exp.9:12:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions three men: Hodijah, Bani, and Beninu. They are Levites, that is, members of the tribe responsible for helping with worship in the temple. Here only their names appear, with no further details.

Nehemiah 10 records a list of those who signed or sealed a covenant with God after the people returned from exile. They committed themselves to keep the law of Moses, to care for the temple, and to support the priests and Levites. The text is not spoken by a character but is a written record. Most likely Nehemiah, or whoever compiled the book, wanted to leave a record of who made this commitment.

For today: God values people who commit themselves to Him, even when no one remembers them. You can serve faithfully in small things and take your promises before God seriously, for He knows your name.
exp.8:29:
This verse says that God was patient with Israel for many years. The first quoted word, "Alargaste," means that God waited and was slow to punish. The second, "Protestásteles," means that he warned them firmly. He did this through his Spirit, speaking by means of the prophets. But the people would not listen, and so God allowed other peoples to rule over them.

This is part of a prayer of confession by the Levites, during a great assembly in the time of Nehemiah. After the return from exile, they review the history of Israel. They acknowledge that the punishment was not unjust, because God had warned them many times. And right after, they highlight his mercy, since he did not destroy them completely.

For today: when you sense a warning from God, whether through his Word or through wise counsel, do not let it pass. His patience is an invitation to return to him, not a sign that it doesn't matter what we do.
exp.6:34:
The explanation says that 320 people from the family of Harim returned to Judea after the exile in Babylon. The phrase "children of" does not refer only to direct sons, but to descendants or members of a clan. It is part of a list of families who went back to their land.

Nehemiah found a record of the first people who returned with Zerubbabel and included it in his book. It was necessary to know who belonged to the people, because Jerusalem was almost empty and needed to be resettled. This list appears almost the same in Ezra 2, and some numbers vary slightly. It is not known with certainty why; there are different explanations, such as the use of records from different periods.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass. Every family and every person counts for Him, even if they are only a number in a list. Today you can serve with confidence in your place, even if no one notices it: God does remember it.
exp.12:23:
Half of the children of those mixed marriages spoke the language of Ashdod, or the speech of other peoples, and no longer knew how to speak the language of the Jews, the tongue of Judah. Ashdod was a Philistine city. The phrase "according to the language of each people" indicates that they used the languages of their foreign mothers.

Nehemiah, governor of Jerusalem, is the one who reports this. He had returned and seen the troubles of the people, and he was concerned that the children were losing the language in which God's law was read and understood. Some scholars see here a risk to the faith and identity of the people; the text gives no further details.

For today: what is taught at home is passed on to the children. Make time to teach them the Bible and to live your faith with them, so that they know it and understand it from an early age.
exp.11:34:
This verse says that among those marching with trumpets were sons of priests. Zechariah is named, and his list of ancestors is given back to Asaph, the famous musician from the time of David. "Son of" here can mean descendant, not always a direct father. The trumpets were metal instruments used to announce and celebrate.

Nehemiah, or whoever wrote his account, tells of the dedication of Jerusalem's wall, now rebuilt. For this, two praise groups were formed that walked on the wall. This verse describes those in one of them. The list of names shows that God remembers each servant and that the people valued their spiritual heritage.

God uses specific people, with name and family, for his work. Serve where he has placed you, even if your task seems small, and give thanks for those who taught you to worship.
exp.12:24:
Nehemiah describes how he confronted some Jews who had married foreign women. He "contended" with them, which means he argued with them sharply, and he "cursed" them, meaning he rebuked them with harsh words, and he "made them swear," meaning he made them promise. He made them promise that they would not marry their children to people from those nations.

Nehemiah, governor of Jerusalem, speaks when he returns and finds that the covenant with God had been neglected. He was concerned that the children no longer knew how to speak the language of Israel, and that with it the knowledge of the law would be lost. His very forceful manner is part of the account, but the Bible does not say that we should imitate it.

For today: take care with what shapes the faith of your family. This is not about looking down on anyone, but about teaching your children the Word consistently and seeking God's guidance in your most important decisions, always treating others with respect and patience.
exp.10:18:
This verse tells us that the gatekeepers of Jerusalem were Akkub, Talmon, and their brothers. They were guards of the city's gates, and their number was one hundred seventy-two. The gatekeepers were the ones assigned to watch over the entrances and look after them. They were Levites with a simple task, but a necessary one.

The book of Nehemiah presents a list of those who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile. The city had been rebuilt, but it had few inhabitants, so one out of every ten families was chosen to live in it. The text is a record, and it is not known with certainty who wrote this particular list. Tradition attributes the book to Nehemiah, though some think he used older documents. The gatekeepers are named to show that service in the city was organized.

God notices those who serve in places that are not very visible. These men did not lead the praise, but they guarded the gates and protected the community. Today we can serve faithfully in quiet tasks in the church or the family, trusting that God values that work.
exp.8:5:
This verse declares that Jehovah is the only God. He made everything: the heaven, the highest parts of creation, the heaven of heavens, all the host of heaven (that is, the heavenly beings and probably the stars too), the earth, and the seas. Preserving means that God gives and sustains the life of everything He has created. Even the heavenly hosts worship Him.

The Levites speak here, leading the people of Israel in a public prayer. After the return from exile and the reading of the law, the people gathered to confess their sins and praise God. They begin by remembering who God is as Creator, and soon move on to His faithfulness to Abraham.

For today: before asking God for anything, take a moment to remember who He is. Looking up at the sky or at nature and thanking Him for sustaining your life can bring you peace and confidence in the middle of your worries.
exp.6:43:
This verse is part of a list of families who returned from exile in Babylon. It says that 148 descendants of Asaph, a family of singers, went back to Jerusalem. The singers were the ones responsible for the music and praise in the temple. In other passages, Asaph is linked to the music of worship, and several psalms bear his name.

Nehemiah, the governor, found this record when he wanted to resettle Jerusalem and arrange the people by families. The list distinguishes priests, Levites, singers and gatekeepers. It is almost identical to the one in Ezra 2, although some figures and details differ, and it is not known for certain why. It was necessary to know who belonged to the service of the temple.

For today: God notices the services that seem small. Here singers are recorded by family, with no personal fame. Serve with your gift, whether singing, helping, or simply being present, even when no one applauds.
exp.6:29:
They are part of a list of families and towns that came back from exile in Babylon. The word "men" here means adult men, and it is used to count the inhabitants of each place.

The book of Nehemiah tells how Jerusalem was rebuilt. Nehemiah, the leader, found an old record of those who had returned first, and he copied it. This list serves to show who made up the restored people and to organize the community according to their origin. Ramah and Geba were neighboring towns in the region of Benjamin.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even the small names. Every person counts in his work. You can serve with confidence wherever you are, even if your labor seems quiet; God sees it and values it.
exp.2:12:
This verse tells how Hanun and the people of Zanoah repaired the Valley Gate. They rebuilt it, hung its doors, and put in its locks and bars (the parts that kept it closed and secure). They also repaired a thousand cubits of wall, about 450 meters, as far as the Dung Gate, which was the entrance through which the city's trash was carried out.

The book is told by Nehemiah, the cupbearer of the Persian king, who returned to Jerusalem to rebuild its walls, which had been broken down for decades. Here he lists the groups who worked, each one on their own section. Zanoah was a town near Jerusalem. Its help shows that the work belonged to many people.

God uses both people with important positions and ordinary people, and every task matters. Ask yourself what your section is today: in your family, your church, or your work. Do it faithfully, even when no one notices, or even when it seems as humble as repairing the gate for the trash.
exp.2:20:
Meremoth, son of Urijah and grandson of Koz, repaired another section of the wall of Jerusalem. His portion ran from the entrance of Eliashib's house to the far end of that same house.

The narrator of the book, who most likely follows the memoirs of Nehemiah, records in detail who rebuilt each section of the wall. Eliashib was the high priest, and his house served as a point of reference. Meremoth appears again in verse 4, so he worked on more than one section. This shows that the whole people took part in the work.

For today: God values faithful work that seems small or little noticed. Do steadily the part that is yours, without comparing yourself to others, and trust that it adds to something greater.
exp.8:10:
It says that God divided the Red Sea (the "sea" and the "Red Sea" are the same sea) so that his people crossed on dry ground, that is, on solid land. Then the Egyptians who were chasing them sank into the depths, like a stone falling into huge waters.

It is part of a prayer of confession by the Levites in the time of Nehemiah. The people had returned from exile and gathered to hear the Law and acknowledge their sins. To do this, they recall their history: God was faithful from Egypt onward, and they were often not faithful.

For today: when you feel trapped, remember how God has helped you before. Remembering his faithfulness can give you confidence to pray and keep going, even if you cannot yet see how the path will turn out.
exp.12:15:
It says that some merchants from Tyre were living in Jerusalem, a coastal city outside Judah. They brought fish and all kinds of goods, and they sold them on the sabbath to the people of Judah. The word "ware" means goods for sale, and "sold on the sabbath" means that they did business on the day of rest.

Nehemiah, governor of Jerusalem, speaks and tells what he saw when he returned to the city. God's law called for rest on the sabbath, and the people had become used to working and buying on that day. Nehemiah sees this as a serious offense, and that is why he later rebukes the leaders.

For today: ask yourself what things, even if they seem normal, are taking away from God the time of rest and worship. You can set aside a fixed moment each week to rest, pray, and be with your family or your church.
exp.4:11:
The explanation says that the nobles and rulers agreed to return what they had taken from the poor and to stop charging them. Nehemiah was not satisfied with the promise alone: he called the priests and had them swear an oath in front of everyone. "Then I called the priests, and took an oath of them" is the phrase in the verse, so the words about the oath are simply the verse's own wording.

Nehemiah was governing Jerusalem while the wall was being rebuilt. Many poor Israelites, because of hunger and debts, had lost their lands, their houses, and even their sons and daughters into servitude, at the hands of their own brothers. Nehemiah was outraged and asked them to correct that injustice, setting the example himself.

For today: if someone has placed their trust in us or owes us something, let us deal with justice and mercy. And when we promise to correct a wrong, let us put that promise into action and be accountable, as this people did before God.
exp.6:51:
This verse is part of a list of families. It names the descendants of Besai, of Meunim, and of Nephishesim. These are names of groups that returned from exile. The phrase "the children of" indicates family or lineage, not always direct children.

About the exact origin of these names, scholars are not certain. Some think Meunim and Nephishesim may come from foreign peoples, but that is a possibility, not a settled fact.

Nehemiah, who writes much of the book, found a record of the families who returned to Judah from Babylon. He includes it to rebuild the community after the wall of Jerusalem was raised. The list shows order and memory: each group mattered and had its place among God's people.

For today: God knows people by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. Today you can value and thank those who serve quietly, and remember that your hidden work also counts before God.
exp.2:7:
It says that Uzziel, a goldsmith, repaired a section of the wall of Jerusalem, and beside him worked Hananiah, the son of one of the apothecaries. "Repaired" means they restored what had been damaged. An apothecary was someone who prepared perfumes and ointments. The phrase "unto the broad wall" points to a stretch reaching a thicker section of the wall, though it is not known exactly where that was.

The account is told by Nehemiah, who returned to Jerusalem to rebuild its ruined walls. Chapter 3 lists who repaired each section. Priests, rulers, and ordinary people take part. Here we find craftsmen who were not builders by trade, but goldsmiths and perfumers, who set aside their usual work to help.

For today: God uses ordinary people with different occupations. You do not need to be an expert or famous to serve; it is enough to offer what you have and work alongside others in the part that is yours.
exp.8:13:
It says that God made known to Israel his holy sabbath, the day of rest set apart for Him. He also gave them commandments, statutes, and laws through Moses, his servant.

It is part of a long prayer of confession that the Levites offer before the people, after the return from exile, in the time of Nehemiah. They review Israel's history: how God guided them, spoke to them at Sinai, and gave them his law. They do this to remember God's goodness and to acknowledge that the people often disobeyed him.

For today: God gives us his commandments as a gift, not as a burden. You might set aside a time each week to rest, pray, and thank him, trusting that he cares for your life.
exp.9:33:
It says that all the people, priests, Levites, and ordinary folk, cast lots to decide which families would bring the wood to the temple and on what dates. "Cast lots" was like a drawing to share the duty fairly. That wood kept the fire burning on the altar. Everything was done "as it is written in the law."

The people of Israel are speaking here, after returning from exile in Babylon. Under the leadership of Nehemiah, they made a signed commitment to obey God and to support worship in the temple. The Bible does not detail here how the drawing was done, only that each father's house had its turn.

For today: God's work moves forward when everyone takes part, not just a few. Ask yourself what simple task, even if it seems small, you could take on faithfully in your church or community.
exp.11:43:
On the day of the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, men were appointed to be in charge of the storerooms of the temple. There the offerings were kept, the firstfruits (the first of the harvest) and the tithes (the tenth part). They were to gather from the fields of the cities the portion that the Law assigned to the priests and Levites. There was great joy in Judah because of them, because they served in the temple.

This is part of Nehemiah's account of the celebration after the wall was rebuilt. The narrator tells how the people, full of joy, arranged for the support of those who served in worship. This followed what the Law of Moses required.

For today: giving with order and joy helps sustain the service of God. We can support those who minister, with generosity and gratitude, not out of cold obligation.
exp.2:3:
This verse says that several men rebuilt a section of the wall of Jerusalem, one beside the other. Meremoth, son of Uriah, worked on one stretch. Then, next to him, Meshullam, son of Berechiah, did his part. Next came Zadok, son of Baanah.

This is part of a list in the book of Nehemiah, which tells how the people rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem after returning from exile. The narrator records the names of those who took part. The city was exposed and in ruins, and Nehemiah encouraged everyone to work together. Nehemiah 3 remembers that each person had an assigned section.

For today: God values steady work, even when it is simple and almost no one notices it. Faithfully do the part that belongs to you, in your family, your church, or your job, and trust that God joins everything together with the work of others.
exp.12:3:
This verse says that Eliashib, a priest in charge of the storerooms of the temple, had become related by marriage to Tobiah. The word "oversight" means that he was in charge, and "chamber" means a room or storeroom. "Allied" means that he was joined to him through family ties, perhaps by marriage, although the text gives no further details.

Nehemiah speaks, recounting what happened while he was away from Jerusalem. Tobiah had been an opponent of Nehemiah, and he claimed a place set apart for God. The reading of the law had just reminded the people that they must separate themselves from whatever drew them away from God. Even so, Eliashib let Tobiah in and prepared a room for him in the temple.

For today: those who hold responsibility over the things of God must take care with whom they form alliances. Closeness without care can open the door to what harms faith. Let us ask for wisdom and firmness.
exp.4:3:
This verse presents the complaint of a third group of poor Jews. They say they borrowed money to pay the tax demanded by the king of Persia, and that to do so they put up their fields and vineyards as security. "Tribute" means tax.

The ones speaking are Jewish families who had returned from exile and were living in Jerusalem during the rebuilding of the walls. There was famine, and on top of that the taxes were heavy. Their wealthier brothers lent to them, but they ended up losing their fields and even their sons as servants. That is why they cried out, and Nehemiah became angry when he heard them.

For today: if you have more resources, do not take advantage of the need of others. Help generously, without abusing, and treat with justice anyone who is in hardship, because they are your brother or your sister.
exp.8:25:
The explanation says that the people of Israel, after receiving so much good, turned against God. "They provoked you" means they offended him. "Cast your law behind their backs" means they stopped paying attention to his teaching. They even killed the prophets, who warned them to turn back to God. "Great provocations" refers to actions that were very serious and abhorrent in God's eyes.

Here the Levites speak in a public prayer of confession, in the time of Nehemiah, when the people had returned from exile. They review the history of Israel: God was faithful and generous, and they failed again and again. They acknowledge their sin and also God's patience, who listened when they cried out.

For today: when everything is going well for us, it is easy to forget God. Let us remember his kindnesses, give him thanks, and listen to his Word with humility, especially when someone corrects us with love.
exp.8:32:
This verse says that God is just in everything that has happened to the Israelites. He acted with righteousness and faithfulness, while they were the ones who did wrong.

It is part of a long prayer of confession spoken by the Levites in Jerusalem, when the people gathered with fasting and mourning clothes after rebuilding the wall. They review the history of Israel and acknowledge that their sufferings, such as being ruled by foreign kingdoms, were not due to any injustice on God's part. They and their ancestors did not obey the law, despite the many blessings they had received.

For today: when we face the consequences of our mistakes, we can avoid blaming God or others and humbly recognize our own part. That honesty brings us closer to his mercy, because he is merciful and forgives.
exp.5:17:
The verse says that many in Judah were bound by oath to him, because he was the son-in-law of Shechaniah the son of Arah; and his son Johanan had married the daughter of Meshullam the son of Berechiah. So they were tied to him by family connections.

The one speaking is Nehemiah, the leader who was directing the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem. Tobiah was one of his opponents. Although the enemies recognized that the work came from God, there were influential people among the people who kept up correspondence with Tobiah. Nehemiah tells this to show that the pressure did not come only from outside, but also from within.

For today: take care that your loyalties and friendships do not pull you away from what God has entrusted to you. Love your family and your friends, but do not let their influence dull your obedience.
exp.12:19:
The explanation says that the merchants and sellers of all kinds of goods, unable to enter Jerusalem on the Sabbath, stayed outside the city, camping beside the wall, once and then again. "Merchants" are the traders, and "goods" are what is bought and sold.

Nehemiah, the governor of Jerusalem, speaks here. He returned to the city and found that people were trading on the Sabbath. He remembered that Israel had suffered exile for disobeying God, so he ordered the gates shut at dusk on Friday and posted guards. He wanted to protect the day of rest that God had given his people.

For today: God invites us to set limits on our work and our earnings so that we keep time to rest and worship him. We can ask ourselves which gates we need to close so that worry does not take over everything.
exp.9:37:
This verse says that a priest, a descendant of Aaron, would be present with the Levites when they received the tithe (the tenth part of the harvests) from the people. Then the Levites would in turn bring a tenth of what they received, "the tithe of the tithes," to the house of God, to the chambers or storerooms of the treasure house, which were rooms for keeping supplies.

The Israelites who had returned from exile speak here. Under the leadership of Nehemiah, they signed a commitment to obey God's law. They wanted the temple to have what it needed and those who served there to be supported. The presence of the priest brought order and oversight to the process.

For today: God values order and honesty in how we handle what is given for his work. If you support your church, give generously and trust that it will be managed with transparency. If you manage resources belonging to others, do so with integrity.
exp.11:28:
This verse continues the list of places from which the Levite singers came for the dedication of the wall. It names the house of Gilgal, and the fields of Geba and Azmaveth. The reason it gives is that the singers had built themselves villages, that is, they had built their own small towns, around Jerusalem.

Nehemiah tells the story himself, in the first person. The wall was already finished, and a great festival of thanksgiving with music was being prepared. That is why they gathered the singers from all the surrounding areas. It is not known with certainty where each place mentioned was located, but all of them were near the city.

For today: God values those who serve with their gifts, and praise must be prepared for. These singers lived nearby so that they would be available. We can ask ourselves how to organize our lives to serve God and the church with steadiness and joy.
exp.4:9:
Nehemiah says that he, his relatives, and his helpers had also lent money and grain to the people. Now he proposes to stop collecting that burden.

Nehemiah is speaking as governor of Judah. The people were going hungry and had fallen into debt; some had even handed over their lands and their children as security. Wealthy Jews took advantage of that need. Nehemiah does not place himself above them: he includes himself among those who lent, and he sets the example before asking others to change.

For today: if we have more resources, we should not take advantage of someone who is in a tight spot. We can ease a debt, be patient with a payment, or help without exploiting the situation. And whoever wants to correct others should begin with their own conduct.
exp.2:10:
Verse 11 says that two men, Malchijah son of Harim and Hashub son of Pahath-moab, repaired another section of the wall, and also the tower of the furnaces. That tower was probably named for being near the place where bread was baked or where furnaces were worked; this is not known for certain.

Nehemiah tells how the wall of Jerusalem was repaired after the exile. Here it is not God who speaks, but the narrator, who carefully records the names of each family and place. He wants it remembered who took part in the work, whether their share was large or small.

For today: God values the faithful work of every person. Do with joy the part that falls to you, even when no one sees it, because in his work every one of us is needed, and he does not forget anyone.
exp.4:2:
Here some of the people describe their situation: to have food during a time of famine, they handed over their lands, their vineyards, and their houses as security. "Mortgaged" means to leave something of your own as a pledge in exchange for a loan, with the risk of losing it if the debt is not paid.

They speak as poor Jews who had returned to Jerusalem and were working to rebuild the wall. There is famine, debt, and taxes owed to the king. They complain that their own Jewish brothers, who were richer, lent them money and grain taking advantage of their need, until they ended up with their property. Nehemiah is angered by this injustice.

For today: if someone around you is in need, do not see their crisis as an opportunity to gain. Ask yourself how you can help them with generosity and justice, especially if they are part of your family or your church.
exp.8:31:
This verse is part of a prayer of confession. The people address God with reverence, acknowledging him as great, mighty, and "terrible," which here means that he inspires a reverent awe. God keeps his covenant and his mercy. They ask him not to consider the suffering they have lived through as small: to take it fully into account before him. That hardship reached everyone, from the kings down to the common people, from the time of the kings of Assyria until today.

The Levites speak together with the people of Israel, now returned from exile, in the days of Nehemiah. They have gathered to read the law, fast, and confess their sins. They recall their history: God warned them through the prophets, they did not listen, yet God did not abandon them completely.

For today: we can pray with sincerity, bringing our pain before God without hiding it, while also acknowledging our own part. God is just and also merciful.
exp.11:46:
It says that all Israel, both in the days of Zerubbabel and in the days of Nehemiah, gave each day what was needed for the support of the singers and the gatekeepers of the temple. The "portions" were the daily shares of food and provision. "Set apart" means they set that part aside for God. The people set aside their share for the Levites, and the Levites in turn set aside a part for the priests, the sons of Aaron.

The text is from the narrator, who closes the account of the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem. He looks back to two different periods to show that the people steadily supported the service of the temple. He also recalls the order that David and Solomon had established. The reason is that the praise and worship could continue without interruption.

For today: service to God needs steady support. We can think about how to sustain, with generosity and regularity, those who serve in our church, and also give in our own way.
exp.4:1:
This verse shows a group of poor families explaining their problem. They say they have many sons and daughters, and that because of this they needed to "take up corn," that is, to get wheat or barley, so that they could eat and stay alive. The word "taken" here means receiving grain on credit, or as a loan.

The speakers are the common people of Judah, during the rebuilding of Jerusalem. There was famine, and they also had to pay taxes to the king of Persia. Some of the wealthier Jews would lend to them, but apparently at the cost of their lands and houses. That is why the outcry was against their own brothers.

For today: when someone around you is in need, do not look only at your own comfort. Help with generosity and justice, without taking advantage of their distress. Listening attentively to the cry of the needy is already a good first step.
exp.9:10:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions three Levites: Micha, Rehob and Hashabiah. These were men who, together with their brothers, signed a commitment before God. The names appear in the older style of spelling, so they look different from how we read them today.

The book of Nehemiah tells how the people of Israel returned from exile and rebuilt Jerusalem. In this chapter, leaders, priests and Levites put their seal on a written covenant to obey the law of God. The narrator records their names so that there is a lasting record. The Levites served in worship and taught the law to the people.

God looks at specific people, not only at crowds. These men hardly appear in other stories, but their names were written down because of their commitment. Today we too can serve faithfully in small things, without seeking applause, trusting that God sees and remembers every act of obedience.
exp.8:4:
Here the Levites call the people to stand up and praise God. To "bless" means to speak well of God and give him thanks. The phrase "from age to age" means "forever," from eternity to eternity. They say that his name is so great that no human praise can reach it.

This happens after the people heard the law, confessed their sins, and worshiped. The Levites, who guided the people in spiritual matters, now lead a prayer aloud. The names are repeated in a somewhat different way in verses 4 and 5, and we do not know the reason for certain. What we can see is that the prayer begins with praise.

For today: before asking or confessing, begin your prayer by remembering who God is. Take a moment to praise him, even if your words feel few.
exp.3:13:
Nehemiah looks at the situation, stands up, and encourages the leaders, the officials, and all the people. He tells them not to be afraid of their enemies, to remember that the Lord is great and worthy of respect ("terrible" here means that he inspires reverence), and to fight for their families: their brothers, sons, daughters, wives, and homes.

Nehemiah, who was leading the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem, is speaking. The enemies of the Jews threatened to attack, and many were tired and afraid. Nehemiah placed the people by families, armed, behind the wall. Afterward, God frustrated the enemies' plan, and the work continued with half working while the other half stood guard.

For today: when fear paralyzes you, remember who God is and think of the people you love. Pray, and then take the responsible step that is yours to take, without abandoning your task.
exp.5:5:
This verse is part of the letter that Sanballat sent to Nehemiah. It says that a rumor is going around among the neighboring nations, and that Gashmu also claims it, that Nehemiah and the Jews plan to rebel against the king of Persia. According to the letter, that is why they are rebuilding the wall, and Nehemiah himself wants to make himself king.

Sanballat and his allies had already tried four times to trick Nehemiah into leaving Jerusalem. Now they use an open letter, which anyone could read, to spread fear and pressure. It was a very serious political accusation, and Nehemiah rejects it as their invention.

For today: when someone slanders you or tries to frighten you into stopping what God has entrusted to you, do not stay in fear or in endless argument. Respond with calm and truth, pray, and keep working.
exp.8:33:
This verse says that the leaders and ancestors of Israel did not obey God's law. Kings, princes, priests and fathers did not put it into practice, meaning they did not live by it. They also did not pay heed to his commandments or to his warnings, the reminders through which God spoke to them with insistence in order to correct them.

The people of Israel speak in a prayer of confession, after returning from exile, in the time of Nehemiah. They acknowledge that God was right to discipline them. They do not blame God, but admit the sin of the whole nation, from the leaders down to the common people.

For today: honesty before God is the first step toward returning to him. Instead of justifying ourselves or blaming others, we can recognize where we have failed and ask him for his mercy.
exp.2:14:
It says that Shallun, a leader from the region of Mizpah, repaired the Fountain Gate. He rebuilt it, put a roof of beams over it, and set in place its doors, locks, and bars. He also repaired the wall of the Pool of Siloam (Shelah), beside the king's garden, all the way to the stairs that go down from the City of David.

The narrator is Nehemiah, who tells how the wall of Jerusalem was repaired after the exile. Each group or leader received a section to work on. In this way the city was rebuilt, with many people taking part, so that the people could live safely and worship God.

God values faithful work, even when it is hardly seen. Shallun appears in a list, but his effort was necessary. Today you can serve in your family, your church, or your work with steadiness, trusting that God sees every task done with care.
exp.7:7:
The explanation says that the Levites read the book of God's law aloud, clearly, and explained its meaning so that everyone could understand what they were hearing. "Gave the sense" means giving the explanation or meaning of the text. Some scholars think this also included translating or clarifying the ancient Hebrew, although this is debated.

The people of Israel had returned from exile and rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem. They gathered in a public square and asked Ezra, the scribe, to read the law of Moses. The Levites helped him, teaching the people in groups, while the people listened attentively and responded with reverence.

Reading the Bible is not enough; we must understand it. Today we can look for a good explanation, study in a group, or ask someone with experience, so that the Word reaches the heart and transforms our lives.
exp.6:24:
This verse says that 95 descendants of Gibeon returned from exile in Babylon. "Children of" means descendants or relatives, not only direct sons. In the list in Ezra 2:20 the same number appears with the name "Gibbar," so some think it is another form of the name; this is not entirely certain.

Nehemiah, governor of Jerusalem, found a record of the families who had returned with Zerubbabel years earlier. He copies it here to organize the population of a city that was only beginning to be rebuilt. Gibeon was a nearby town, and its people had served in temple duties since the days of Joshua. Each number shows that someone returned to help rebuild.

For today: God does not overlook small people or quiet work. Even if no one mentions you, your faithfulness counts. Serve where you are, with steadiness and gratitude.
exp.10:8:
Joel, son of Zichri, had charge over the men of the tribe of Benjamin who settled in Jerusalem. "Prefect" means leader or person in charge. Judah, son of Senuah, is described as "second over the city," meaning a second in command, serving as an assistant or lesser administrator. The text does not make clear exactly what authority each one held.

The book of Nehemiah tells how Jerusalem was rebuilt. Once the walls were finished, there were few inhabitants, so lots were cast so that one family in ten would live inside the city. The narrator carefully lists those who accepted that commitment, along with their leaders and their numbers, so that their names would not be forgotten.

For today: God sees and values the service of those who work in positions of responsibility, whether great or small. Serve where you are asked, faithfully, without worrying about who is first or second.
exp.8:14:
It says that God gave Israel bread from heaven when they were hungry, and brought water out of the rock when they were thirsty. Furthermore, He told them to go in and take the land that He had promised with a raised hand, that is to say, with a solemn oath. The sentence that speaks of God giving them bread and bringing forth water is rendered in the verse you are reading as "gavest them bread from heaven" and "broughtest forth water."

It is part of a prayer of confession by the Levites, in the time of Nehemiah, when the people gathered after rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem. They recall the story: God cared for their ancestors in the wilderness, even though they rebelled. The bread is the manna, and the water from the rock recalls what happened in the desert.

For today: when you doubt that God will sustain you, remember how He has cared for you before. Giving thanks for what God has already done strengthens trust and helps us obey Him with humility.
exp.8:30:
This verse says that although the people of Israel rebelled again and again, God did not finish them off or fully abandon them. The reason is his great mercy. The verse uses the idea of destroying completely, and it describes him as someone who forgives and treats people with kindness.

It is part of a long prayer of confession that the Levites make before the people, in the time of Nehemiah, after the return from exile. They review the history of Israel: God rescued them and spoke to them through the prophets, but they became stubborn and refused to listen, as the text describes them stiffening their necks. Even so, God was patient.

For today: when you fail, do not hide from God or think that there is no hope left. Come back with sincerity, admit your mistake, and trust that his mercy is greater than your stubbornness.
exp.9:19:
This verse is part of a list of names. These are three leaders of the people: Magpiash, Meshullam, and Hezir. They are mentioned among those who put their seal to, or signed, a covenant. Their names appear without further explanation, and the exact meanings of the names are not the point of the text.

The book is told by Nehemiah, along with the details of his time. After the wall of Jerusalem was rebuilt, the people made a written commitment to obey the law of God. Leaders, Levites, and priests signed first. The names were recorded so that it would be known who had committed themselves. Nothing more is said about these three men in this passage.

God values specific people, not only crowds. These men were written down for having stood up and made a commitment. Today we can do the same: take on clearly a commitment to obey God in something specific, such as honesty, prayer, or service, and let others know about it so they can encourage us.
exp.9:2:
These verse names three men: Pashur, Amariah, and Malchijah. They are part of the list of those who signed, that is, put their seal, on a covenant. Nehemiah, the governor, is the one referred to here.

After the wall of Jerusalem was rebuilt, the people of Israel gathered, confessed their sins, and decided to commit themselves to God. This list appears in the account in the book of Nehemiah, and the names in this group seem to belong to priests or heads of priestly families. The names recur in other lists, and we do not know with certainty any further details about each person.

God values people who commit themselves to Him, even when we know only their names. Today we too can take concrete steps of obedience, without seeking applause. A simple and faithful commitment, such as attending church, praying, or serving others, has value before God.
exp.4:13:
Nehemiah says that for twelve years, from the twentieth year to the thirty-second year of King Artaxerxes, he served as governor of Judah. During all that time, neither he nor his brothers (his relatives and co-workers) ate the governor's food allowance, that is, the food and taxes that the people would normally have been expected to give their ruler.

Nehemiah speaks as the governor appointed by the Persian king. He has just corrected the wealthy who were taking advantage of the poor through unjust debts and loans. To show that he was not asking of others what he himself did not do, he recalls that he never burdened the people with the costs of his table, unlike the governors before him.

For today: whoever holds authority should set a good example. If we are given the task of leading at work, in the church, or at home, we can ask ourselves whether we are serving or being served, and live with generosity and reverence toward God.
exp.8:1:
This verse tells that the people of Israel separated themselves from all foreigners. Then, standing, they acknowledged their sins and the wrongs of their ancestors. "Seed" means descendants, and "iniquities" are the wicked deeds or serious offenses.

The account is narrated by the author of the book, without a specific speaker. The people had just celebrated the Feast of Tabernacles and now gather in fasting, wearing mourning clothes and with dirt upon them, a sign of grief and humility. This separation probably refers to turning away from the practices and alliances that were leading them away from God, according to many interpreters. Others see it as a stricter ethnic separation. Even so, the heart of the passage is repentance.

For today: it is not enough to feel guilt in silence. God invites us to confess our failures honestly and also to recognize the harmful patterns we inherited, so that we can change direction with his help.
exp.10:23:
It says that a man named Pethahiah, a descendant of Zerah, son of Judah, served as an advisor or representative of the king in all matters that concerned the people. Being at the king's side means that he was close to him, as a trusted helper. "Matters" means affairs or business.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the account that presents the list of those who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile. Leaders of the Levites, singers, and other officials are named. This Pethahiah probably served as a link with Persian authority, although the text gives no further detail. That is why his task seems to have been important for the order of the community.

God uses both those who sing and serve in the temple and those who work in administrative affairs. If you have a practical task today, such as organizing, advising, or handling paperwork, do it faithfully, for it is also service to God and to others.
exp.4:10:
Nehemiah asks the wealthy among the people to return to the poor, this very day, what they had taken from them: their fields, vineyards, olive groves, and houses. They are also to return "the hundredth part," which was probably the monthly interest (one percent) they charged on the money, grain, wine, and oil they had lent. Some understand that phrase in other ways, but the idea is clear: stop charging abusive interest.

Nehemiah, the governor of Jerusalem, is the one speaking. Many poor Israelites, in the midst of a famine, had mortgaged their lands and even given their sons and daughters into servitude to pay their debts. Their own brothers in faith were taking advantage of them, and this offended God and harmed the witness before the neighboring nations.

For today: check whether in your work, your business, or your lending you are taking advantage of someone in need, and correct it with generosity and justice, as Nehemiah did.
exp.6:25:
It says that 188 men of Bethlehem and Netophah returned from the exile in Babylon. The word "men" here means men, and it refers to families who came back to settle in those two nearby villages of Judah.

Nehemiah speaks as both narrator and leader. After rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem, he found a record of the first people who returned from exile and copied it. He wanted to reorganize the people according to their families and their cities. In Ezra 2 there is a similar list, but with slightly different numbers. It is not known for certain why, and several explanations are offered.

For today: God knows and remembers each person, even when a name seems to be only a number in a list. You can trust that your life and your simple service matter to him. Also value those who work quietly in your church or family.
exp.1:12:
Nehemiah goes out by night through the Valley Gate and makes his way along the south side of Jerusalem, passing toward the Dragon's Well and the Dung Gate, where the city's refuse was thrown out. He looks carefully at the fallen walls and the burned gates. The word "viewed" means that he examined the scene closely and with attention. The exact location of the Dragon's Well is unknown.

Nehemiah speaks in the first person. He was cupbearer to the king of Persia, and he came to Jerusalem to rebuild its walls. He surveys the city in secret and at night, with only a few men, because he had not yet told anyone the plan that God had placed in his heart. He first wanted to see the reality with his own eyes.

Before you act, take time to look honestly at the real situation. Pray, observe, and gather information, without rushing or exaggerating, so that your decisions will be wiser and firmer.
exp.10:2:
This verse opens a list of the people who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile. The word "province" refers to Judah, which was part of the Persian empire. The sentence "they dwelt" means they lived, and the "possession" is the inherited land. The "Nethinims" were helpers at the temple, and the "children of Solomon's servants" were descendants of workers from his time. The text says that some stayed in Jerusalem and others remained in their own cities.

The narrator is the writer of the book of Nehemiah, who records the resettling of Jerusalem. The walls had already been rebuilt, but the city had few inhabitants. For that reason the leaders stayed there, and the rest cast lots so that one family in ten would move there.

For today: God values those who serve where help is needed, even when it costs them. Think about where you can offer yourself willingly in your church or community, knowing that God sees and remembers every act of service.
exp.5:12:
This verse says that Shemaiah was paid to frighten Nehemiah. They wanted Nehemiah, out of fear, to do something contrary to the will of God, that is, to sin. That way they would have a reason to speak badly of him and damage his reputation. A word that appears in the verse, "hired," means paid in secret to act in a certain way. "Reproach" means to be shamed publicly.

Nehemiah leads the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem. His enemies, Tobiah and Sanballat, try to stop him with threats and deception. They hire a false prophet who advises him to hide in the temple. Entering the temple was permitted only to the priests, so doing so would have been disobedience. He recognizes that this message did not come from God.

Today, not every piece of advice that sounds spiritual comes from God. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and do not act out of fear. Keep your integrity even when you are pressured.
exp.11:6:
This verse ends a list of names. It mentions Sallu, Amok, Hilkiah, and Jedaiah, and says that they were the chief of the priests, that is, the heads or leaders of the priestly families. Along with their brothers, or fellow members of their lineage, they served in the days of Jeshua, the high priest who returned from exile in Babylon.

Nehemiah 12 is a record of the priests and Levites who returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. The text presents not a speech but a narrative with lists. Its purpose is to preserve the memory of those who sustained the worship of God when the people were rebuilt. Some details of these lists are difficult to reconstruct, and scholars explain them in various ways.

God knows and remembers those who serve, even when almost no one notices them. Today you can serve faithfully in simple things, without seeking applause. What you do for the Lord has value.
exp.12:29:
He says that Nehemiah cleansed the people of every foreign influence and organized the priests and Levites again, each one in his own service group, so that each would do his assigned task. The sentence that explains the wording of the verse has been removed, since it refers to words that do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Nehemiah speaks at the end of his book. He had returned to Jerusalem and found that some had mixed the life of the temple with interests foreign to the faith, such as a grandson of the high priest who had married the daughter of Sanballat, an enemy of the people. His cleansing seeks to protect faithfulness to God's covenant, not to despise people. Some scholars stress the spiritual danger; others remind us that the Bible also shows welcome to foreigners who believe, such as Ruth.

Today: examine which influences weaken your faithfulness to God, and serve with order and constancy in the task He has given you.
exp.6:21:
This verse is part of a list. It says that the descendants of the family of Hashum, who returned from exile, numbered three hundred twenty and eight. "The children of" does not refer only to direct sons, but to the members of a family or clan. In Ezra 2:19 a similar list appears, with figures somewhat different for other names; scholars explain this in several ways, and it is not certain what the exact reason is.

Nehemiah, the governor of Jerusalem, found a record of the families who had come back from Babylon. He includes it to put the people in order, to repopulate the city, and to show that God had kept his promise to bring his people back.

Today it reminds us that God knows people one by one, including those whom almost no one mentions. Your service may go unnoticed by others, but not by him. Serve faithfully, without seeking applause.
exp.11:4:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions Miamin, Maadiah, and Bilgah, who were heads of priestly families. The word "princes" in the next verse means the "heads" or "leaders" of each priestly group.

The author, traditionally Nehemiah, records the priests who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. This list keeps a record of who served in the temple and maintained the worship of God. Some names are spelled a little differently in other lists, and it is not always possible to know for certain why.

For today: God does not forget those who serve him, even when their names seem unimportant. Your faithful service, even the quiet kind that receives no applause, has value before him. Today you can do a simple task with care in your church or family, knowing that God sees it.
exp.1:8:
Nehemiah reports that he came to the governors on the other side of the river Euphrates, that is, the Persian authorities of that region. He gave them the letters of King Artaxerxes, which granted him permission to pass through without trouble. In addition, the king sent him with a military escort: captains of the army and horsemen (men on horseback). The phrase "let them pass freely" means that they should let him go through without hindrance.

Nehemiah speaks in the first person. He was the king's cupbearer, and he wanted to go to Jerusalem to rebuild its walls. Earlier he had prayed, and he himself acknowledges that the king granted him everything because the good hand of God was upon him. Soon opponents such as Sanballat and Tobiah would appear.

For today: Nehemiah prayed and also acted with order, asking for letters and permissions. We can trust God and, at the same time, responsibly do what is ours to do, thanking him for his help in the details.
exp.10:30:
The text says that the descendants of Benjamin lived in several towns north of Jerusalem: Geba, Michmash, Aija, Beth-el, and the nearby villages. The "villages" are the small settlements around a main town. "Lived" means they settled there to dwell.

The book of Nehemiah presents a list of where the people lived after returning from exile in Babylon. The narrator is Nehemiah, or a writer who gathered his records. Jerusalem had been rebuilt and needed inhabitants, so some lived in the city and others in towns of Judah and Benjamin. The list shows that each tribe recovered its territory.

For today: God pays attention to places and people who seem small. Each has their place and their contribution. Serve faithfully where God has put you, without comparing yourself to others, because your work also counts in his work.
exp.3:20:
This verse tells that the people kept building the wall of Jerusalem, while half of the men stood guard with spears. They worked from the rising of the morning until the stars appeared, that is, from sunrise to nightfall.

The speaker is Nehemiah, the leader who was directing the rebuilding of the wall. The enemies of the Jews threatened them and wanted to stop the work. For this reason Nehemiah organized the people to work and to defend themselves at the same time, trusting that God would fight for them.

For today: faith and effort go together. We can trust God and, at the same time, be responsible, steady, and careful in what He has entrusted to us, without neglecting either the work or prayer.
exp.8:26:
Therefore, the explanation says, God allowed Israel's enemies to oppress them because of their disobedience. But when, in the midst of their suffering, they cried out to God, he heard them from heaven. Out of his great compassion, he would send them deliverers, that is, rescuers who saved them from their oppressors.

This is part of a long prayer of confession in Nehemiah 9. The Levites lead it before the people, who had now returned from exile, and they retell the history of Israel. They recall a repeated pattern: blessing, rebellion, punishment, crying out, and rescue. They do this to acknowledge their own failures and the faithfulness of God.

For today: when you go through difficulties because of your own mistakes, do not hesitate to return to God. He remains merciful and listens to a sincere cry. And in the good days, do not forget to thank him.
exp.6:19:
This verse mentions the descendants of Adin, a family or clan, and says there were 655 of them. "Children of" does not mean only direct sons and daughters, but the whole family that came from one ancestor.

The speaker is Nehemiah. After rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem, he found a record of the families who had returned from exile in Babylon and copied it. He wanted to repopulate the city and organize the people by their families. In Ezra 2:15, Adin appears with 454 people. The difference can be explained in several ways, such as a different moment of counting or changes made while copying, but it is not known for certain.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass. Every family and every person counts for Him. Today you can value those who serve quietly in your church or community, and remember that your name is also important to God.
exp.2:31:
The explanation says that the last part of the wall of Jerusalem, between the corner room and the Sheep Gate, was repaired by the goldsmiths and the merchants. The word "merchants" here means people who bought and sold goods. The goldsmiths were craftsmen who worked with gold.

Nehemiah 3 is an account of who rebuilt each section of the wall after the exile. Nehemiah narrates the work, and this verse closes the list. The Sheep Gate was the point where the chapter began, so the circle is complete. People of ordinary trades are mentioned here, not only priests or leaders.

God uses people with everyday jobs for his work. Your trade, whatever it is, can serve to build up something good in your church and community. Ask yourself which section you can help repair.
exp.7:15:
What it says: After hearing the law, the people went out to gather branches and built booths. They put them up in different places: on the roofs of their houses (the flat roofs of the homes), in their courtyards, in the courtyards of the temple, and in two squares of Jerusalem, near the Water Gate and the Gate of Ephraim.

Context: Ezra was reading the law to the people who had returned from exile. There they discovered God's command about the Feast of Booths, which remembered how Israel lived in booths after leaving Egypt. The account says that for a long time they had not celebrated it this way, and there was great joy.

For today: When you read the Bible, do not stop at understanding; take a concrete step of obedience. Ask yourself what God is asking of you today and do it with joy, even if it is simple, and it is better if you do it together with other believers.
exp.0:6:
Nehemiah says that the people behaved very badly before God. The word "corrupted" is not the source word here, so the comment on it is removed. They did not keep the commandments that God gave through Moses. The commandments, statutes, and judgments are his laws, his rules, and his just decisions. To "transgress" or "break faith" means failing on purpose in what must be kept.

Nehemiah speaks as the cupbearer to the king of Persia, who is far from Jerusalem. He learns that the city is in ruins and the people are in trouble. Before doing anything, he prays and confesses the sins, including his own and those of his family. Then he reminds God of his promise to gather together those who return to Him.

For today: when something is going wrong, begin with a sincere prayer. Acknowledge your failings without excuses, and trust that God receives with mercy anyone who turns back to Him.
exp.5:11:
Nehemiah reports that he came to recognize something: Shemaiah claimed to speak on behalf of God, but in reality God had not sent him. That "prophecy" was directed against Nehemiah, because Tobiah and Sanballat had paid him. Being "hired for wages" means he had been engaged with money.

Nehemiah, who leads the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls, is the one speaking. His enemies wanted to frighten him into hiding in the temple. Going in there was not his place, and it would have been a sin. In doing so he would have lost the respect of the people and abandoned the work.

For today: not every message that sounds spiritual comes from God. Test it against the Bible, ask for wisdom, and notice whether it pushes you toward fear or toward disobedience.
exp.6:50:
This verse is part of a list of families called "netineos," that is, people dedicated to service in the temple. Three groups are named here: the descendants of Gazzam, of Uzza, and of Phaseah. Older spellings vary in other versions (Gazam, Uza, Paseah). Nothing more is said about them.

The book of Nehemiah presents a record of those who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem. Nehemiah found it and copied it to organize the people while the city was being rebuilt. The temple servants helped the Levites in temple tasks. Scholars do not know for certain the origin of each family, and it is not wise to claim more than the text says.

For today: God remembers names that we barely read. No simple service is small before Him. Today you can serve faithfully in your church or family, even though no one notices, trusting that God does see it.
exp.6:41:
The verse says that the descendants of Harim, a family of priests, numbered one thousand and seventeen people. It is part of a list of the priests who returned from exile: Jedaiah, Pashur, Immer and Harim. The phrase "the children of" means the descendants of that family.

Nehemiah copies here a record he found of the first ones who came back from Babylon to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel. He uses it to know who had the right to live in the city and to serve as a priest. The figures in this list and those in the book of Ezra almost coincide, although there are small differences that scholars explain in several ways.

God does not see faceless crowds; every family counts and was remembered. Your name and your service, though they may seem small, matter to Him. Today you can thank someone who serves without being noticed.
exp.11:9:
This verse is a list of high priests. The word "begat" is an older way of saying "was the father of." This names the succession: Jeshua, then Joiakim, then Eliashib, and then Joiada. In lists like this, generations are sometimes skipped, so "begat" can also mean "was an ancestor of."

The one who tells the story is the author of the book, who records who served in the temple after the return from exile. This list of priests and Levites shows that worship of God followed an orderly line. It is not known with certainty who put the final names of the list into their final form.

For today: God notices faithful service, even when it goes unseen. Today you can serve steadily in your family or in your church, knowing that God remembers what you do.
exp.6:8:
This verse is part of a list of families who returned from exile in Babylon. It says that the descendants of Shephatiah, that is, his clan or family, numbered three hundred seventy and two people. The phrase "children of" here means descendants, not only direct sons. The list counts the men of the people.

Nehemiah copies this record from the first ones who came back with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, many years before. He finds it when he wants to reorganize the people of Jerusalem. This same list appears in Ezra 2, with small differences in some numbers, and scholars explain these in several ways. The record served to know who belonged to the people and to which family.

For today: God does not see his people as an anonymous mass. Each family was counted and remembered. You can trust that your name and your story also matter to him, even when no one else notices them. And it is an example for valuing ordinary people who sustain the work of God.
exp.6:16:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that from the family of Azgad, two thousand three hundred and twenty-two people returned. "The children of" means descendants, not only direct sons.

Nehemiah speaks in the first person. After rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem, he found the record of those who had come back from exile in Babylon. He wanted to organize the people and repopulate the city. This list resembles the one in Ezra 2, but some figures differ. It is not known with certainty why; it may be due to copying errors or to the count being taken at different times.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass. Every family was remembered. You can trust that God knows your name and your story. And you too can value those who serve without being noticed.
exp.4:18:
Nehemiah asks God to remember him for good, because of everything he did for the people. "Think upon me" does not mean that God has forgotten him, but that God will take it into account and act with kindness.

Nehemiah, governor of Judah after the return from exile, speaks here. Shortly before, he tells how he did not collect the tax that was due to him as governor, and how he paid out of his own pocket for a generous table for many people. He did this because the people were already heavily burdened. His prayer does not boast before others; it is a simple plea before God. Some think it reveals a trusting heart, others notice a certain insistence on his own merits, and the Bible does not make this clear.

Today we can serve others without taking advantage of our position, and leave the recognition in God's hands. If you help someone, do it generously and pray with humility, trusting that God sees what no one else notices.
exp.3:11:
The explanation says that the Jews who lived near the enemies came and warned Nehemiah again and again. The ten times probably means many times, not an exact number. They warned him from every place they passed through when they returned. The phrase about the word that means "but" and the word meaning a warning are about the original wording, so they are left out here.

Nehemiah, who was leading the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem, is the one speaking. His enemies were planning a surprise attack, and the people were tired and afraid. These Jews, who lived among the opponents, heard their plans and passed them on. Thanks to these warnings, Nehemiah was able to organize the defense of the families.

For today: God often cares for us through people who warn us with sincerity. Let us listen to the advice of wise brothers and sisters, and when we face danger, let us pray and act with prudence, trusting in the Lord.
exp.10:32:
This verse names three places where descendants of the tribe of Benjamin lived: Hazor, Ramah, and Gittaim. It is part of a list of towns and villages. The word "lived" here means they settled there to make their homes.

Nehemiah 11 describes how Jerusalem was resettled after the return from exile in Babylon. Some families stayed in the capital, and others went back to their hometowns in Judah and Benjamin. The author, who according to tradition is Nehemiah or someone close to his work, records these places as a careful account of how the people recovered their land.

For today: God pays attention to places and people who seem small. Your faithful work in your town, neighborhood, or family, even when nobody notices, counts before Him. Serve with joy where you have been placed to live.
exp.3:17:
It says that each builder worked with his sword fastened at his side (the word for the waist or hips is the part of the body where a belt sits, and the word for girded means bound on or tied fast). In this way they built the wall, ready to fight. Beside Nehemiah stood the man who blew the trumpet, to sound the alarm if danger came.

Nehemiah speaks about the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem. The enemies of the Jews, Sanballat, Tobiah and others, mocked them and threatened to attack. So Nehemiah organized the people: some stood guard armed, and others built, without abandoning the work or neglecting the defense.

For today: when you do something good that God has placed in your heart, there will be opposition and weariness. Pray, stay alert and keep working, without letting fear stop you. And do not do it alone: seek the support of other believers.
exp.3:18:
Nehemiah speaks to the leaders, the officials, and all the people. He tells them that the work of rebuilding the wall is enormous and stretches over a great distance. That is why they are scattered, each group in its own section, quite far from one another. The words "nobles" and "rulers" name the chiefs and the officials who governed.

Nehemiah leads the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem. Israel's enemies threatened to attack, and the people worked with one hand on the building and the other on the sword. Because they were separated, Nehemiah made a plan: the sound of the trumpet would serve as a signal to gather wherever the danger was. Then he reminds them that God will fight for them.

When the task is great and we feel alone or far from others, we need to organize ourselves and stay united. Seek out your church or your family, support them, let them support you, and trust that God is with you.
exp.8:27:
It says that when Israel had peace, they again did evil before God. Because of this, God allowed their enemies to rule over them. But when they turned back to God and cried out, God heard them from heaven. Many times he rescued them because of his compassion. The sentence about the archaic word has been removed, and the phrase is translated directly as "compassion" in the context of the verse, which speaks of his mercies.

This is part of a long prayer of confession by the Levites, in the time of Nehemiah, after the return from exile. They remember Israel's history in order to acknowledge their sin and God's patience. The cycle repeats: peace, forgetting God, punishment, crying out, and deliverance.

For today: let us not wait for difficulty to seek God. When all is going well, it is also right to thank him and obey him. And if you have drifted away, remember that God still hears the one who sincerely returns to him.
exp.8:11:
This verse says that God led Israel with a pillar of cloud during the day and with a pillar of fire during the night. In this way he gave them light so they would know where to walk. The word "give them light" in the verse above is the phrase to focus on, and it means giving them light, and "they should go" means they had to go.

Here a group of Levites is speaking, in a prayer of confession in the time of Nehemiah, when the people had already returned from exile. They review the history of Israel, from Egypt to Sinai, to remember God's faithfulness and to acknowledge how much they had failed him. This verse tells what happened in the exodus, after crossing the sea.

For today: God remains faithful to guide his children. He does not always show the whole path, but he gives the light needed for today's step. Trust him and ask him for direction with humility.
exp.2:26:
The people of Tekoa, called Tekoites, repaired another section of the wall. It lay across from a large tower that stood out and reached as far as the wall of Ophel, a raised area of Jerusalem. The word "restored" means to repair and rebuild.

Nehemiah tells this account in the first person. He had been cupbearer to the king of Persia, and he returned to Jerusalem to rebuild its fallen walls. His list of workers names each group. The Tekoites had already worked on another section (verse 5), though there it says their nobles did not help. Here we see that the people kept working.

Today, God values steady service, even when it is little seen. Ask yourself where you can help again in your church or family, without expecting applause or public recognition.
exp.12:8:
This verse says that Nehemiah ordered the rooms of the temple to be cleaned, the chambers where things were stored. Then he brought back into them the vessels of the house of God, the grain offerings, and the frankincense. The word "vessels" here does not mean jewels, but the objects and utensils used in worship. "Frankincense" is the perfume referred to.

Nehemiah speaks as one who has already returned to Jerusalem. He found that the priest Eliashib had given Tobiah, an opponent of Nehemiah, a chamber within the courts of the temple. Nehemiah removed Tobiah's belongings and restored the place to its original purpose. He then also corrected the neglect of the Levites and of the house of God.

For today: examine whether there is something in your life that occupies the place that belongs to God, such as habits, distractions, or commitments. With humility, clean house and give that space back to prayer, to the Word, and to serving others.
exp.7:3:
Verse 4 tells us that Ezra the scribe stood on a high platform of wood, made especially for that occasion. The word here refers to a raised stand, so that everyone could see and hear him. On his right hand and on his left stood thirteen men, who accompanied him before the people.

The writer of the book recounts how, after returning from exile and rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem, the people gathered to hear the Law of God. Ezra read it aloud for hours. We cannot be certain who all the companions were or what each one did, though some think they helped the people understand the reading.

For today: giving God's Word a central place. We can set aside time to listen to it or read it with attention, and also support those who teach it, so that we do not go alone.
exp.0:5:
Nehemiah asks God to listen closely. The phrase "Let thine ear now be attentive, and thine eyes open" is a way of asking God to really pay attention to his plea. He says he prays day and night for the people of Israel. He also confesses the sins of everyone, and he includes himself and his family: "both I and my father's house have sinned." The word "servant" means someone who serves God.

Nehemiah was living in Persia, where he served the king. He had just heard that Jerusalem was still in ruins and that those who had returned were living in great distress. So he wept, fasted, and prayed. He acknowledges that the people had broken their covenant with God.

For today: when you see a big problem, begin by praying honestly. Nehemiah does not blame only others; he admits his own part. Today you could ask God to forgive your failures and those of your community, and ask him what you can do yourself.
exp.9:17:
This verse is part of a list of names: Hodijah, Hashum and Bezai. They are leaders or heads of the people who signed a covenant. There are no difficult words; they are simply Hebrew names. The Bible gives no further details about them in this passage.

The book of Nehemiah tells how the people of Israel returned from exile and rebuilt Jerusalem. In chapter 10, after hearing God's law, the leaders, the Levites and the priests sealed with their signatures a commitment to obey it. The narrator records only the names, like an official document. Some of these names also appear in other lists, but it cannot be known with certainty whether they refer to the same people.

For today: God values people, even those whom almost no one remembers. These men put their names to a public commitment before God. We might ask ourselves: what promise of obedience should I make sincerely and responsibly, regardless of whether others see me or remember me?
exp.8:17:
This verse recalls the sin of the golden calf. A "molten calf" is an image of metal that has been melted and shaped, an idol. The people said that this calf was the God who brought them up out of Egypt, and in doing so they committed great provocations, that is, acts that God hates.

This is part of a prayer of confession by the people of Israel, in the time of Nehemiah, after their return from exile. The Levites review the history, from Egypt up to that day, to acknowledge the failures of their ancestors. But the account does not stop at the sin: it emphasizes that God, being merciful and patient, did not abandon them.

For today: it is easy to attribute to created things, such as money, success, or our own ideas, what only God has done. Today you can sincerely thank Him for what He has done in your life and confidently confess your mistakes to Him, because He remains merciful.
exp.10:0:
The rulers of the people settled to live in Jerusalem. The rest drew lots: of every ten people, one would move into the city, and the other nine would stay in the other towns. Drawing lots was a way of deciding with stones or marks, trusting that God guided the result. Dwelling there means living there. The holy city is Jerusalem, where the temple stood.

After the walls were rebuilt, Jerusalem had few inhabitants and was vulnerable. The account comes from the story of Nehemiah, which describes how the people were organized to populate it. The leaders set the example first. The exact details of how the drawing worked are not explained precisely.

For today: serving sometimes costs something, because it means leaving comfort behind. The leaders went first, and the people shared the burden in an orderly way. Ask yourself where you can take the step and serve in your church or community, without waiting for others to do it for you.
exp.2:17:
Their companions kept on repairing the wall of Jerusalem. Bavai, son of Henadad, took over the next section. "Repaired" here means mended or rebuilt, and "ruler" means the leader or governor of a district. Keilah was divided into two districts, and Bavai led one half.

This is part of the list of the builders of the wall in Nehemiah 3. Nehemiah himself is usually considered the narrator, and he records who worked and where. Jerusalem lay in ruins, and the people organized themselves by sections to rebuild it quickly.

Today: God values the steady work of every person, even when no one applauds it. Ask yourself what your own "section" is in your family, your church, or your work, and do it faithfully, alongside others.
exp.10:16:
This verse names three Levites who lived in Jerusalem. Mattaniah, a descendant of Asaph, was the leader and directed the song of praise and thanksgiving at the time of prayer. Bakbukiah was his second, and Abda came from the family of Jeduthun, another line of temple musicians.

Nehemiah recounts how Jerusalem was resettled after the exile. Some were chosen to live in the holy city, and their names and duties are recorded. It is a list of royal servants with specific roles. The passage says nothing more about what that prayer was like, so it is best not to imagine details.

For today: God notices those who serve quietly, and also those who go to the front. Some lead the praise and others support it. Ask yourself what place is yours to fill, and serve it with gratitude, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.11:31:
This verse says that Hoshaiah, together with half of the leaders of Judah, was walking behind the first group that gave thanks on the wall. "Princes" means the leaders or authorities of the people. "Went after them" means he followed them in the procession.

The one telling the story is Nehemiah, speaking in the first person. The wall of Jerusalem had already been rebuilt, and now it was being dedicated to God with purification, music, and two great choirs marching in opposite directions. This verse is part of the list of those who took part. Not much more is known about Hoshaiah, so I prefer not to assume anything.

For today: the leaders also march in the celebration; they do not only direct from a distance. We can give thanks to God alongside others, and those who carry responsibility can set an example by taking part with humility and joy in the life of the community.
exp.7:8:
The explanation says that Nehemiah, called "the Tirshatha" (a Persian title for the governor), together with the priest and scribe Ezra and the Levites, told all the people that this day was holy to God. For that reason they should not mourn or weep, even though the people were weeping as they heard the law.

Ezra read from the book of the law, and the Levites explained it clearly so that everyone could understand.
