When the people grasped how far they had strayed from what God required, they were moved to tears. The leaders did not despise that sorrow, but they reminded them that it was a day of celebration and thanksgiving to God.

When God's word confronts us, it is good for our hearts to ache. But we should not stop there: God calls us to turn back to Him with confidence and to receive His joy, which sustains us.
exp.8:20:
It says that God cared for Israel for forty years in the wilderness. They lacked nothing. Their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell. The phrase "sustained them" means "you upheld them and provided what they needed." "Swelled" refers to the swelling that comes from walking a great deal.

These words are part of a long prayer of confession that the Levites offer in Jerusalem, in the days of Nehemiah. The people have heard the law and are remembering their history. They recount how God was faithful, even though Israel was often rebellious. Some scholars see the detail about the clothing as a way of highlighting God's care; the text does not explain how it happened.

For today: when you go through a long and difficult season, remember how God has sustained you before. Write down the times he helped you. That strengthens trust and encourages you to give thanks, even when you do not have all the answers.
exp.2:0:
Here is what the text says: Eliashib, the high priest, got up together with the other priests, and they rebuilt the Sheep Gate. Then, according to other translations, they consecrated it. They worked on the wall as far as the tower of Meah and as far as the tower of Hananel, two points on the wall of Jerusalem.

The one telling the account is Nehemiah, who led the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls after the return from exile in Babylon. This chapter lists who built each section. It is notable that the priests are the first to work. The Sheep Gate was near the temple, and the animals for the sacrifices probably entered through it, although the text does not explain this.

For today: leaders set the example when they are the first to serve. If God places you in a responsibility, begin yourself with humility and without waiting for others to go first.
exp.12:26:
Nehemiah asks firmly: are we really going to listen to you and commit this great evil? The word "prevaricate" means to betray or be unfaithful to a commitment; here, being unfaithful to God. "Foreign women" refers to women from neighboring peoples who did not follow the God of Israel.

Nehemiah, governor of Jerusalem, speaks when he returns and finds that many Jews had married women from other peoples. He sees in this a danger to the people's faithfulness to the covenant, and he remembers the case of Solomon. His reactions, such as striking some of them, are harsh; the Bible recounts them, but it does not say that we should imitate them.

For today: think about which commitments to God you might be neglecting under pressure from others. Ask God for help to remain faithful, and do so with resolve, but also with respect and love toward others.
exp.6:12:
Verse 13 says that eight hundred forty-five descendants of the family of Zattu returned from exile in Babylon to Judah. It is part of a list of families, counted by surname or clan. The phrase "the children of" means descendants, not only direct children.

Nehemiah, governor of Jerusalem, tells that he found a record of the families who first returned with Zerubbabel. He looks for it to organize the people after the wall was finished. The list also appears in Ezra 2, where the number for Zattu is 945; scholars explain the difference in several ways, such as copying errors or counts made at different times, but it is not known with certainty.

For today: God does not see faceless crowds; each family counts and is remembered. You can trust that your life, even one that seems small or anonymous, has a place in God's plan. Serve faithfully wherever you are.
exp.6:35:
This verse is part of a list, and it says that 345 descendants of families who had lived in the city of Jericho returned. "Children of" does not speak only of children, but of people who belonged to a family or place.

The one speaking is Nehemiah, who tells how he found the record of the first Jews who came back from exile in Babylon. After rebuilding the wall, he wanted to organize the people and resettle Jerusalem. An almost identical list appears in Ezra 2, and the differences in some of the numbers are explained in several ways.

For today: God overlooks no one. Even though 345 people may seem few, they were recorded and remembered. Your simple and steady service also counts in God's work, even when no one applauds it.
exp.6:9:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that the descendants of Arah, that is, his clan or family, numbered six hundred fifty-two. The phrase "children of" does not speak only of direct sons, but of the whole family that came from one ancestor.

Here Nehemiah speaks, or at least he presents this record. God put it on his heart to gather the people and count them by their genealogies. He found the book of those who had returned from exile with Zerubbabel. Ezra 2:5 gives a different figure for Arah, seven hundred seventy-five. The reason is not known with certainty; copying errors or counts made at different times have been proposed.

For today: God does not see faceless crowds. Every family is counted and remembered. You can serve with confidence that your place, though it may seem small, matters to God.
exp.3:4:
He says that Nehemiah asks God not to leave the wickedness of his enemies unpunished or to erase their sin from his sight. The reason he gives is that they have stirred up anger and mocked those who were rebuilding the wall.

The speaker is Nehemiah, the leader of the Jews who were rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem. Sanballat and Tobiah mocked the work and looked down on it. Nehemiah does not respond with violence but brings the matter to God in prayer. It is a harsh prayer, similar to the psalms that ask for justice. Some see it as a legitimate cry, while others note that Jesus later taught people to pray for their enemies.

For today: when people mock you or hinder you for doing what is right, do not seek revenge. Tell God honestly what you feel, leave justice in his hands, and keep working.
exp.10:19:
This verse says that the rest of the people, that is, the other Israelites, priests, and Levites who did not stay in Jerusalem, lived in the other towns of Judah. Each one was in his own inheritance, which is the land or property that had come to his family from long ago.

Nehemiah 11 tells how Jerusalem was resettled after the return from exile. Lots were cast so that one out of every ten families would live in the holy city, and others offered themselves willingly. This passage is part of a record of names and places, told in the third person. It shows that Jerusalem needed people, but that the rest of the people also had their place.

For today: God works through those who serve in very visible places and through those who do so in simple ones. Ask yourself where he has placed you and serve him faithfully there, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.7:2:
Ezra read the book of the law in the open area in front of the Water Gate. He read from early morning until midday, in front of the men, the women, and all who could understand. The people who could understand were those old enough and able to grasp what was read. And all the people listened with great attention.

The people had returned from exile, and Jerusalem already had its walls rebuilt. It was the first day of the seventh month, and the people themselves asked Ezra to bring the law of Moses. The text reports the event; it does not say how many hours it lasted, only that it was a long reading.

Today we can give the Bible unhurried time without distractions. Try turning off your phone and reading a whole passage, really listening to what God says. If possible, do it together with other believers, as that people did.
exp.11:45:
This verse says that music and praise to God were not something new in Israel. From the time of King David and Asaph, many years earlier, there were already chief singers, that is, the directors or leaders of the singers. They guided the songs of praise and thanksgiving to God.

The narrator of the book tells how the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem was celebrated. He explains that the people cared for the service of the temple, including the singers, following the order that David and Solomon had left. The tradition is recalled to show that the people were returning to what God had established.

For today: praise needs order, care, and steadiness. If in your church or your home there are those who lead the music, support them and thank them for their service. You can also make thankfulness to God a daily habit, not only an occasional moment.
exp.6:37:
The explanation says that the descendants of Senaah, who returned from exile, numbered three thousand nine hundred and thirty people. It is part of a list of families and towns. "The children of" means descendants, not only direct sons.

Nehemiah tells how he found the record of the first people who returned from Babylon to Judah. He explains it himself in this chapter: God put it on his heart to gather the people and register them. This list appears almost the same in Ezra 2, with some differences in certain numbers. It is not known for certain why; some think of different copies or dates of counting. Senaah was probably a place or a clan, and its number is among the largest.

For today: God does not see crowds without faces; every family and person counts for Him. Today you can value your simple place in the church or the family, and also recognize with gratitude those who serve without anyone noticing them.
exp.9:3:
This verse names only three people: Hattush, Shebaniah, and Malluch. They are part of a list of priests who signed, that is, who sealed a covenant. The names may sound unusual to modern readers because they are spelled in an older way.

Nehemiah 10 follows the great reading of the law and the confession of sins by the people (chapters 8 and 9). Here no single character speaks: it is a written list of those who committed themselves before God to live according to his law. First appears Nehemiah, the governor, and then the priests. They are named one by one so that the commitment would be public and real.

For today: God values commitments with a name attached. It is worth deciding on one concrete act of obedience, telling it to someone you trust, and carrying it out. God knows your name, just as he knew the names of these men.
exp.3:10:
The enemies of Israel make a secret plan. They want the Jews not to find out or see anything, until they suddenly arrive in the midst of the people, kill them, and bring the building of the wall to a stop. "Let us cause the work to cease" means they want to stop the work completely.

The ones speaking are Sanballat, Tobiah, and the other opponents of Nehemiah. They had already mocked the Jews, and now they move on to threats. The Jews who lived near them warned Nehemiah about this plan. That is why he prayed, posted guards, and organized the people with their weapons behind the wall.

When we do something good for God, opposition may come. Nehemiah teaches us to pray and also to act with wisdom, without neglecting what we have to take care of. Trusting God does not remove the responsibility to stay alert.
exp.6:39:
This verse gives the number of descendants of Immer who returned from exile: one thousand fifty-two people. "Children of" means descendants of a family, not only direct sons. Immer was a family of priests, that is, men dedicated to service in the temple.

Nehemiah records that he found the register of the first people who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem. He notes it while he is reorganizing the city, already rebuilt. This list helped people know who belonged to the community and who could serve as priests. The figure matches Ezra 2:37.

For today: God pays attention to people and remembers them by name and family. No one is a mere number to Him. You can serve with confidence in your place, whether it is large or small, because God sees and values what you do.
exp.1:13:
Nehemiah keeps riding through the streets of Jerusalem by night, inspecting the walls. He reaches the Fountain Gate and the King's Pool, but the rubble was so heavy that his mount could not get through. The word "beast" refers to the animal he was riding.

Nehemiah speaks as the cupbearer of the king of Persia, who came to Jerusalem with permission to rebuild its walls. He examines the damage in secret before telling anyone about his plan. He wants to see the situation clearly and act wisely. The exact details of the route are debated, but the point is clear: the destruction was great.

For today: before undertaking something important, take time to observe reality calmly and to pray. Seeing the problem honestly, without rush or exaggeration, helps you move forward with wisdom and trust in God.
exp.7:5:
Ezra blesses the Lord, whom he calls "the great God." All the people respond, "Amen, Amen," which means "so be it" or "we agree." They lift up their hands, bow down, and worship with their faces to the ground.

The people of Israel gathered in Jerusalem after returning from exile and rebuilding the wall. Ezra, the scribe, stood on a wooden platform so that everyone could see him. Before the law of God was read, the people listened carefully. Their response shows respect and reverence before God and his word.

When you read the Bible, do not treat it only as information. Before you read, offer a short prayer of praise and ask God for an attentive and humble heart. In this way your reading can become an encounter with God, not only a duty.
exp.2:2:
This verse tells how the family of Hassenaah built the Fish Gate of Jerusalem. They laid the wooden beams, set the gate's doors in place, and fitted it with locks and bars. Laying the beams refers to putting the wooden framework in place, and the bars are what secure the gate shut.

Nehemiah, cupbearer to the king of Persia, returned to Jerusalem to rebuild its ruined walls. In this chapter the account lists the groups who worked, one by one, each on its own section. It does not say why the gate was called the Fish Gate; some think it was because it was near where fish were sold, but that is a guess.

God uses the work of many people, not only the leaders. A task that seems small, like fitting a lock, matters for the good of everyone. Ask yourself: what part can I do faithfully today, in my family, my church, or my community?
exp.6:64:
He says that the governor ordered those men, whose family records could not be found, not to eat of the most holy offerings, that is, the part of the sacrifices reserved only for the priests. They would have to wait until there was a priest who could inquire of God with the Urim and Thummim. "Tirshatha" is a Persian title for the governor, here Nehemiah.

Nehemiah was speaking after the exiles had returned to Judah. When they checked the lists of families, some priests could not prove their lineage, so they were set apart from service. A final decision was expected through the Urim and Thummim, objects used to seek God's answer. The Bible does not explain in detail how they worked, and we do not know whether the matter was resolved.

For today: God deserves to be served with reverence and order. When a decision is difficult, we can wait patiently and ask him for direction instead of rushing ahead.
exp.12:30:
This verse closes the book of Nehemiah. It says that Nehemiah also arranged the offering of wood for the altar, which was brought at appointed times, and the firstfruits, that is, the first produce of the harvest that was given to God. It ends with a simple prayer: "Remember me, O my God, for good."

Nehemiah, the governor of Jerusalem, is speaking. Once the city had been rebuilt, he returned and found disorder in the temple and in the service of the priests. He corrected these things and put each person back in his work. At the end he does not boast about himself, but leaves his work in God's hands.

For today: when you serve God, do it with steadiness, even in small and orderly things, such as being punctual and faithful. Then rest in God without seeking applause, and pray with humility, asking for his goodness.
exp.9:31:
It says that the people committed themselves to give each year a third part of a shekel to support the temple. The phrase "made ordinances for us" means they placed this obligation on themselves. The shekel was a unit of weight in silver, and this amount was small, but it was given by everyone together.

The speaker is the people of Israel, along with their leaders, after their return from exile in Babylon. They signed a covenant to obey God's law. They had already promised to keep the marriage laws, the Sabbath, and the seventh year. Now they commit themselves to worship: bread, sacrifices, and the whole service of the temple. The law of Moses mentioned half a shekel (Exodus 30:13), so the difference is usually explained by the economic situation or the period, though this is not known for certain.

For today: if we love God, our commitment shows in our care for his work. Decide on a regular offering, even a modest one, and give it cheerfully and consistently to your local church.
exp.5:4:
This verse says that Sanballat sent his servant to Nehemiah for the fifth time with the same request: that he meet with him. This time the messenger carried an open letter, that is, one that was not sealed. "Servant" means a servant or assistant.

Nehemiah is rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem, and Sanballat, who opposed the work, had already asked him four times to come and see him. Nehemiah always answered that he could not leave the work. An open letter could be read by others along the way, so it probably helped spread rumors. Some think it was meant to pressure him, although the text does not fully explain this.

For today: when someone insists on distracting you from what God has entrusted to you, do not give in out of weariness. Stand firm, with calm and steadiness, as Nehemiah did.
exp.10:27:
This verse is part of a list of towns in the south of Judah where some Israelites settled after the return from exile. Ziklag and Mekonah were towns, and "its villages" refers to the smaller settlements that depended on them. In other words, people did not live only in the main cities, but also in the surrounding area.

The book is told as a record of the rebuilding of Jerusalem. Earlier, lots were cast so that one out of every ten families would live in the holy city, and the rest stayed in other towns. This list shows how the promised land was resettled. Scholars are uncertain about the exact location of Mekonah.

For today: God values those who serve in small and little-known places, not only in the important centers. Your faithfulness in your village, your neighborhood, or your family counts with Him, even when few notice it.
exp.3:6:
This verse tells us that Nehemiah's enemies became extremely angry when they learned that the walls of Jerusalem were making progress. The "gaps" are the openings or breaches in the wall, and "began to be stopped" means the holes were beginning to be filled in. "Were very wroth" means they were filled with rage. Among the opponents were Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabians, the Ammonites, and the people of Ashdod.

Nehemiah speaks in the first person. He had returned to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem after the exile. The neighboring peoples saw that the work was prospering, and this threatened their influence in the region. That is why they first mocked and now grow furious. The exact motives of each group are not spelled out, but the text shows that they opposed the advance of the work.

For today: when you do something good and begin to see progress, opposition can appear. Do not lose heart. Like Nehemiah, pray, and also act with wisdom, without abandoning what God has placed in your hands.
exp.12:0:
This verse tells us that on a certain day the book of Moses was read aloud, and the people heard it. In it they found written that the Ammonites and the Moabites were never to enter the congregation of God, that is, the assembly of the people of Israel.

The one telling the story is Nehemiah, now that the walls of Jerusalem have been completed. The public reading of the law led the people to examine their lives. The text that was read comes from Deuteronomy 23:3-6, and the passage that follows explains the reason: those peoples did not help Israel, and they hired Balaam to curse them.

For today: reading the Bible should not stop at gaining information. If we let the Word speak to us, it will show us what we need to correct. We can ask God for a heart willing to obey when something makes us uncomfortable.
exp.12:21:
Nehemiah instructs the Levites to purify themselves and come to guard the gates of Jerusalem, so that the Sabbath would be kept as a day set apart for God. Then he prays: "remember me" and "spare me" according to the greatness of God's mercy. To sanctify something means to set it apart for God.

Nehemiah, governor of Jerusalem, speaks after seeing that merchants were selling on the Sabbath. He had already confronted and warned them, and they stopped coming. Now he places the Levites as guards to uphold that order. His prayer shows that, even with his zeal, he knows he needs God's mercy. Some think he is humbling himself; others think he is asking God to value his effort.

For today: when you work to do what is right, do it with firmness, but with humility. Set limits that protect your time with God, and rest in his mercy, not in your own merits.
exp.2:23:
This verse says that a man named Binnui, son of Henadad, rebuilt another section of the wall of Jerusalem. That section ran from the house of Azariah to the bend of the wall and on to the corner.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, closely following the recollection of Nehemiah. After Jerusalem lay in ruins, the people organized themselves to raise the wall. This chapter lists the families and groups who worked, each on a specific stretch, many of them near their own homes. The exact locations of these places are difficult to pinpoint today.

For today: God values steady, concrete work. Your part may seem small or unremarkable, but it adds to a greater task. Faithfully do the section that falls to you.
exp.12:14:
In those days Nehemiah saw people in Judah working just as on any ordinary day: they were treading grapes in the winepresses, bringing in bundles of grain, and loading donkeys with wine, grapes, figs, and all kinds of goods, which they brought into Jerusalem on the Sabbath. "I warned them" means that he spoke to them firmly and rebuked them, especially for selling food on that day.

Nehemiah, the governor of Jerusalem, speaks here after returning and finding that the people had neglected their covenant with God. The Sabbath was a day of rest that God had commanded Israel as a sign of their relationship with Him. Nehemiah tries to correct this neglect and protect the spiritual life of the people.

For today: setting aside regular time to rest and to be with God helps us remember that we do not live by work alone. We can ask ourselves what we are giving priority to.
exp.3:16:
They said that everyone who was rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem, both those who set the stones and those who carried materials, worked with one hand and held a weapon in the other.

Nehemiah is the one who tells the story. He was leading the rebuilding of the walls after the return from exile. His enemies, among them Sanballat and Tobiah, mocked them and threatened to attack. Nehemiah did not abandon the work or let fear paralyze him. He organized the people to keep building and, at the same time, to be ready to defend themselves.

For today: when we do something good, obstacles or discouragement sometimes come. We can keep working with steadiness and, at the same time, stay alert and pray, trusting that God sustains us. We should not abandon the task, but neither should we lower our guard.
exp.3:12:
Nehemiah reports that he placed the people in the lowest and most exposed spots behind the wall, and also in the higher parts of the rocks. He set them by families, each with their swords, spears, and bows. The lower places were the unprotected areas where the wall still had gaps.

He is speaking as the leader of the rebuilding of Jerusalem. His enemies were planning a surprise attack to stop the work, and some Jews who lived nearby warned him several times. So he organized the defense, and shortly after, he encouraged the people to trust in God and not be afraid.

For today: when we face threats, Nehemiah prayed and also acted with prudence. We can take care of what God has entrusted to us, relying on family and community, without living in fear, because we trust in God.
exp.11:19:
This verse is part of a list of priestly families. It says that, in the house of Sallai, the head was Kallai, and in the house of Amok, the head was Eber. They are only names, but each one recalls a family that served God in the temple.

The book of Nehemiah is a narrative, and here the author, whom tradition usually identifies with Nehemiah, though this is not entirely certain, records the heads of the priestly houses in the time of the high priest Joiakim. They were noted down to keep the order of worship and the identity of the people after the return from exile in Babylon. This list shows us that God cared that service in his house be orderly and remembered.

For today: God values people who serve faithfully, even when almost no one knows them. Today you can serve in your church with steadiness and simplicity, knowing that God sees and remembers your work.
exp.6:63:
These men of priestly family looked for their record of genealogies, that is, the list that proved whom they descended from, and did not find it. Therefore they were "put from the priesthood," that is, removed from priestly service, because they could not prove their lineage.

The author, Nehemiah, copies the list of the families who returned from exile in Babylon. Only the descendants of Aaron could serve as priests, so the records were checked with great care. The verses that follow say that the governor forbade them to eat of the most holy things until a priest arose who could consult with the Urim and Thummim. We do not know for certain how these objects worked.

For today: God cares about order and faithfulness in his service. Yet today our identity in Christ does not depend on a human record, for through faith we are his children (John 1:12). Let us serve with humility and gratitude.
exp.9:21:
Pelatiah, Hanan, and Anaiah are three more names in a list of the people's leaders. They were real people who signed, or "sealed," a commitment before God. The names alone tell us nothing more about them; the Bible gives no details here about their lives.

The book of Nehemiah tells how the people returned from exile and rebuilt Jerusalem. In this chapter, the leaders, the Levites, and the priests sign a written agreement to obey God's law. The writer includes the list to keep a record of who made the commitment. This part names the heads of the people.

For today: God values people who commit themselves simply and without fame. Although we know nothing about Pelatiah, his name was written down. We can make concrete commitments to God, such as praying, serving, or being honest, knowing that He sees every faithful decision, even the one no one else notices.
exp.8:7:
It says God saw that Abraham's heart was faithful and made a covenant with him, that is, a solemn agreement or promise. He promised to give his descendants the land of several peoples: the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, and the Girgashites. "Descendants" here means offspring, the people who would come after him. God kept what he promised because he is righteous, that is, upright and trustworthy.

This is part of a prayer by the Levites, guiding the people of Israel after they returned from exile. They were gathered to confess their sins and renew their commitment to God. They recall the story from creation and Abraham, to show that God has always been faithful, even when they failed.

When you doubt that God will keep his promises, remember how he has been faithful before. Write down today one promise of God and one time he helped you, and give him thanks.
exp.6:48:
This verse is part of a list of families. It mentions the descendants of Hanan, of Giddel, and of Gahar. These are three ancestors' names, and their "children" (that is, their descendants) formed family groups. In this section, these groups belong to the temple servants. We do not know much about the exact meaning of each name.

Nehemiah 7 is a record of the people who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah. The author, traditionally Nehemiah, tells how he found this list and used it to organize the people after the wall was rebuilt. It was important to know who belonged to each family and to each service.

For today: God overlooks no one. Although these names hardly appear anywhere else, they were written down. Your quiet, simple work for God also matters. Serve faithfully, even when no one notices.
exp.8:36:
The good harvest of the land, which God gave to Israel, now goes to the foreign kings. God allowed those kings to rule because of the people's sins. They have authority over their bodies and their livestock to do as they please, and the people live in great distress. The explanation of "have dominion" is that they rule with total power, and the explanation of the animals is that they are the working animals and livestock.

The people of Israel, led by the Levites, speak in a public prayer of confession. They have returned from exile, but they remain under the dominion of the Persian empire. They remember the history of their fathers, who did not serve God in abundance, and they acknowledge their own guilt. For this reason they make a written covenant to return to obedience.

For today: when we go through difficulties, we can pray with sincerity, without blaming others, acknowledging our faults and asking God for help to change. Honesty before God opens the way to a new beginning.
exp.7:16:
It says that all who had returned from the exile in Babylon built booths, or shelters of branches, and lived in them during the feast. Since the days of Joshua son of Nun, the people had not kept it in that way. "Captivity" refers to the exile, and "there was very great gladness" shows the joy of the people.

The author is the narrator of the book of Nehemiah, and it is believed he used memoirs of Nehemiah and Ezra. The people had just heard the law and discovered that the Feast of Tabernacles was to be kept in this way. That feast recalled how God cared for Israel in the wilderness. The statement about Joshua is understood in different ways: perhaps it indicates that they had never done it with such enthusiasm and unity.

When we know God's Word, the natural response is to obey it with gladness. Today you can read the Bible and put into practice something concrete that you learn, without seeing it as a burden.
exp.12:28:
Nehemiah asks God not to forget those who "defile" the priesthood. Here, "defile" means to make dirty or dishonor something set apart for God. "The covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites" refers to the sacred commitment God made with those who served in the temple. It is a prayer, not a personal revenge.

Nehemiah speaks near the end of his book, when he returns to Jerusalem and finds problems. A grandson of the high priest had married the daughter of Sanballat, an enemy of the people. This put the purity of the temple service at risk. Nehemiah drove him out and then reorganized the priests. Some interpret the problem as more a matter of faithfulness to God than of ethnic origin.

For today: those who lead others carry a greater responsibility. Guard your integrity, and entrust to God what you cannot correct.
exp.7:4:
It says that Ezra opened the book of the law in the sight of all the people, because he was higher up than the people. As soon as he opened it, everyone paid attention. The words "in the sight of" mean that everyone could see him, and "paid attention" means they listened with interest and respect.

The people of Israel had returned from exile, and Jerusalem already had its walls rebuilt. They gathered in the square in front of the Water Gate. Ezra, the scribe, read God's law from a wooden platform, with other men at his side. He did it from early morning until midday, and the people wanted to hear the Word.

Today we can imitate that attitude. Before reading the Bible, let us pause, set aside distractions, and open our hearts with attention. Reading it with respect and a desire to obey helps us let God really speak to us.
exp.12:12:
This verse tells that Nehemiah appointed four men as officers in charge of the temple storerooms: Shelemiah, a priest; Zadok, a scribe; Pedaiah, a Levite; and Hanan, as their helper. The word "supervisors" here means people in charge or overseers. They were chosen because they had a reputation for being faithful, and their job was to distribute what was received among their fellow Levites.

The one speaking is Nehemiah, governor of Jerusalem. When he returned after some time away, he found that the people had stopped bringing the tithes. The Levites had gone off to work their fields so they could eat, and the temple had been neglected. Nehemiah corrected the leaders, the people began bringing the tithe again, and he arranged its care and distribution with trustworthy people.

For today: when it comes to offerings, time, or helping others, faithfulness matters more than talent. If you are entrusted with something in your church or family, take care of it with honesty and order. And if you have to choose someone, look first for the person who is reliable.
exp.9:38:
This verse says that the people of Israel and the Levites were to bring the offerings of grain, wine, and oil to the storerooms of the temple. The storerooms were rooms for keeping supplies beside the house of God. There were kept the holy items used in worship, and those who served there: priests, gatekeepers, and singers. The people end with a promise: "we will not forsake the house of our God."

The people speak, together with their leaders, after their return from exile. They had signed an agreement to obey God's law (Nehemiah 10). This promise made sure that those who served in the temple would have support and that the worship would continue.

For today: God is worthy of our constant faithfulness. We can support our local church, its ministers, and its work with generosity and consistency, so that it is not neglected.
exp.1:19:
Nehemiah answers with firmness: the God of heaven is the one who will give them success, and they, as his servants, will arise and build. To the mockers he says that they have no part, no right, and no memorial in Jerusalem.

Nehemiah, the king's cupbearer, speaks here after arriving in Jerusalem to rebuild its walls. Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem mocked him and accused him of rebelling against the king. Nehemiah does not argue with them; he answers with confidence in God and clarity about his mission. He had received permission from the king, and for that reason the accusation was false.

When someone mocks or doubts what you do to serve God, you do not need to defend yourself in anger. Pray, trust that God gives success, and keep working with humility and steadiness.
exp.8:12:
This verse says that God came down to Mount Sinai and spoke with his people from heaven. He gave them right judgments, true laws, good statutes and commandments. "Right judgments" are decisions and just rules; "statutes" are established rules; "gavest them" simply means "you gave them."

It is part of a prayer of confession that the Levites offer in the time of Nehemiah, when the people, now returned from exile, gather to hear the law and acknowledge their sins. They review their history: the open sea, the cloud and the fire, and now the law at Sinai, as signs of God's care.

For today: God's word is a gift from a Father who guides, not a burden. You can read it this week with gratitude, asking him to teach you to live with justice and truth.
exp.0:3:
Nehemiah tells how, on hearing the bad news about Jerusalem, he sat down and wept. He mourned for several days, fasted, and prayed to God. The word "mourned" means he dressed and lived in visible signs of deep sorrow.

Nehemiah speaks as a Jew who lived far from his homeland, serving the king of Persia. His brother Hanani had told him that the survivors in Judah were suffering disgrace and that the walls of Jerusalem still lay in ruins. Nehemiah did not remain indifferent; he brought his people's pain before God, and his prayer continues in the following verses with a confession of sins.

For today: when you learn of a problem that hurts, let it move you and bring it to God in prayer first. Before you act, ask him for direction and sensitivity to help.
exp.2:8:
This verse says that Rephaiah, son of Hur, worked on repairing the wall right beside the groups before him. He is called "ruler," which here means governor or leader, of the half of the Jerusalem district. The rebuilding of his section is what the text describes as repairing it.

Here the book's narrator speaks, listing in detail who rebuilt each part of the wall under Nehemiah's direction. The people had returned from exile and the city lay in ruins. It is striking that an important leader worked with his own hands, just like goldsmiths and perfumers. Scholars understand this to have been an administrative district, though we do not know exactly how it was divided.

For today: no one is too important to serve in the ordinary tasks. Ask yourself where you can help alongside others in your church or community, without seeking recognition. God notices every section of the wall.
exp.1:16:
Nehemiah speaks to the people and reminds them of the sad condition of the city: Jerusalem lies empty, that is, without life or protection, and its gates have been destroyed by fire. Then he invites them to rebuild the wall so that they will no longer live in disgrace, meaning shame or dishonor.

Nehemiah was cupbearer to the king of Persia and had received permission to go to Jerusalem. After inspecting the walls at night and in secret, he now presents the plan to the people. He shows them the problem and encourages them to work together, trusting that God supports them.

For today: God often moves his people to act, not just to lament. Think of something broken in your family, your church, or your community, and ask yourself what concrete step you can take, together with others, to help repair it.
exp.11:26:
When the time came to dedicate the wall of Jerusalem, the people sent for the Levites from all the places where they lived. They wanted to bring them to the city to celebrate with praise, songs, and music. The instruments named in the verse were stringed instruments and metal cymbals.

The one telling the story is Nehemiah, the governor, who writes in the first person later in this chapter. The wall had already been rebuilt, and the people wanted to thank God publicly. The Levites were in charge of the music and of the service in the temple, and they were scattered among the villages nearby.

For today: when God helps us finish something difficult, let us not simply move on. Let us stop and thank him, and better still, do it together with other believers, with joy and sincere gratitude.
exp.6:72:
This verse says that everyone settled in their cities: the priests, the Levites (who assisted in worship), the gatekeepers (who guarded the doors), the singers, and the common people. Also the Nethinim, who were servants devoted to the service of the temple. When the seventh month came, everyone was already in their places.

The account comes from the memoirs of Nehemiah, although scholars debate how the book was put together. After rebuilding the wall and recording those who returned from exile, the author shows that the people were now settled. The seventh month was important in Israel, and in the following chapter they gather to hear the Law.

For today: God uses each person in their place, whether with visible or simple tasks. Do faithfully what is yours to do, and prepare your heart to listen to his Word.
exp.6:60:
This verse mentions a group of people who returned from exile from places in Babylon called Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer. When they arrived, they could not prove with documents or records that their families belonged to Israel.

Nehemiah copied a list of those who returned to Judah after the exile. He was organizing the people and rebuilding the life of the community. Family records mattered for inheriting the land and for service in the temple. For that reason, those who had no proof were left in doubt, although the Bible does not say that they were false.

Today we can remember that our security before God does not depend on papers or on a good record. In Christ, God welcomes those who trust in him. We can approach him with humility and gratitude, and also treat others with the same grace.
exp.5:13:
Nehemiah asks God not to forget what Tobiah and Sanballat, his enemies, have done. He also mentions Noadiah, a prophetess, and the other prophets who wanted to frighten him.

Nehemiah speaks while he is rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem. His enemies tried to stop the work with threats and deception, and they even paid false prophets to scare him and lead him into sin. Nehemiah did not take revenge on his own; he left the matter in God's hands. Soon afterward the wall was finished.

When someone tries to intimidate you into giving up what is right, do not respond with revenge. Pray, hand the situation over to God, and stay steady in your work. He sees what others do and knows how to care for you.
exp.2:21:
After him the priests repaired the wall, the men who lived in the surrounding area. The phrase "the men of the plain" indicates that these were men who lived in the region around Jerusalem, not inside the city. The word "repaired" means that they fixed and rebuilt that section of the wall.

Nehemiah, who writes in the first person for much of the book, recounts how the work on the wall of Jerusalem was divided after the exile. Each group and family received a section. This passage mentions priests alongside the house of the high priest Eliashib. Some scholars think that "the plain" refers to the Jordan Valley or the nearby rural area, but the text does not specify this.

For today: God uses everyone, regardless of their position or where they come from. Look for the place where you can serve in your church or community, even if your part seems small. Every section counts toward the whole work.
exp.6:54:
This verse names three families: the children of Barkos, of Sisera, and of Tamah. They are part of a longer list of the Nethinim, that is, people set apart to serve in the temple. Here "the children of" means descendants or members of a family.

Nehemiah writes this record of the families who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem. He found this book of genealogies and included it to show who returned and how the people organized themselves to rebuild their life. About these names we know almost nothing more; the Bible mentions them only here and in Ezra 2.

Today it reminds us that God knows and values every person, even those who go unnoticed. Humble service, done faithfully in the church or in the family, is not forgotten by God. Today you can thank someone who serves quietly.
exp.6:61:
This verse names three families: the descendants of Delaiah, of Tobiah, and of Nekoda, who together numbered 642 people. "Children of" means descendants. They were people who had returned to Judah after the exile in Babylon.

Nehemiah is copying the list of those who first returned. These families came from towns in Babylon, but they could not prove with documents that they were of Israel. Ezra 2:60 has the same list with a different figure, 652, and it is not known with certainty why the numbers differ.

Today we can remember that God knows each person, even when no one else remembers their story. Our place with Him does not depend on papers or family names, but on His grace. And in the church, let us respectfully value those who go unnoticed.
exp.7:1:
This verse tells how the priest Ezra brought the law of Moses before the whole assembly: men, women, and all who were able to understand what was being read. It was on the first day of the seventh month.

It is part of Nehemiah's account, after the wall of Jerusalem had been rebuilt. The people themselves asked Ezra to bring the book. That seventh month was special in the law of Moses, since it included a feast of trumpets (Leviticus 23:24). The text does not say more about why that day was chosen, so it is best not to claim more than it says.

For today: come to the Bible with hunger and attention, as those people did. Set a fixed time to read it, with your family or your church, and ask God to help you understand it and put it into practice.
exp.11:3:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions Iddo, Ginnetho, and Abijah, who were heads of priestly families. In this older version, some names sound different from other Bibles; for example, "Ginnetho" appears in other translations as Ginnethon or Ginnetoi.

Nehemiah 12 lists the priests and Levites who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. No one speaks here; the author, whom tradition often associates with Nehemiah, simply leaves a record. It was kept to preserve the order of service in the temple and to remember who belonged to each family. About some of these names we know very little.

For today: God notices people, even those almost no one remembers. Your simple, steady service, though it goes unnoticed, has value before Him. Serve faithfully, without seeking applause.
exp.1:1:
Here King Artaxerxes notices that Nehemiah's face is sad, even though he does not appear to be sick. The king concludes that it is a sorrow of the heart, that is, a deep pain of the soul. Nehemiah says that he was very afraid, meaning he felt great fear.

Nehemiah was the king's cupbearer, the one who served him wine. He had just received news that Jerusalem lay in ruins and its people were suffering. Showing sadness before the king could be dangerous, which is why he was afraid. Even so, his grief was sincere, and he had been carrying it for months. After this moment, the king asks him what he wants, and Nehemiah prays before he answers.

Today, God can use the burdens we carry for others as the beginning of something new. You do not have to hide your pain before Him. Bring it to Him in prayer, and ask Him for courage to act when the opportunity comes, even when you feel afraid.
exp.3:5:
It says that the people kept building the wall of Jerusalem, and that the whole wall was joined together up to half its height. "Joined together" means the parts were brought together so that no gaps were left. The phrase about having a mind to work means that the people were willing and had the strength to labor.

This is related by Nehemiah, who was directing the rebuilding. Shortly before, Sanballat and Tobiah had mocked the Jews, and Nehemiah prayed to God asking for help. After praying, the people went back to the work. Soon more serious threats would come, as the following text shows.

For today: when others mock you or discourage you, pray and continue with what God has entrusted to you. Steady work, step by step, goes far, especially when it is done with a united heart.
exp.4:15:
Nehemiah says that he devoted himself fully to the work of rebuilding the wall. "I held firm to my share" means that he stayed committed and worked on his own portion. A "piece of land" is a property or plot of ground, and "servants" are his attendants or helpers. He bought no land, and all his helpers gathered there to work.

Nehemiah was the governor of Judah. For twelve years he did not collect the taxes and food supplies that were due to him. The governors before him had burdened the people with abuses. He wanted to relieve a people who were already weighed down, and he acted this way out of fear of God. Some understand that he did not buy land so as not to take advantage of the poverty of others.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we use our position, work, or influence to benefit ourselves or to serve others. A leader who fears God takes care of others, works alongside them, and does not seek to get rich at the expense of others.
exp.2:24:
This verse continues the list of those who repaired the wall of Jerusalem. Palal, son of Uzai, worked opposite the corner and the high tower that stood out from the king's upper house, beside the court of the guard. After him, Pedaiah, son of Parosh, repaired another section.

The narrator is Nehemiah, who tells how the people rebuilt the wall after the exile. Each family received a section, often near their own home. We do not know exactly where that tower was, and scholars debate it. What is clear is that the work was orderly and shared.

For today: God values simple, unremarkable work. Do faithfully the section that falls to you, without comparing yourself to others, and trust that your effort, joined with that of others, serves a greater purpose.
exp.8:22:
It says that God made the descendants of Israel grow until they were as numerous as the stars of the heaven. Then he brought them into the land he had promised to their forefathers. "Brought them in" is the sense of the verb, and "possess it" means taking it as an inheritance.

This passage is part of a long prayer of confession that the people make in the time of Nehemiah, after returning from exile. They review the history of Israel to acknowledge that God was faithful, even though they failed many times. Here they remember that God fulfilled what he promised to Abraham and to his descendants.

For today: when you doubt that God will do what he says, remember how he has been faithful before. Write down three things that he has done for you and thank him today.
exp.12:10:
Nehemiah confronts the officials, that is, the leaders or authorities of the people. He firmly asks them why the house of God had been neglected. Then he gathers the Levites who had left and returns them to their posts of service. "Set them in their place" means that he restored them to their work.

Nehemiah is speaking, the man who had returned to Jerusalem after being away and found that the people had stopped bringing their tithes. The Levites, without support, had gone off to work their fields so they could live. That is why the worship had been left abandoned, and the blame fell on the leaders.

For today: what God has entrusted to us calls for constant attention. If we neglect our church, our offering, or those who serve, the ministry suffers. Ask yourself which area of your commitment to God needs to return to its place.
exp.3:1:
This verse shows Sanballat mocking the Jews in front of his companions and the soldiers of Samaria. With several scornful questions, he says the Jews are weak and will not be able to finish the work. Where the explanation quotes "will they let them do it?", it means: are they going to let them finish? The phrase "will they sacrifice?" is hard to understand, and some believe it speaks of offering sacrifices when the work is complete. The "heaps of the rubbish" are the piles of burned stones and debris.

Sanballat was one of Nehemiah's opponents. The Jews were rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem, which had been destroyed years earlier. When he saw their progress, Sanballat became angry and used mockery to discourage them.

For today: when others mock what God has placed in your heart, do not let their words stop you. Do as Nehemiah did: pray and keep working in faith.
exp.6:45:
It says that, within the list of those who returned from exile, the Nethinims appear. They were helpers of the temple, assigned to service tasks for the priests and Levites. Three families are named here: the children of Ziha, of Hashupha, and of Tabbaoth. The word "Nethinims" comes from a Hebrew term meaning those given over to the service of the temple.

Nehemiah is recording the list of the families who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel, years earlier. He found it and used it to organize the people. The Nethinims come after the singers and gatekeepers, and before the servants of Solomon. Their exact origin is not entirely clear, but their service was well known.

God takes into account those who serve in less visible places. Their names were written down. Today, if you help in simple tasks at your church, keep doing it with joy: God sees and values your service.
exp.9:27:
This verse says that all the rest of the people joined the commitment: priests, Levites (the temple helpers), gatekeepers, singers, and Nethinims (temple servants). Also joining were those who had separated themselves from the neighboring peoples to follow God's law, along with their wives, sons, and daughters, and everyone who could understand and reason. The phrase "understanding" refers to those who were old enough to grasp what they were promising.

Nehemiah tells how, after the reading of the law and the confession of sins, the leaders signed a covenant. Now the rest of the people accept it with an oath. They want to return to God and avoid the mistakes that led them into exile.

Today, following God is not only a matter for leaders. It is a decision made with understanding, within the family, and in the community. We might ask ourselves: what specific commitment to God do I need to renew, and who can walk with me in it?
exp.7:14:
This verse tells that an order was given to announce to all the people, with a public proclamation in all the cities and in Jerusalem. They were to go up to the mountain and bring back branches of olive, pine, myrtle (a shrub with fragrant leaves), palm, and other leafy trees, to build booths, that is, simple shelters made of branches. The phrase "proclaim in all their cities" means to make an announcement out loud.

Ezra and the leaders were reading the law of Moses and discovered the command to live in booths during the feast of the seventh month. The people had returned from exile, and the Scripture says that for a long time they had not celebrated this feast in this way. The leaders passed on the order.

For today: when you read the Bible, do not stop at understanding it; take a concrete step of obedience. This people heard, acted, and lived a great joy.
exp.9:23:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions three leaders of the people: Lohes, Pilha and Sobec. They were heads of families who signed a commitment before God. We are told nothing more about them, so we do not know details of their lives.

Nehemiah 10 follows the great prayer of confession in chapter 9. After acknowledging their sins, the people of Israel made a written covenant to obey the law of God. Nehemiah, the priests, the Levites and the leaders of the people signed first. The text does not explain why each name appears, but it shows that the commitment was public and personal.

God values every person, even those whom almost no one remembers. Today we too can commit ourselves to Him in concrete ways: perhaps by praying every day, serving in the church or being honest at work. A simple commitment, made with sincerity, has value before God.
exp.8:8:
This verse says that God saw the suffering of Israel's ancestors when they were slaves in Egypt, and that he heard their cry for help by the sea. "Affliction" means pain and oppression. The sea is named in the verse as the Red Sea, though some scholars think the Hebrew text speaks of a "Sea of Reeds," and this is debated.

The Levites are praying aloud, in a ceremony of confession for the people, after returning from exile and rebuilding Jerusalem. They recall the history from Abraham onward to praise God for his faithfulness, and to acknowledge that he always kept his word, even when the people failed.

God is not indifferent to your pain. When you feel that no one is listening, pray with sincerity, for he sees and hears. Remembering how he helped you before can give you hope today.
exp.6:30:
This verse says that 122 men of Michmash returned from exile in Babylon. "Men" here refers to heads of families or citizens of that town, and the word "men" in the verse above is the one that captures this. Michmash was a village in the tribe of Benjamin, north of Jerusalem.

Nehemiah copies a list of the families who went back to Judah with Zerubbabel years earlier. Nehemiah is the one telling the story, and he reviews the list in order to organize the people and repopulate Jerusalem, now that its walls had been rebuilt. This list also appears in Ezra 2, with small differences that scholars explain in various ways.

For today: God forgets no one. Here is a small town with only 122 men, and yet it was recorded. Your simple and quiet service also has value before God. Do your part faithfully today, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.12:27:
It says that a grandson of the high priest Eliashib, son of Joiada, had married the daughter of Sanballat the Horonite. When Nehemiah saw this, he drove him away from himself.

Nehemiah, governor of Jerusalem, speaks here during his second stay there. He was concerned that the family of the high priest was joining itself with Sanballat, an opponent of God's people. A priest was expected to guard the faithfulness of the covenant. Some scholars believe Nehemiah acted with such firmness because the alliance could influence the whole community. The text gives no further details about what happened to this man afterward.

For today: those who lead others must guard their alliances and decisions, since their example carries great weight. Let us ask God for wisdom in choosing with whom we join ourselves in what matters most, and for courage to correct with firmness and with love.
exp.11:13:
The verse continues a list of priests. It says that from the priestly family of Melicu, the head was Jonathan, and from the family of Shebaniah, the head was Joseph. These are the names of family leaders, called "heads" in the text.

This passage records the heads of the priestly families in the days of Joiakim, the chief priest after the return from exile. The book of Nehemiah is traditionally attributed to Nehemiah, though some think other hands added lists like this one. The purpose seems to be to preserve the order of service in the temple and to remember who served God in that generation.

For today: God values those who serve faithfully, even when almost no one remembers them. Serve God steadily in what is yours to do, without seeking applause. He knows your name and your effort.
exp.9:20:
The explanation says that Meshezabeel, Zadok, and Jaddua are three more names in a list of leaders of the people. They were real people who signed a commitment before God. The names are written in this version's older spelling, and not much is known about each one outside this list.

Nehemiah and the people of Israel had just returned from exile and rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem. After hearing the law of God, the leaders sealed a covenant: they committed themselves to obey the law, not to marry neighboring peoples who worshiped other gods, to keep the Sabbath, and to support the temple. The passage is a list of those who put their names to that covenant.

God values people who commit themselves to Him, even though almost no one remembers them. You can make a concrete decision of obedience today, such as praying every day or being honest at work, and keep it faithfully even when no one notices.
exp.11:11:
This verse begins a list of the priests who were heads of families in the days of the high priest Joiakim. Each name with "of" refers to a priestly house: for example, Meraiah was the head of the family of Seraiah, and Hananiah, of the family of Jeremiah. "Fathers" in the verse means the leaders or heads of each clan, and "begat" in the verse is "was the father of".

Here no particular person speaks; it is the record of the book of Nehemiah. After the return from exile in Babylon, the people took great care of the records of priests and Levites so that worship in the temple would stay in order. Many of these names appear only here, so we know little about them.

For today: God remembers names that the world forgets. Serve faithfully in what is given to you, even when it is little seen; God sees it and values it.
exp.1:9:
This verse tells how Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant heard that Nehemiah had arrived. It greatly displeased them that someone had come to seek the welfare of the people of Israel. The phrase about seeking the good of others means working to help and benefit them.

The one telling the story is Nehemiah, cupbearer to the king of Persia. He had just received the king's permission and letters to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem. Sanballat and Tobiah were leaders of neighboring peoples. The texts do not explain their motives in detail, but later it becomes clear that they oppose the project, perhaps out of fear of losing their influence.

For today: when you do something good for others, someone may be bothered by it. Do not lose heart. Pray, act with wisdom, and keep going, trusting that God sustains what He Himself has placed in your heart.
exp.3:8:
This verse says that the people prayed to God and, at the same time, posted guards to protect themselves from their enemies. Those are the sentences that explain the wording, so they are rewritten or omitted as needed: the guards were watchmen posted to keep careful lookout, and the verse's phrase "because of them" refers to the threat those enemies posed.

Nehemiah, who was leading the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem, is the one speaking. Sanballat, Tobiah and other neighboring peoples became angry when they saw the work moving forward, and they planned to attack the city. Nehemiah tells how the people responded: they did not stop at complaining or at action alone, but did both.

For today: when you face a problem, pray sincerely and also do what is within your reach with wisdom. Prayer does not replace responsibility, and responsibility does not replace trust in God. Ask Him for guidance, and then take the practical steps that fit the situation.
exp.10:34:
This verse names three places where people from the tribe of Benjamin lived: Lod, Ono, and "the valley of craftsmen." Craftsmen means artisans, people who worked with their hands making objects and tools. The exact location of the valley is not certain.

The book of Nehemiah presents a list of who settled in Jerusalem and in other towns after the return from exile. It is thought that Nehemiah, or whoever gathered his writings, used official records. The purpose was to show that the land was being populated again and that each family had its place.

For today: God pays attention to the everyday, even to manual work and to small places. You can offer your trade with dedication, trusting that what you do where you live also serves his purpose.
exp.1:6:
Nehemiah asks the king for official letters addressed to the governors beyond the Euphrates River. Those letters would serve so that they would let him pass without trouble until he reached Judah. The phrase "If it please the king" means "if it pleases the king." "Let letters be given me" means "that they be handed over to me." "That they may convey me over" means "that they let me pass freely."

Nehemiah speaks as the cupbearer of King Artaxerxes. He had just received permission to go and rebuild Jerusalem. Now he thinks about the details of the journey, because it was long and he had to cross territories with authorities who were not always friendly. Later he himself acknowledges that the good hand of God was with him.

For today: praying and trusting God does not remove the responsibility to plan. Nehemiah asked for concrete help and thought about the obstacles. We can do the same: pray with faith and also prepare our steps well.
exp.7:13:
This verse says that, while the people were studying the law, they found a command that God had given through Moses. It ordered the Israelites to live in booths during the feast of the seventh month. The sacred feast is the festival the people were to keep, and the booths were simple shelters made of branches.

The narrator tells what happened after Ezra read the law to the people. On the next day, the heads of the families, the priests and the Levites gathered with Ezra to understand it better. There they discovered this command. According to Leviticus 23, the feast remembered how God cared for Israel when they left Egypt and lived in the wilderness.

For today: hearing the Word once is not enough; it is good to keep studying it with others and to obey it with joy. This week, read a Bible passage with a brother or friend, and ask one another: "What is God asking us to do?"
exp.8:6:
This verse says that God was the one who took the initiative with Abram. He chose him, brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans (an ancient city in Mesopotamia), and gave him the name Abraham.

The name Abraham is usually understood to mean "father of many nations," according to Genesis 17.

The levites speak during a great prayer of confession and praise, after the people returned from exile and heard the law. They begin by remembering that God is the Creator, and then they review the history of Israel. They start with Abraham, because that is where the covenant began that holds together the whole story they tell.

For today: our faith does not begin with our merits, but with God's call. If today you feel small or far from the place where you should be, remember that God still calls and guides. Thank him for seeking you first.
exp.2:19:
He says that Baruch, son of Zabbai, worked with great zeal to repair another section of the wall of Jerusalem. That section ran from the corner to the entrance of the house of Eliashib, the high priest. "Earnestly repaired" means he worked with great eagerness and determination. "High priest" is what we today call the chief priest.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, traditionally associated with Nehemiah. He is recording who rebuilt each part of the wall after the return from exile. The list is long: leaders, priests, and ordinary people all work, each in their own section. It is striking that, of all of them, only Baruch is singled out for his zeal.

For today: you do not need an important position to serve God. Do your part, even if it is small, with enthusiasm and from the heart. God sees your effort, and together with others, great works are accomplished.
exp.6:67:
This verse is part of a list of what the Jews who returned from exile in Babylon had. It says they brought seven hundred thirty and six horses and two hundred forty and five mules. Mules were pack animals, useful for transport and work.

Nehemiah reports that he found the record of the families who had returned to Jerusalem years earlier, with Zerubbabel. He copies it to identify the people and to reorganize them after rebuilding the wall. An almost identical list appears in Ezra 2, and some figures differ slightly. Scholars explain this in different ways, and there is no single certain answer.

For today: God pays attention to the concrete and the small. Not even the animals were forgotten in this account. Think about your resources, your time, and your abilities, even when they seem ordinary, and offer them with gratitude to serve others and God.
exp.5:18:
Nehemiah says that some nobles of Judah were speaking well of Tobiah in front of Nehemiah, praising his good deeds. They also kept reporting to Tobiah what Nehemiah was saying. Meanwhile, Tobiah kept sending letters to frighten him. The phrase "put me in fear" means to scare me or intimidate me.

Nehemiah is the one speaking, recounting his own memoir. He had just rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem despite the opposition of Tobiah, an enemy of the project. But Tobiah had family ties and alliances with important people in Judah. Because of this, Nehemiah was surrounded by pressures: praise for his adversary, information that was leaking out, and written threats.

For today: not everyone who speaks well of someone tells you the whole truth. Be careful with divided loyalties and with the information you share. When you are intimidated, do as Nehemiah did: keep doing your task and pray that God will strengthen you.
exp.9:32:
This verse says what the money the people promised to give each year would be used for. It was for the showbread (the twelve loaves placed before God in the sanctuary), for the continual grain offering and the continual burnt offering, for the Sabbaths, the new moons and the set feasts, and for the holy things, and for the sin offerings, which served to make atonement, that is, to cover the guilt of Israel. It was also for all the work of the house of God.

Nehemiah speaks together with the people who sealed a covenant after returning from exile. They wanted to obey God's law and not neglect the temple, as had happened before. They promised to give a third of a shekel each year.

For today: God deserves what comes first and what is constant, not what is left over. You might decide on a regular, planned gift for your church or for helping others, giving it with gratitude and not out of obligation.
exp.6:13:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that 760 descendants of Zaccai returned to Judah. "Children of" does not mean only direct sons and daughters, but the whole family or clan that came from one ancestor.

Nehemiah speaks in the first person. After rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem, God put it on his heart to gather the people and record the families. He found the list of those who had returned from exile in Babylon. They were written down to know who belonged to the community and to repopulate the city. This same record also appears in Ezra 2.

For today: God does not see anonymous numbers, but families with names. Although Zaccai is hardly mentioned anywhere else, he was recorded. You also count for God, even if your service is quiet. Do your part faithfully today, without seeking applause.
exp.5:3:
Nehemiah tells us that his enemies sent him the same message four times, inviting him to meet with them. And each of the four times he gave them the same answer. The word "á" is the old way of writing the preposition "a," and "por cuatro veces" means "four times in a row."

Nehemiah speaks while leading the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem. Sanballat and Geshem wanted to stop the work, and the invitation to come together in the plain of Ono hid a trap to harm him. He answers that he is doing a great work and cannot leave it.

For today: you do not need to change your answer every time someone insists that you drop what God has given you to do. If you are sure of your calling, you can respond with calm, with firmness, and with the same clarity, without giving in to the pressure.
exp.8:9:
It says that God performed signs and wonders against Pharaoh, against his servants, and against all the people of Egypt. He did so because he knew they had treated the Israelites with arrogance, that is, with pride and harshness. In this way God made a great name for himself, and that name is still remembered "como este día," that is, until today.

It is part of a prayer of confession by the people of Israel, in the time of Nehemiah, after returning from exile. They review their history: God promised the land to Abraham, saw the suffering of their ancestors in Egypt, and rescued them. Remembering this helped them recognize God's faithfulness and their own need to return to him.

For today: when you feel oppressed or without a way out, remember how God has acted before. Write down something he has done for you and give him thanks; that strengthens trust.
exp.5:16:
In this verse, while the wall of Jerusalem was being finished, several important leaders of Judah kept writing regularly to Tobiah. He would send them letters, and they would reply. The word "nobles" refers to people of high rank or influence, and the phrase "many letters" shows that the exchange was constant.

Nehemiah, the governor, is the one telling what happened. Tobiah was an opponent who had mocked the work and had tried to stop it. Even so, he had family ties with some families of Judah, and for that reason several people supported him. Nehemiah reports this to show that the threat did not come only from outside, but also from within the people.

For today: pressure does not always come from declared enemies; sometimes it comes from comfortable alliances with those who do not share what God has asked of us. It is worth asking ourselves which friendships or commitments are pulling us away from our task, and asking God for wisdom to stay firm without losing love.
exp.9:11:
They are Levites, that is, men from the tribe in charge of service in the temple. The Bible says nothing more about them in this passage.

The book records it as an official list. After hearing the law and confessing their sins, the people made a written agreement to obey God. Leaders, Levites and priests signed it with their seal. These names show that each one took on the commitment personally and publicly.

For today: God values those who serve without being famous. Today you can commit yourself to Him in a concrete way. Choose one single decision of obedience, such as praying every day or serving in your church, and carry it out faithfully.
exp.6:70:
Here it says that some of the heads of families gave to the treasury of the work 20,000 drams of gold and 2,200 pounds of silver. The "pounds" were an ancient measure of weight (minas in Hebrew), and the "drams" were gold coins. Their exact value is uncertain.

This is part of the list of those who returned from exile, recorded in the time of Nehemiah. The gifts are noted to show how the people supported the rebuilding and the service of the Lord. A similar list in Ezra 2 has somewhat different figures, and there are several possible explanations.

For today: God's work moves forward when each person contributes according to what they have. The leaders set the example, and everyone else takes part too. Ask yourself what you can give joyfully: money, time, or talents.
exp.10:7:
After him, Gabbai and Sallai, two other men of the tribe of Benjamin, also settled in Jerusalem. Together with their families or their people they add up to nine hundred twenty-eight. The phrase "after him" means "after him," and the wording about settling means "lived." The text is very brief and says nothing more about these two men.

This chapter is a list recording who went to live in Jerusalem after the return from exile. The city had many rebuilt walls, but few inhabitants. So lots were cast so that one out of every ten families would move there (Nehemiah 11:1). The author notes the names and the numbers carefully. Some scholars think the numbers count the men, others that they count all the people of each family; the text does not make this clear.

For today: God notices ordinary people, even those almost no one remembers. Your humble and steady service, such as moving to a difficult place or supporting your church, does not go unnoticed by Him.
exp.0:4:
Nehemiah begins his prayer by speaking to God with reverence. He calls him "God of heaven," strong, great, and "terrible," which here means worthy of awe and reverence, not cruel. He says that God keeps covenant and mercy with those who love him and obey his commandments. A "covenant" is the solemn promise God made with his people.

Nehemiah speaks as the king's cupbearer in Persia, living in exile. He has just heard that the survivors in Jerusalem are living in distress and that the city's walls lie in ruins. He sits down, weeps, fasts, and prays. Before asking for anything, he remembers who God is and that he is faithful to his word.

For today: when you face a big problem, before asking, pause to remember what God is like and what he has promised. This calms the heart and strengthens confidence to pray with humility and hope.
exp.8:35:
This verse says that the people today live as servants, that is, under the control of others, right in the land that God had given to their ancestors. That land was meant to provide them with food and well-being. The words "Behold, we are" are the same as "here we are," and "its fruit and its good" refers to their harvests and their blessings.

The speakers are the Levites, in a prayer of confession that the people make in the days of Nehemiah, after returning from exile. They remember God's goodness and acknowledge that their leaders and their fathers did not obey his law. They are still under the rule of the Persian empire, and they feel great distress.

For today: when we go through difficulties, we can be honest with God, acknowledge our failures without blaming others, and return to him with humility. A sincere confession opens the way to a renewed commitment.
exp.11:17:
This verse is part of a list of priestly families. It names two priestly houses and the head of each: in the house of Bilgah, the head was Shammua; in the house of Shemaiah, it was Jehonathan.

The book of Nehemiah records here the names of the heads of the priestly families in the days of the high priest Joiakim, after the return from exile. Tradition attributes much of the book to Nehemiah, although some scholars think the list was completed later. Its purpose was to keep a record of who served in the temple and to maintain order in worship.

For today: God values those who serve quietly, even though almost no one remembers their name. Faithfully do your service in your church or family, without seeking applause. God sees it and remembers it.
exp.6:14:
This verse is part of a list of Jewish families. It says that from the family of Binnui, six hundred forty-eight people returned. "The children of" here means descendants or members of that family, not only direct sons.

Nehemiah reports that he found the record of the first exiles who came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel. He writes it down to organize the people, to repopulate Jerusalem now rebuilt, and to confirm who belonged to the people. In Ezra 2:10 the name appears as Bani with 642, and it is not known for certain why the name and the number differ. It may have been another form of the name, or a record from a different time.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless crowd, but as families and persons with names. Remember that your service, even when it is simple and little seen, matters to God and to his work.
exp.1:15:
The verse says that the city's leaders did not know where Nehemiah had gone at night, or what he was doing. The word "rulers" here refers to the city's officials. The "nobles" were the important families. Nehemiah had not yet told his plan to anyone: not to the Jews, not to the priests, and not to those who would do the work.

Nehemiah speaks in the first person. He had been the cupbearer of the king of Persia, and he arrived in Jerusalem with permission to rebuild its walls. First he secretly inspected the damage, and then he presented the plan to everyone.
