For today: before announcing an important project, it is wise to pray, to observe the situation carefully, and to prepare. That way, when we speak, we do so with clarity, with prudence, and with confidence that God is guiding us.
exp.5:6:
This verse is part of the letter that Sanballat sends to Nehemiah. He accuses him of having appointed prophets in Jerusalem to proclaim him as king over Judah. Then he threatens: these reports will reach the king of Persia, so let us take counsel together.

Nehemiah was rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem, and his enemies wanted to stop him. Since they could not prevail by force, they used rumors and fear. This is the fifth time they insist, and this time they send an open letter so that everyone can read it. Nehemiah answers that everything is their own invention (v. 8).

For today: when people falsely accuse you or try to frighten you into giving up what God has entrusted to you, do not get distracted by endless arguing. Respond with the truth and pray as Nehemiah did, asking God to strengthen your hands.
exp.4:4:
Here the people say that they are the same as the other Jews: the same flesh, the same children. Even so, because of debts, they have had to hand over their sons and daughters as servants. The phrase about being brought into bondage means being forced to work as slaves. The point that they have no power to redeem them means they have neither the means nor the money to buy them back, because their lands and vineyards already belong to others.

These are poor Jews who had returned from exile and were rebuilding Jerusalem with Nehemiah. There was famine, taxes owed to the king, and debts. Some of their wealthier brothers were lending to them at usury, that is, charging abusive interest. That is why they cried out, and Nehemiah became angry when he heard them.

God cares about the pain of those who suffer, and he expects us not to take advantage of the need of others to gain more. Today we can ask ourselves: do I help someone who is under pressure, or do I profit from their situation?
exp.11:37:
This verse tells us that there were two groups of singers, called choirs, who walked in opposite directions on the wall of Jerusalem. The second choir went toward the side opposite the first. Nehemiah followed them, together with half of the people, and they walked the wall from the Tower of the Furnaces to the Broad Wall.

The one speaking is Nehemiah, who tells what he himself experienced. The wall had already been rebuilt, and the people dedicated it to God with praise, music and thanksgiving. The two choirs marched in opposite directions and then met in the house of God. The exact locations along the route are not known with certainty.

For today: thank God for what he has done in our lives, and do it together with others. Even though each of us may take a different path in our service, we can all end up together worshiping him.
exp.8:2:
The verse tells that the people stood in their place and listened to the reading of the book of the law of God for a fourth part of the day, about three hours. Then they spent another fourth part of the day confessing their sins and worshiping the Lord. "Jehovah" is the name of God, and "worshiped" means that they bowed down and gave honor to him.

The account speaks of the Israelites who had returned from exile. They gathered in fasting, dressed in sackcloth and with dust on their heads, signs of humility and mourning. They had already separated themselves from foreigners, and they confessed their own sins and those of their fathers. The text does not say who wrote the passage, but the book is traditionally associated with Nehemiah.

For today: give time to the Word of God and then respond with sincerity. Read a passage calmly, ask God to show you what needs correcting, confess it honestly, and finish by giving him thanks and praise.
exp.5:14:
This verse says that the wall of Jerusalem was finished on the twenty-fifth day of the month of Elul, after fifty-two days of work. "Was finished" is the meaning here. Elul is the sixth month of the Hebrew calendar, which roughly corresponds to August and September.

Nehemiah is the one speaking, telling what he lived through. He had returned to Jerusalem to rebuild its walls. Enemies such as Tobiah and Sanballat threatened him and tried to frighten him with deceptions so that he would abandon the work or act wrongly. Even so, the people kept working. Then the enemies understood that God was with them.

For today: when there is opposition, fear, or pressure, do not abandon what God has placed in your hands. Keep going with prayer, perseverance, and one step at a time, trusting that God sustains your effort.
exp.10:9:
This verse begins the list of the priests who went to live in Jerusalem. It names Jedaiah, son of Joiarib, and Jachin. These are names of people, although some scholars think they might also refer to priestly families. That cannot be known for certain.

The book of Nehemiah tells that, after the wall was rebuilt, Jerusalem had few inhabitants. So lots were cast so that one out of every ten families would move into the city. The author carefully records who did so: first other groups, and now the priests, who served in the temple.

For today: God notices the service that seems small and quiet. Even if your name appears only in a list, those people sustained the life of the city. Serve faithfully where you are, even when no one applauds; God sees it and remembers it.
exp.9:6:
This verse is part of a list of names. Meshullam, Abijah and Mijamin are three men who signed, along with others, a covenant with God. According to verse 8, all of them were priests. These are little-known Hebrew names, and the Bible gives us no further details about each one.

Nehemiah and the leaders of the people had just returned from exile in Babylon. After hearing the Law read and confessing their sins, they made a written pact to obey God. The priests signed with their names, as a public witness that they were personally committed. Some of these names match priestly families mentioned in other lists, although nothing more can be asserted.

God knows each person by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. Your everyday faithfulness also counts. Think of one concrete commitment to God, such as praying every day or serving in your church, and keep it with steadiness.
exp.6:62:
Explanation says that three families of priests, the children of Habaiah, of Koz, and of Barzillai, could not prove their priestly descent. Of Barzillai it is said that he married a daughter of Barzillai the Gileadite and took the name of his father-in-law.

The account records the list of those who returned from exile in Babylon. To serve as a priest one had to prove one's lineage with a written record. These men searched for theirs and did not find it, so they were set apart from the priesthood for the time being. The Tirshatha, who was the governor, forbade them to eat of the most holy things until a priest arose who could consult with the Urim and Thummim. We do not know for certain how those objects were used.

For today: God cares for order and faithfulness in his service. We can examine our lives and ask whether our service rests on humility and truth, not only on the name we carry.
exp.1:2:
Nehemiah greets the king with respect: "Let the king live for ever" was a polite formula of courtesy. Then he explains why he is sad: Jerusalem, where his ancestors are buried, still lies in ruins. "Waste" means abandoned and destroyed, and "consumed with fire" means burned.

Nehemiah was the king's cupbearer, Artaxerxes' trusted servant who tasted the king's wine. He was a Jew and lived far from his homeland. He had received news that Jerusalem was in ruins, and this grieved him deeply. That is why the king noticed his sadness, and Nehemiah felt fear, since showing grief before the king could be dangerous.

For today: do not hide the pains that God has placed in your heart. Bring them before him with respect, sincerity and prayer, and trust that God can open a door for you to act.
exp.2:5:
This verse tells that Jehoiada and Meshullam repaired the Old Gate of Jerusalem. They put beams on it, set the doors in place, and fitted it with locks and bars, that is, the fastenings that let it be closed securely. Some believe the gate was called "Old" because of its age, though this is not known for certain.

Here the narrator of the book, who is Nehemiah or is based on his memory, speaks. After the exile, the walls of Jerusalem still lay in ruins. Nehemiah organized the people to rebuild them, and this chapter lists who worked on each section. It is like a roll of honor, with the names of ordinary people from different families and trades.

For today: God values the faithful work of each person, even when it is small and little seen. Your part in the church, in your family, or in your community matters. Do your section well, with steadiness, alongside others.
exp.0:8:
God promises that if his people return to him, obey his commandments and put them into practice, he will gather them together, even if they are scattered in the farthest place. The explanation of "cast out" (the expulsion or exile) and of "the uttermost part of the heaven" (the farthest end of the earth) is omitted here since those words do appear in the verse as shown. God would bring them to the place where he had chosen to have his name dwell, that is, Jerusalem and its temple.

Nehemiah, the king's cupbearer in Persia, prays when he learns that Jerusalem lies in ruins. He confesses the sins of the people and reminds God of the words he spoke to Moses. Nehemiah relies on that promise of restoration.

For today: if you have moved away from God, do not think you are too far away. Return to him sincerely, and begin by obeying in one concrete matter today. He still welcomes whoever comes back.
exp.6:11:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that the descendants of Elam, an ancient ancestor or clan leader, numbered one thousand two hundred fifty and four people who returned to Judah.

Nehemiah copies here the record of the families who came back from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel, years earlier. He found it written down when he wanted to organize the people and resettle Jerusalem. It is almost identical to the list in Ezra 2, although some of the numbers differ a little, and scholars explain this in several ways, with no single answer that is certain. The list shows that the people remembered their history and their identity.

For today: God does not see His people as a faceless mass. Every family, and every person, counts for Him. Also value your place in the community of faith, even when your service seems small or hardly visible.
exp.10:25:
This verse is part of a list of towns in southern Judah where some families settled after the exile. It names three places: Jeshua, Moladah, and Beth-phelet. The word "villages" refers to small settlements around a main city.

The book of Nehemiah tells how Jerusalem was rebuilt. Since few people wanted to live in the city, lots were cast so that one out of every ten families would move there (11:1). The others spread out to other towns. The author, traditionally associated with Nehemiah, records these names carefully, because each place was part of the restoration of the people. Little is known about these particular sites.

For today: God notices small places and little-known people. Your faithful work in a simple corner, whether your home, your church, or your neighborhood, also matters to Him and is part of what He is building.
exp.8:3:
This verse tells how a group of Levites stood up on a raised platform and from there cried out to God with a loud voice. "Cried out" here means to speak or pray with intensity, from the heart. Their names are listed, which shows they were real people with a specific task.

This happens after the people had gathered to fast, hear the law, and confess their sins. The Levites were responsible for teaching and leading worship. They lead the people in prayer, and what follows is a long prayer that recalls God's faithfulness and Israel's failures.

For today: when we recognize our wrongs, we do not stop at sadness. We can lift our voices to God with sincerity, and pray together with others, encouraging one another to return to Him.
exp.9:30:
The people of Nehemiah's day made two promises in this verse. First, if people from the surrounding nations brought goods or food to sell on the Sabbath or on another holy day, they would not buy anything from them. Second, every seventh year they would let the land rest and would forgive debts. The words "also" and "moreover" are the sense of the original connecting these promises, and "forgiveness" or "cancellation" means letting a debt go.

The people of Israel, now returned from exile and living in the time of Nehemiah, make a solemn oath to live according to the law given through Moses. Their leaders head the commitment. They wanted to avoid the mistakes that had once turned them away from God. The law spoke of weekly rest and of the seventh year (Exodus 23:10-11; Deuteronomy 15:1-2).

For today: think about which things in the marketplace and in the rush of life might take first place away from God. Choose one concrete habit of rest, generosity, or forgiveness, and practice it with consistency.
exp.9:25:
This verse continues a list of names. Ahijah, Hanan, and Anan are three leaders of the people who put their signature or seal on a document. They are proper names, and the Bible tells us nothing more about them in this passage. With the next verse, the list of leaders comes to an end.

Nehemiah describes how the people of Judah, now back from exile and with the walls of Jerusalem rebuilt, made a solemn covenant with God. After hearing the law and confessing their sins, the leaders sealed the commitment to obey what God had commanded through Moses. Then the rest of the people join in, and mention is made of those who had separated themselves from the customs of other peoples in order to follow God's law.

For today: God values commitments made with sincerity. Putting your name to something, that is, truly committing yourself, is a concrete step of obedience, even when no one else notices.
exp.11:12:
This verse is part of a list of priestly families. It says that in the days of the high priest Joiakim, Meshullam was the head of the priestly house descended from Ezra, and Jehohanan was the head of the house of Amariah. The phrase "heads of families" refers to the leaders of each group of priests. This priestly Ezra may be the name of a family, and not necessarily the scribe Ezra; scholars interpret it in different ways.

The author of the book records who served in the temple after the return from exile in Babylon. It is not a particular person who speaks, but the account keeps an orderly record. These lists show that the service of God continued from generation to generation, and that God cared for the worship of his people.

God knows and values each person who serves him, even if their name is almost never mentioned. Today you can serve faithfully in simple things, without seeking applause, trusting that God sees and remembers your work.
exp.9:35:
This verse says the people promised to bring to the house of God the firstborn of their sons, and the firstlings of their animals: the first young of their cattle and sheep. These would be given to the priests who served there.

Here the people of Israel are speaking after returning from exile in Babylon. Under the leadership of Nehemiah, they made a signed covenant to obey the law of Moses. They wanted worship in the temple not to be neglected. According to the law, the firstborn belonged to God; for sons, a ransom was paid in their place (Exodus 13:11-15).

For today: we can ask ourselves what we put first in our time and money. Giving God the first, and not what is left over, is a way of saying that we trust Him.
exp.11:8:
This verse mentions two more Levites, Bakbukiah and Unni, and says that they and their brothers were "over against them in the watches." That is, each had his place and his task in the service of the temple. "Watches" here means service, assigned work. The phrase is usually understood to mean that they stood opposite the other Levites, in turns or groups of service, although the Hebrew expression can be translated in several ways.

Nehemiah is not a speech but a written record. The author lists the priests and Levites who returned from exile with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. This list shows who cared for the worship of God and how the continuity of service in the restored temple was maintained. The names mattered because the people wanted to remember their lineage and their responsibility.

For today: God notices those who serve even when few know them. Do faithfully the task you have, in your church or in your family, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.12:9:
Nehemiah discovers that the Levites had not been given the portion that was due to them. Because of this, the Levites and the singers, who served in the temple, abandoned their work and went back to their fields.

Nehemiah, governor of Jerusalem, speaks here after returning from an absence. He finds that the people had neglected the temple. The Levites had lived on the tithes and offerings, so without them they had to look for their livelihood elsewhere. The service of God was left without attention.

For today: the work of the church and of those who serve in it needs the support of everyone. We can ask ourselves whether we are sustaining, with generosity and steadiness, those who dedicate their time to serving, so that the work of God is not left abandoned.
exp.11:27:
This verse says that the Levite singers gathered for the celebration of the wall. They came from the area around Jerusalem, the open land near the city, and also from the villages of Netophathi, a place near Bethlehem. The phrase "sons of the singers" means the members of the families devoted to music in the temple.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, describing how the dedication of the rebuilt wall under Nehemiah was celebrated. The singers lived in villages outside the city, so they had to be summoned to come and give praise to God. The text does not explain all the details of how they were organized.

For today: praise is best lived out in community. If God has given you a gift, whether singing, serving, or helping, offer it gladly when your church gathers, even if you have to make an effort to get there.
exp.10:12:
This verse continues a list of priests who lived in Jerusalem. It says that the relatives of Adaiah, heads of their families, numbered two hundred forty-two men. Then it presents Amashai, with his lineage: son of Azareel, of Ahasai, of Meshillemoth, and of Immer. The phrase "heads of the fathers' houses" means chiefs or heads of ancestral households.

Nehemiah 11 tells who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile. The city was sparsely populated, and some were chosen by lot to live there. The author, who according to tradition is Nehemiah or someone close to his work, records names and figures to keep a written account. In this way it is seen that the priests sustained the service of the temple.

For today: God pays attention to the service of people who sometimes seem unknown. Today you can serve faithfully in your church or family, even when no one applauds it.
exp.6:32:
The explanation says that 52 men from the other Nebo returned from exile to Judah. They are counted by their town of origin. "Men" means men, and the word "other" in the name shows that there was another place called Nebo, so this one is told apart from it. We do not know for certain where exactly this Nebo was.

Nehemiah tells us that he found the record of those who came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel, years earlier. After rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem, he wanted to resettle the city and arrange the people according to their families and places. That is why the list is so detailed: each group had a place among God's people, even if it was small.

For today: God does not overlook anyone, neither the small groups nor the little-known ones. Their names were written down. You can trust that your simple and quiet service also matters to God. Value and thank someone today who serves without being noticed.
exp.6:53:
This verse names three families: the children of Bazlith, of Mehida, and of Harsha. They belong to a list of the Nethinim, who were servants of the temple. "Children of" here means descendants of a family or clan.

The book of Nehemiah presents this record of those who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem. According to the account, Nehemiah finds this list and uses it to organize the people. The names are written down to confirm who belonged to each group and had their place in the community. About the exact origin of these clans we know no more than the names.

God does not overlook the humble. Although today these names may seem to us just a list, they were recorded because their service mattered. Today you can remember that your quiet work, without applause, also has value before God. Serve him faithfully wherever you are.
exp.9:26:
This verse names only three more men: Malluch, Harim, and Baanah. They are part of a long list of the people's leaders who signed, with their names, a solemn commitment before God. The names are not explained here, and this passage tells us nothing more about them.

Nehemiah 10 follows a great reading of the law and a prayer of confession (chapters 8 and 9). After acknowledging their failures, the Israelites who had returned from exile made a written covenant. The leaders sealed the document, and then the rest of the people joined in with an oath to obey the law given through Moses.

For today: when we commit ourselves to God, it helps to do so in a concrete way and in view of others. Writing down a decision, sharing it with trusted brothers and sisters, and asking them to walk alongside us can strengthen our steadiness in obeying God.
exp.2:22:
This verse tells that Benjamin and Hasub repaired the section of the wall that lay in front of their own houses. Afterward, Azariah, son of Maaseiah and grandson of Ananiah, repaired the stretch next to his own house. "Repaired" means they fixed or rebuilt it. "Over against their house" means right in front of where they lived.

This is not a character speaking in a speech. It is Nehemiah's account of the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem, set out as a list of those who worked. Nehemiah records name by name and section by section, so that it would be written down who took part. Many worked in the area near their own homes.

God uses the simple work of ordinary people. You may not be able to do something great, but you can care for and improve the place closest to you: your family, your home, your church, or your neighborhood. Do it faithfully, even when no one else notices.
exp.11:2:
This verse is part of a list of names: Shechaniah, Rehum and Meremoth. They are heads of families of priests and Levites who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel and the priest Jeshua. The explanation's note on the older spelling of the names is omitted here, since the reader's verse already gives them in their current form.

The one who wrote this is the author of the book, traditionally associated with Nehemiah, although some scholars think other hands added the lists. His purpose was to keep a record of who served in the temple and which families they came from. In this way it was shown that the worship of God had been restored in an orderly way, and that the people kept their history and their service.

For today: God notices people even when no one else remembers them. There are those who serve in silence, without applause, and their work has value before Him. Today you can serve faithfully in small things and be grateful to those who do.
exp.6:7:
This verse is part of a list and says that from the family of Parosh, two thousand one hundred and seventy-two people returned. The phrase "children of" here means descendants, that is, a clan or a large family. This list counts the men of the people.

Nehemiah copies the record of the families who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel and other leaders. He tells us that he found this book of genealogy and used it to organize who belonged to Jerusalem and Judah. The list also appears in Ezra 2, and some of the figures differ a little; it is not known for certain why, and there are several possible explanations, such as copying errors or censuses taken at different times.

God does not see the people as a faceless mass. Every family was remembered, and every person who returned to rebuild had a place. Today you can serve in small ways, even when no one applauds you, knowing that God knows you and values your part in his work.
exp.3:15:
This verse tells that, from that day on, the young men were divided into two groups. Half worked on rebuilding the wall, and the other half stood guard with spears, shields, bows and breastplates (armor for the chest). The servants are the young men, and the leaders were the chiefs who stood behind all the people of Judah to support them.

Nehemiah is the one telling the story. The Jews were rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem, but their enemies threatened to attack them. Nehemiah had encouraged the people not to be afraid and to remember that the Lord is great. Then he organized the work and the defense at the same time.

For today: trusting God does not remove our responsibility to be careful. We can keep on with our task while also looking after what God has entrusted to us, supporting one another with encouragement and unity.
exp.4:7:
Nehemiah reminds them that he and other Jews have bought back, as far as their means allowed, fellow Jews who had been sold to other nations. Then he asks them with grief: are you now selling your own brothers, so that we have to buy them back again? The words "I said" and "sell" in the older wording are simply the verse's "said" and "sell." "Held their peace" means they fell silent, with no answer.

Nehemiah, governor of Jerusalem, is speaking while the wall is being rebuilt. The poor were crying out because, through hunger and debt, they had mortgaged their fields and even handed over their sons and daughters as servants to other wealthy Jews who were charging interest. Nehemiah was angry and confronted the leaders. His argument is simple: what you are doing contradicts what we have done.

For today: let us examine whether our advantages, businesses, or loans help those in need or crush them. If we have taken advantage of someone's need, let us offer them a just and merciful way out.
exp.1:5:
The king responded to Nehemiah with interest: he wanted to know how long his journey would last and when he would return. The king accepted the idea of sending him, and Nehemiah gave him a specific date. The text mentions that the queen was sitting beside the king; it says nothing more about her.

Nehemiah was the king's cupbearer, serving in the palace in Persia, under King Artaxerxes. He had just learned that Jerusalem lay in ruins. Before answering the king, he briefly prayed to God. Now the king not only listens to him but asks practical questions, a sign that he took the request seriously.

For today: when you have a plan you believe comes from God, pray first and then prepare in an orderly way. Nehemiah trusted God, but he also thought about dates, permissions, and materials. Faith and good planning can go together.
exp.2:9:
It says that Jedaiah, son of Harumaph, repaired the section of the wall that was across from his own house. Beside him worked Hattush, son of Hashabniah. "Repaired" means to mend or rebuild, and "beside" means next to.

It is part of a list in the book of Nehemiah, which tells how the wall of Jerusalem was rebuilt after the return from exile. The account is written in the third person and remembers by name the families and people who did the work. Many repaired near their own homes, so each one had a specific task.

For today: God values faithful work in the place where we are. No glorious task is required; we can serve steadily in our home, neighborhood, or church, and work alongside others.
exp.11:24:
This verse names six Levites: Mattaniah, Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, and Akkub. They were gatekeepers, meaning watchmen who guarded the entrances and storerooms at the gates of the temple. The verse's wording of "keeping the ward" points to shifts of watch duty. The spelling of the names in the older text differs somewhat from how we see them today.

Here the speaker is not a character in the story; it is Nehemiah's account, which records lists of Levites and their duties. After the wall was rebuilt, the service of the temple was organized. This list appears alongside the list of singers and worshipers, showing that each role had its place. Scholars disagree about when the list was compiled, but its purpose is to keep an orderly record.

For today: God values quiet service, like watching over a door. If your task seems small or little noticed, do it faithfully, because in God's house every sincere service counts.
exp.6:52:
This verse names three more families: the children of Bakbuk, of Hakupha, and of Harhur. They are part of a long list of those called "temple servants," people dedicated to service in the temple. Here "children of" means descendants or clans, not only direct sons.

The book of Nehemiah presents a record of the families who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem. It is believed that Nehemiah found this census and copied it to organize the people after the walls were rebuilt. An almost identical list appears in Ezra 2:51. About the exact origin of these names, we know little, and scholars debate it.

For today: God remembers every name, even those that no one else remembers. Your simple and little-seen service also matters to Him. Today you can do your part faithfully, without seeking applause, trusting that God sees it and values it.
exp.3:3:
Here Nehemiah speaks to God with great candor. He tells God that his people are being despised and asks that the mockery of their enemies fall back on their own heads. The reproach is what is meant by the word "reproach" in the verse, and to give them as plunder means that they should be taken as spoil. "Captivity" is the exile.

Nehemiah and the Jews were rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem. Sanballat and Tobiah mocked them, saying that the work was weak and useless. Nehemiah does not answer with insults but brings his pain to God in prayer. It is a harsh prayer, and many understand it as a cry for justice rather than as a model of personal revenge.

When you are mocked or belittled for doing what is right, do not hold on to the wound. Lay it before God honestly, leave justice in His hands, and keep working, as the people did.
exp.8:16:
This verse says that the people refused to listen to God and did not remember the wonders he had done for them. "Stiff-necked" means stubborn, like someone who will not bow their neck. "Captain" means a leader or chief. In their rebellion, they decided to appoint a leader to take them back to Egypt, where they had been slaves. Even so, God is forgiving, compassionate, patient, and full of mercy, and he did not abandon them.

This prayer is spoken by the Levites in Jerusalem, after returning from exile, when the people gather to confess their sins. They recall the history of Israel in the wilderness: their disobedience and God's faithfulness.

For today: when it is hard for you to trust God, remember what he has already done in your life. And if you have failed, do not run away; return to him, for he is patient and forgives.
exp.11:35:
This verse names a group of Levites, brothers of Zechariah, who walked in procession with the musical instruments of David, whom it calls a man of God, meaning a man devoted to God. Going before everyone was Ezra the scribe, who was the expert teacher of the law of Moses.

Nehemiah tells in the first person about the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, now rebuilt. To celebrate it, he formed two great choirs that gave thanks to God and walked on the wall in opposite directions. Here the first group is described. Using David's instruments joined the praise of that moment with the worship of earlier generations.

For today: when God helps us finish something, it is worth stopping to give him thanks together with others. And praise is enriched when we remember the faith of those who came before us.
exp.5:10:
Nehemiah responds firmly: a man in his position should not run away or hide. He says he will not go into the temple to save his life.

Nehemiah is leading the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem, and his enemies want to frighten him. Shemaiah, perhaps paid by Tobiah and Sanballat, proposes that he hide in the temple on the pretext that they are out to kill him. Nehemiah was not a priest, so entering that part of the temple would have been against the law, and it would also have shown fear. He recognizes it as a trap.

For today: when someone gives you advice that seems prudent but pushes you to disobey God or to abandon what He has entrusted to you, stop and pray. Not every piece of advice with a religious tone comes from God. Ask Him for courage and wisdom.
exp.11:32:
This verse is part of a list of people who marched behind the first choir of thanksgiving. It names three men: Azariah, Ezra, and Meshullam. The explanation does not say exactly who they were; it only states that they were part of the group that followed Hoshaiah and half of the leaders of Judah.

Nehemiah speaks in the first person, recounting the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, now rebuilt. He organized two large choirs that walked on the wall in opposite directions, with songs, music, and gratitude to God. This Ezra could be the well-known priest and scribe, but the text does not make it clear, and some interpret him as another man with that name.

For today: God values every person who takes part, even those who appear only as names in a list. Serve where you are, without worrying about being seen; your presence and your gratitude count in God's work.
exp.9:16:
This verse is part of a list of names: Ater, Hizkijah, and Azzur. They are leaders of the people who sealed a covenant. There are no hard words here; they are simply names of people, and each one represents a family or household of Israel.

Chapter 10 of Nehemiah follows the great reading of the law and the people's prayer of confession. After returning from exile, the Israelites made a written commitment to obey God's law. The narrator lists the leaders who sealed it. Some names repeated here, such as Ater and Hizkijah, also appear in other lists, and it is not always known whether they refer to the same descendants. We cannot say that with certainty.

For today: God pays attention to people by name. When you commit yourself to Him, your decision matters and can encourage others. Put your name to your commitment: decide on one concrete act of obedience today and carry it out.
exp.6:27:
This verse is part of a list of families and towns. It says that 42 men from Beth-azmaveth returned from exile. "Men" here means adult men who were counted in the record. Beth-azmaveth was a town near Jerusalem, and in other passages it appears under the name Azmaveth.

The book of Nehemiah presents this record as the list of those who came back to Judah after the exile in Babylon. Nehemiah says that he found this list and copied it, while Jerusalem still had few inhabitants and had not yet been fully rebuilt. The list is very similar to the one in Ezra 2, although some details differ, and it is not known for certain why.

God pays attention to small towns and modest numbers. Forty-two people were recorded, and that reminds us that no contribution is insignificant in God's work. Today you can serve faithfully where you are, even if you are few or no one applauds you.
exp.6:55:
The text says that among the people who returned from exile in Babylon there were two families: the descendants of Neziah and those of Hatipha. They are part of a list of the temple servants. The word "children" here means descendants or clan, not only direct sons.

The book is narrated by Nehemiah. After rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem, he finds a record of the families who had come back with Zerubbabel. This list serves to order the community, to know who belonged to the people and who served in the temple. Nothing more is known about these two families; the Bible only preserves their names.

For today: God does not overlook ordinary people or those who serve in silence. Even if no one remembers your name, your faithful service has value before God. Serve with joy, without seeking applause.
exp.10:5:
This verse says that the descendants of Perez who settled in Jerusalem numbered 468 valiant men, or capable men. "Dwelt" means "lived," and "valiant men" can refer to men of courage, fit for service or defense. Perez was a son of Judah.

The book of Nehemiah presents a list of those who stayed to live in Jerusalem after the exile. The city had been rebuilt, but it had few inhabitants, so some were chosen by lot and others offered themselves willingly. The author, who according to tradition is Nehemiah or someone close to his work, records the names and numbers with care.

For today: God notices those who commit to sustaining his work, even when they are part of a long list. Your steady service in your church or community, though it may seem small, has value before him.
exp.9:9:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions five Levites: Shebaniah, Hodijah, Kelita, Pelaiah, and Hanan. They are called "brethren" of the Levites named before, that is, fellow workers in the same service in the temple. The Levites were the tribe responsible for helping in worship and teaching the law.

We are after the return from exile, when Jerusalem was being rebuilt. After the reading of the law and a prayer of confession (chapters 8 to 9), the people made a written covenant, and their leaders signed it. Nehemiah appears at the beginning of the list. These Levites committed themselves to obey God and to support the temple. About these people we know nothing more than their names.

God values those who serve without fame. These men are almost never remembered, yet their names were kept in Scripture. Today we can commit ourselves to God in simple and steady things: attending, helping, praying, and serving in the church, even when no one applauds us.
exp.6:36:
This verse is part of a list of families who returned from exile in Babylon. It says that the people of three neighboring towns, Lod, Hadid, and Ono, numbered seven hundred twenty-one persons. These towns are in the territory of Benjamin and the nearby area, and here they are counted together as one group.

Nehemiah tells that, after rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem, he found an old record of those who had come back with Zerubbabel. He wanted to gather the people by families and put the life of the city in order. This list also appears, with some differences in the numbers, in Ezra 2, and scholars explain those differences in several ways.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even those who appear only as a number. Think of a person in your church or community who goes unnoticed, and today greet them by name and thank them for their service.
exp.2:11:
It tells us that Shallum, son of Halohesh, repaired the section of the wall that followed the one before it. He was "ruler of the half part of Jerusalem," that is, a leader over half of a district. The word "repaired" means that he mended and rebuilt. What stands out is that he worked along with his daughters, who helped in the work.

Context: chapter 3 is a list of those who rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem, with Nehemiah as leader, after the return from exile. The narrator records the names to remember each person's labor. It is not known for certain whether the daughters laid stones or helped in some other way; the text does not make this clear, and it has been understood in several ways.

For today: no service is too small, and no one is unnecessary. An important leader worked alongside his family. Ask yourself what concrete task you can do in your church or community, and look for ways to include your family.
exp.2:13:
Malchiah, the leader of the district of Beth-haccerem, rebuilt the Dung Gate. The Dung Gate was the place where the city's rubbish was carried out. He also set up its doors, its locks, and its bars (the beams that secured the gate).

Nehemiah recounts how the people of Jerusalem and the nearby towns rebuilt the wall after the return from exile. Each group took charge of a section. This list shows that the work was done as a team, and that an important leader was given a gate that was unglamorous but necessary.

Today, God values faithful service, even when no one applauds it. There are hidden tasks, such as cleaning, organizing, or helping quietly, that sustain the life of a family or a church. Do well the part that is yours.
exp.1:11:
Nehemiah says that he got up at night with a few men. He did not tell anyone what God had put in his heart to do in Jerusalem. He took only the animal he was riding. The word "beast" refers to the animal used for riding, and "tell" here means to make known or to reveal what he had in mind.

The speaker is Nehemiah, cupbearer to the king of Persia, who came to Jerusalem to rebuild its walls. He had been there for three days. Sanballat and Tobiah had already become upset at his arrival. Because of this, he acted with discretion and went out at night to inspect the fallen walls before telling the people about the plan.

For today: when you sense that God places a burden or a project on your heart, do not rush to announce it. Pray, observe the situation calmly, and seek wisdom. Then share the plan with the right people, at the right time.
exp.10:24:
It says that, in addition to Jerusalem, some descendants of Judah settled in towns in the south, with their nearby villages and their fields. Kiriath-arba (the old name of Hebron), Dibon, and Jekabzeel are named. The sentence "Regarding" introduces this detail, and "villages" are small settlements that surrounded a city.

It is part of a list in Nehemiah 11 about who lived where after the return from exile in Babylon. The book's author tells the story, and the text indicates that lots were cast so that one in every ten families would live in Jerusalem, while the others returned to their lands. Resettling these places helped rebuild the life of the people. Some details of the list are interpreted in several ways.

God cares for small places and ordinary people. Your faithful work in your own place, even when it goes unnoticed, is also part of what God is building.
exp.0:7:
Nehemiah asks God to remember what He said to Moses: if the people disobeyed, they would be scattered among the nations. The word "transgress" in the verse means to break faith, to betray or to disobey on purpose.

Nehemiah speaks as the cupbearer of the king of Persia, who learns that Jerusalem lies in ruins. He prays with sorrow and confesses the sins of Israel, including his own and those of his family. He rests on the word of God: God warned of the punishment, but He also promised to restore those who returned to Him (verse 9).

For today: when you fail, do not hide or make excuses for yourself. Pray with sincerity, acknowledge your mistake, and rely on God's promises, for He forgives and restores those who come back to Him.
exp.12:7:
Nehemiah says that he was deeply grieved when he saw what was happening. So he took Tobiah's household goods and possessions and threw them out of the chamber. The word "goods" here does not mean jewels or valuables, but the furnishings and belongings of the house. The phrase "it grieved me" means that it caused him great sorrow.

Nehemiah speaks as the governor. He had returned to Jerusalem after being away, and he discovered that the priest Eliashib had given Tobiah, a man who had opposed God's people, a room within the temple courts. That space was meant to store the offerings. Nehemiah acted to restore the room to its purpose.

For today: when we discover that something occupies the place that belongs to God in our lives, it is not enough to lament it. It is wise to remove it and reorder our priorities with resolve and humility.
exp.12:20:
Nehemiah speaks firmly to the merchants who camped outside the wall of Jerusalem, waiting for the gates to open on the Sabbath. The phrase "I testified against them" means that he warned them and confronted them seriously. "If ye do so again, I will lay hands on you" means that he would have them detained and would take action against them. After that warning, they no longer came on the Sabbath.

The one speaking is Nehemiah, governor of Jerusalem. He had returned and found that people were trading on the Sabbath, neglecting the day of rest that God commanded Israel. He ordered the gates closed and posted guards. The merchants kept pressing, and then Nehemiah spoke plainly to protect the people's faithfulness.

For today: sometimes loving what is good requires setting clear limits, with firmness and without hatred. We can ask ourselves what habit or work pressure is robbing our lives of rest and time with God, and decide courageously on a concrete boundary.
exp.6:22:
The explanation says that the descendants of the family of Bezai who returned numbered three hundred twenty-four. It is part of a list of families, counted by their name and by the number of people. "Children of" here means descendants or members of a clan, not only direct sons.

Nehemiah, governor of Jerusalem, finds a record of those who came back from exile in Babylon. He writes it down after rebuilding the wall, when he wants to organize and repopulate the city. This list is very similar to the one in Ezra 2, although some figures and names vary a little. The reason is not known for certain; they could be differences from copying or from the date of the count.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless crowd. Even little-known families were recorded. You can rest in the knowledge that your life and your simple service, even when no one notices, are valuable to God.
exp.4:5:
Nehemiah tells how he became very angry when he heard the complaint of the people and their words. "I was very angry" means that he was deeply indignant. "Outcry" is a cry of pain or complaint over an injustice.

Nehemiah, governor of Judah, speaks while the wall of Jerusalem was being rebuilt. Some poor Jews, burdened with debt because of famine and the king's taxes, had been forced to give up their lands and even hand over their sons as servants. The wealthier ones, their own brothers, were charging them interest. His anger was not loss of control: he thought carefully before acting and then confronted the leaders.

For today: when we see an injustice, it is healthy to be indignant, but it is wise to stop and think, and then to act with courage and truth. Ask yourself whether there is someone you could relieve instead of taking advantage of their need.
exp.11:5:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions Shemaiah, Joiarib, and Jedaiah, heads of priestly families. These are men who returned from exile in Babylon together with Zerubbabel and the priest Jeshua. The word "princes" in the following verse means "heads" or "chiefs" of the priests.

Here no character is speaking in a discourse. This is the account of Nehemiah, who records the registers of the priests and Levites of that time. These lists showed that the service in the temple continued in order, from generation to generation, and that each family had its place. Some names appear in other lists with small variations, and scholars cannot always clear up every detail.

For today: God notices people who sometimes seem to be only names on a list. Your service, even when it is quiet, does not go unnoticed by Him. Serve Him faithfully, without seeking applause.
exp.11:16:
This verse is part of a list of heads of priestly families. It means: "Of the family of Abijah, the head was Zichri; of the family of Miniamin and of Moadiah, the head was Piltai." Some translations render this verse differently, because the Hebrew text is brief and the names can be understood in several ways.

The book of Nehemiah records who served as priests in the days of Joiakim, after the return from exile. It is not a speech but an official register. It served to remember who led worship in the temple and to keep order among God's people.

For today: God notices people who seem small or little known. Serve faithfully where you are, even when no one applauds; your name is not lost before God.
exp.6:23:
This verse says that 112 people from the family of Hariph returned from exile in Babylon. "Children of" here means descendants or members of the same clan. It is part of a list of families with their numbers.

Nehemiah records that, after the walls of Jerusalem were rebuilt, he found the register of those who had first returned. He wanted to repopulate the city and organize the people according to their families. In the parallel list in Ezra 2:18, a family called Jorah appears with the same number, 112. Many believe it is the same family under another name, although this is not certain.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass. Even little-known families were recorded. If you feel small or overlooked, remember that God knows you and values your place in his work.
exp.11:30:
Nehemiah says that he brought the leaders of Judah up onto the wall of Jerusalem. There he arranged two great companies who marched in procession, that is, in a solemn parade. One of them went to the right, along the wall, in the direction of the dung gate. This gate is the one for the garbage dump; the word "dung" refers to waste thrown out and left in a place.

Nehemiah speaks in the first person. The wall was already rebuilt, and now its dedication was being made with songs and thanks to God. Before this, priests and Levites had purified themselves, along with the people and the gates. Scholars are not entirely certain of the exact route, but the idea is clear: it was a public and orderly celebration.

For today: when God helps us finish something, let us not let it pass in silence. Let us take time to thank him, together with others if possible, and do it with order and joy.
exp.6:1:
Nehemiah says that he put two men in charge of Jerusalem: his brother Hanani and Hananiah, the commander of the fortress or palace. The phrase "palace official" means that he was in charge of the fortress beside the temple. The verse also gives the reason he chose Hananiah: he was a faithful and trustworthy man, and he feared God more than many others.

The speaker is Nehemiah, who had already finished rebuilding the wall. With the gates in place and the gatekeepers appointed, the city needed protection and order. Before giving instructions for guarding the gates, he chooses people he can trust. Some think that Hanani is the same man who brought him news from Jerusalem in chapter 1, but the text does not say so.

For today: when giving responsibilities, whether in the church, at work, or in the family, do not look only for ability. Look for people who are honest and who respect God. And try to be such a person yourself.
exp.7:12:
The day after the great reading of the law, the chief of the fathers of the people, together with the priests and the Levites, gathered before Ezra the scribe (the one who copied and studied the Scriptures). They wanted to understand the words of the law more fully. The heads of the families here are the chief men of the people.

The book tells us that the people had heard the law and rejoiced when they understood it. Now the leaders were not content with what they had heard the day before, but sought out Ezra to go deeper. That study led them to discover the command to keep the feast of tabernacles, which appears in the verses that follow.

For today: it is not enough to hear the Bible once; it is wise to return to it with humility and ask questions. Set aside time this week to study it with someone more experienced or with your family, and put into practice what you discover.
exp.10:31:
It says that some of the descendants of Benjamin lived in Anathoth, Nob and Ananiah. These are names of towns in the territory of Benjamin, north of Jerusalem. This list continues the one begun in the previous verse, and here it only names places.

Nehemiah records where the Israelites who returned from exile in Babylon settled. Jerusalem needed inhabitants, so some moved into the city and others went back to their hometowns, according to their tribe. He does not speak through a character; it is the account of the chronicler, who carefully notes the places as part of the restoration of the land.

For today: God pays attention to places and people that sometimes seem small. Your town, your neighborhood or your ordinary work matter to Him. Ask Him where He wants you to serve faithfully, even when no one else notices.
exp.1:7:
Nehemiah asks the king for a letter to Asaph, the keeper of the royal forest, so that Asaph will give him timber. He needs it for the gates of the fortress next to the temple, for the city wall, and for the house where he will live. The verse describes the king granting the request, and Nehemiah credits it to the good hand of God upon him.

Nehemiah served as cupbearer to King Artaxerxes. He had wept over Jerusalem, which still lay in ruins, and he asked for permission to go and rebuild it. Before he asked for help, he had already prayed. The exact details about Asaph are not known, only that he took care of the king's forest.

For today: plan carefully and ask boldly, but recognize that success comes from God. When you receive unexpected help, give thanks to Him, not only to the people who helped you.
exp.3:2:
Tobiah the Ammonite was standing beside Sanballat and mocked the Jews. He said that the stone wall they were building was so weak that if a fox climbed on top of it, it would break down.

Nehemiah and the people were rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem. Tobiah and Sanballat, who opposed them, did not want the city to rise again. First they grew angry, and then they turned to ridicule to discourage the workers. Nehemiah answered by praying to God, not by returning insults.

When someone mocks what you are doing with faith and effort, do not let their words define your work. Bring that hurt to God in prayer, as Nehemiah did, and keep going with what He has entrusted to you.
exp.6:58:
This verse continues a list of families who descended from the "servants of Solomon," people who worked in the service of the temple and the kingdom. Here four more groups are named: the children of Shephatiah, of Hattil, of Pochereth-hazzebaim, and of Amon. They are only family names, and of some of them not much more is known.

Nehemiah copies an official record of those who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem. The list was made so that it would be known who belonged to the community and what service fell to each one in the rebuilding. At the end it is said that together they added up to 392 people, among temple servants and descendants of the servants of Solomon.

For today: God does not overlook ordinary people. Many of these names do not appear in other stories, but they were written down. Your quiet work, done faithfully in your church or your family, also matters to God.
exp.3:19:
It says that when the people heard the sound of the trumpet, they were to run to that place and join the others.

It is Nehemiah who speaks, the leader who was overseeing the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem. The enemies threatened to attack, so the people worked with the sword at their belts. Because the wall was long and the workers were spread out, Nehemiah placed a trumpeter beside him to sound the alarm and gather everyone together.

For today: do not face difficulties alone. Stay close to your community of faith, so you can come to help when someone needs it. Work diligently, but trust that God is the one who sustains the work.
exp.11:23:
The explanation says that the chiefs of the Levites were Hashabiah, Sherebiah, and Jeshua, son of Kadmiel. Their companions stood across from them to praise and give thanks to God, following what David had commanded. The word "commandment" in the verse points to a rule or order, and the phrase "ward over against ward" means that they were organized into groups, each serving in its own turn.

This appears in a list from the book of Nehemiah, which tells of the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem. The narrator records who served in the temple and how they did it. The Levites were the tribe responsible for helping in worship. The mention of David reminds the reader that organized praise came from an ancient tradition in Israel.

For today: praise to God deserves order and steadiness, not just a passing mood. Think of a simple service you can do regularly in your church or family, and do it with gratitude, knowing that every turn matters.
exp.6:59:
This verse gives the total of two groups of temple helpers: the Nethinims and the children of Solomon's servants. Together they add up to three hundred ninety-two people. The word "Nethinims" refers to workers who served the priests and Levites in the house of God.

Nehemiah copies here the list of families who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem. He wants to show who came back and what task each one had in rebuilding the life of the people. Even the servants of humble work are included, and this shows that everyone was counted.

For today: God values simple and hidden service. Even when no one applauds you, your faithful work in the church, in the home, or in your community has a place in his work. Serve with joy, because God sees and remembers.
exp.10:21:
This verse says that Uzzi was the head or supervisor of the Levites who lived in Jerusalem. He came from a family of singers, the descendants of Asaph, and he was in charge of the work of the temple, here called the house of God.

Nehemiah 11 is part of the account of how Jerusalem was resettled after the return from exile. The city was almost empty, and lots were cast so that one out of every ten families would move there. The author, who follows the tradition of Nehemiah, records in detail who held each responsibility. In this way it shows that the worship of God was well organized.

For today: God values orderly and steady service, even the kind that almost no one sees. Ask yourself what simple task you can carry out faithfully in your church or community, without seeking recognition.
exp.6:31:
This verse is part of a list of families and towns that returned from exile in Babylon. It says that 123 men came from Bethel and Ai. "Men" simply means men, and here it refers to the heads of families or to those who were counted in the record. These are towns in the old territory of Benjamin and its surroundings.

Nehemiah himself explains that he found this record of those who first returned with Zerubbabel. He uses it to organize the community in Jerusalem, which was rebuilding its walls and its life. This figure appears a little differently in Ezra 2:28 (223), and it is not known with certainty why; there are several possible explanations.

For today: God does not see faceless crowds. Every person and every town, even the small ones, counts for Him. Ask yourself how you can value and serve today those who seem few or barely visible around you.
exp.8:24:
They took strong cities and a rich land, and came into houses full of all good things, cisterns already dug, vineyards, olive groves, and many fruit trees. The quoted words are rendered in the verse as "fat land" and "wells digged", and the sense is that the land was fertile and abundant, and that they had water stored and ready. They ate their fill, grew well-fed and prosperous, and took great delight in the great goodness of God.

The speakers are the Levites, who in a public prayer review the history of Israel. This takes place after the return from exile, when the people confess their sins. They remember God's generosity, but they immediately point out that, once they were comfortable, they rebelled against him.

For today: when God blesses us, it is easy to forget him. Take a moment to thank him for what you have, and ask him for a heart that keeps obeying him also in times of plenty.
exp.11:36:
This verse describes the route of one of the two groups that marched along the wall of Jerusalem. On reaching the Fountain Gate, they kept straight on and went up by the steps of the city of David, along the higher part of the wall, passing by the house of David as far as the Water Gate, toward the east. The word "stairs" here refers to steps.

The book is narrated by Nehemiah. The wall had already been rebuilt, and the people were dedicating it to God with songs, trumpets, and two great choirs walking in opposite directions. Ezra went at the head of this group. The detailed mention of places shows that it was a real and organized act of thanksgiving.

Today we can learn to thank God in concrete ways and together with others. It is not enough to feel gratitude; we can set aside time, gather with fellow believers, and celebrate what God has done in our lives.
exp.6:20:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that 98 people from the family of Ater, from the branch called "of Hezekiah," returned from exile. "Children of" means descendants or members of that family. "Ater of Hezekiah" probably distinguishes this group from others with the same name; it is not known for certain whether it refers to King Hezekiah.

Nehemiah, governor of Jerusalem, found a record of those who had returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel. He reviews it when the city already has walls but few people. The list, very similar to the one in Ezra 2, showed the origin of each family and its right to live in the land.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those who seem a small number. Your humble service, like that of those 98, counts in God's work. Today you can serve faithfully without seeking applause.
exp.11:10:
This verse continues a list of high priests. It says that Joiada had a son named Jonathan, and that Jonathan had a son named Jaddua. The word for "begat" here is an old one that means "was the father of" or "had as a son." In biblical lists, it can sometimes also refer to a more distant descendant.

Here the speaker is not a character; it is the author of the book, which tradition links to Nehemiah, though this is not entirely certain. He records the names of the priests and Levites who returned from exile, to show who served in the temple and that the priestly line was still standing. Jaddua appears at the end of this list, and that helps place the time when it was written.

For today: God pays attention to every person, even to names we barely know. Your faithfulness in everyday life also counts. Serve where you are, and pass your faith on to the next generation.
exp.6:47:
This verse continues a list of families called "nethinim." "Children of" means descendants or members of a family group. Three are named here: Lebana, Hagaba and Shalmai. The nethinim were servants devoted to the work of the temple. Of these families we know only the name.

The book records those who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem. Nehemiah says he found this list and includes it to organize the people, repopulate the city and protect the service of the temple. The same list appears in Ezra 2, with small differences in some names.

God does not forget those who serve in silence. These names barely appear in other passages, yet they were written down. Today you can serve in your church without seeking recognition, trusting that God sees and values what you do faithfully.
exp.12:13:
Nehemiah asks God to remember him for what he did. In other words: "God, do not forget the good I did for your house and for its service."

Nehemiah, governor of Jerusalem, speaks here. He had discovered that the temple was neglected and that the Levites were not receiving their support, so he reorganized the tithes and appointed trustworthy overseers. This prayer appears as a brief personal request in the middle of his work. Some read it as humble trust in God, and others notice a certain tone of complaint; the text does not make this clear.

For today: serve God faithfully and without seeking applause, trusting that he sees what no one else sees. You can offer your work to him in prayer with humility.
exp.3:9:
It says the people of Judah were exhausted. Those who carried heavy material and the heap of stones and dirt from the fallen walls are the ones described here. They were saying that the workers no longer had strength, that there was too much disorder, and that they could not keep building the wall.

The speakers are the inhabitants of Judah, the people who worked with Nehemiah rebuilding Jerusalem. They had already suffered mockery, and now their enemies were planning to attack them. Tiredness, the amount of work, and fear came together, and discouragement came to the surface. Even so, Nehemiah responded with prayer, vigilance, and organization.

When you are weary before a great task, do not hide it. Tell God about it, ask others for help, and take one step at a time. Resting, praying, and working as a team is also a way of obeying.
exp.12:17:
Nehemiah reminds the leaders of Judah that their ancestors also disregarded God's laws, and for that reason punishment came upon the nation and upon Jerusalem. He asks whether they want to increase that anger (God's righteous wrath) by desecrating the Sabbath, that is, treating as ordinary a day that God set apart as holy.

Nehemiah speaks as governor, after returning to Jerusalem. He found that some merchants from Tyre were selling fish and goods on the Sabbath, and that the leaders were allowing it. He corrects them by recalling the history of the exile, which many understand as a consequence of the people's disobedience.

For today: learn from the mistakes of the past. We can set aside time to rest and worship God, even when work or money press upon us.
exp.9:15:
This verse names three more leaders: Adonijah, Bigvai, and Adin. They are part of a list of the heads of the people, that is, leaders of families or clans. These are personal names, and the Bible says nothing more here about these individuals.

Nehemiah 10 speaks of a covenant, a signed promise. After the return from exile in Babylon and the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem, the people decided to commit themselves to obeying God's law. The leaders signed first, on behalf of everyone. Some scholars think these names may also be connected with families that returned from exile, as appears in other lists, though not everything here is certain.

For today: God values those who commit themselves to Him, even when they go almost unnoticed. That your name is written into a pledge of faithfulness, in your home, your church, or your work, matters more than it may seem.
exp.10:22:
This verse says there was a command from the king concerning the singers, and that a rule had been set so that they would have what they needed each day. Many scholars understand it to refer to the daily support of the singers, although the text gives no further detail. There is also doubt about whether the king is the Persian king or King David, who organized the singers in earlier times.

Nehemiah does not speak here as in a speech; rather, the account lists who lived in Jerusalem after the city was rebuilt. The Levites and the singers, descendants of Asaph, who served in the house of God, are mentioned. The author makes it clear that their service was orderly and well cared for.

For today: God values steady service, even the kind that almost no one sees. We can support those who serve in the church with order and generosity, so that they can do so with peace and joy.
exp.9:4:
This verse mentions only three names: Harim, Meremoth, and Obadiah. They are part of a list of leaders, in this case priests, who signed or sealed a covenant. The names are written in the spelling that appears in the King James Version, so they may look a little different from how we read them today.

The book of Nehemiah has no single speaker here; it is a record. After the rebuilding of the wall and hearing the reading of the Law, the people confessed their sins and made a written commitment (chapters 9–10). The leaders, Levites, and priests put their seal on it. Their names are recorded because their commitment was public and real. Some of these names also appear in other lists of priests, but we know no further details about these particular people.

For today: God values people who commit themselves to Him, even when they are little known. Think of one concrete promise of obedience you can take on, and keep it faithfully, without seeking recognition.
exp.8:19:
He says that God, in his goodness, gave his good Spirit to instruct Israel in the wilderness. He also kept giving them the manna, the bread that fell from heaven, and gave them water when they were thirsty. Instructing them means teaching them or guiding them, and never withholding it means that he never stopped giving it to them.

This is part of a prayer of confession in Nehemiah 9, spoken by the Levites before the people who had returned from exile. They recount Israel's history to acknowledge their sin, such as the golden calf, and at the same time God's faithfulness. Although the people failed, God did not abandon them. Some scholars see in the "good Spirit" a reference to his work with Moses and the elders; the text gives no further details.

For today: when you fail, do not run from God. Acknowledge your mistake, and remember that he still offers you guidance and what you need each day. Ask him to teach you and trust in his care.
exp.10:14:
This verse names a Levite called Shemaiah, son of Hashub, and traces his family line: Azrikam, Hashabiah and Bunni. In that time names and fathers served to identify each person and his place within the people. The Levites were the ones in charge of service in the temple.

The book of Nehemiah tells of life in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. Here the narrator makes a list of those who settled in the city, which had been left with few inhabitants. It seems that lots were cast so that one family in every ten would live there (11:1). Shemaiah appears as one of the Levites who accepted that commitment. The text says nothing more about him.

For today: God takes notice of people who serve faithfully, even when almost no one knows them. Your quiet work in the church, the family or the community does not go unnoticed by Him.
exp.9:8:
It says that some Levites signed or put their seal on the covenant: Jeshua son of Azaniah, Binnui of the family of Henadad, and Kadmiel. The Levites were the tribe responsible for helping in worship and teaching the law. This is a list of names, not a narrative.

The people of Israel had returned from exile in Babylon and rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem. After hearing the law and confessing their sins (chapter 9), they made a firm covenant. Nehemiah and the leaders sealed it first, then the priests and the Levites. The names are recorded because the commitment was public and real.

For today: following God is not only something private. When we make a commitment to God and carry it out with responsibility, others are encouraged. Think of one concrete step of obedience and share it with someone you trust so they can support you.
exp.6:26:
It says that 128 men of Anathoth returned from exile in Babylon to their land. Anathoth was a town in Benjamin, near Jerusalem. The phrase "the men of" here means the men of that place, and the number shows how many came back.

It is part of a list of people who returned with Zerubbabel, which Nehemiah finds and reads again. Nehemiah, governor of Jerusalem, had already rebuilt the wall and wanted to repopulate the city and organize the people according to their families and places of origin. It is known that the prophet Jeremiah was from Anathoth, but this verse does not mention him.

For today: God does not forget anyone; every person and every town counts. Today we can imitate that care by valuing each member of our church or family, learning their names, and encouraging them to take part in God's work.
exp.6:15:
It says the descendants of Bebai, a family or clan of Judah, numbered six hundred twenty and eight people. It is part of a list of families who returned to Jerusalem after the exile in Babylon. "Children of" means descendants, not necessarily direct sons. An interesting detail: in Ezra 2:11 the figure for this family is 623, and it is not known for certain why it differs. Several explanations have been proposed, such as different dates of the count.

Context: Nehemiah, the leader who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem, tells that he found the record of those who first returned with Zerubbabel. He wanted to repopulate the city and confirm who belonged to God's people according to their families.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass. Every family and every person counts for him. You can rest knowing that your name matters, and also learn to value those who serve quietly, without anyone mentioning them.
exp.12:18:
Nehemiah says that, when the gates of Jerusalem began to grow dark before the sabbath started, he ordered them shut and commanded that they not be opened until after the sabbath. He also placed some of his servants at the gates so that no burden would be brought in on the sabbath day. "Began to be dark" means that evening was already falling.

Nehemiah speaks as governor of Jerusalem during his second stay in the city. He had seen that some people were selling and buying on the sabbath, and he had already rebuked the leaders of Judah. He reminded them that the people had suffered exile in part because they despised God's commands, the sabbath among them. That is why he acted with firmness.

Today we might ask what things leave no room for our time with God and for rest. Just as Nehemiah set concrete limits, we can choose a weekly time to rest, worship, and be with family, guarding it from hurry and from work.
exp.4:14:
The former governors who came before Nehemiah burdened the people with heavy costs. They took forty shekels of silver from them, besides bread and wine. Their servants also "lorded it over" the people, that is, they commanded harshly and took advantage of them. Nehemiah says that he did not act this way "because of the fear of God," that is, out of reverent respect for God.

Here Nehemiah speaks as governor of Judah under King Artaxerxes. Shortly before, he had rebuked the wealthy who charged interest to their poor brothers. Now he offers his own example: he could have demanded his rights as governor, but he chose not to add to the load of a people already in debt. Scholars debate whether the forty shekels were daily or total amounts, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: if you have authority or influence, at work, in the family, or in the church, ask yourself whether you use it to serve or to gain an advantage. The fear of God teaches us to care for others, even when we could take advantage of them.
exp.6:71:
This verse says that the rest of the people also gave to the work: twenty thousand gold coins, two thousand pounds of silver, and sixty-seven garments for the priests. The explanation of the old coin and the unit of weight is removed here, since those words do not appear in the verse. The exact amounts are hard to calculate today.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who recalls how the rebuilding of Jerusalem was supported. First the governor, called Tirshatha, and the heads of the families gave. Then the common people gave. It is a record of offerings for the treasury of the work and the service of the temple. Some figures differ between this passage and Ezra 2, and the reason is not known for certain.

For today: God values the participation of everyone, not only that of the leaders. Even if your contribution seems small, whether it is time, talent, or money, it can help a good work be accomplished in your church or community.
exp.11:33:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions Judah, Benjamin, Shemaiah, and Jeremiah among the people who walked in the procession. There are doubts about whether "Judah and Benjamin" are persons or represent the tribes, and scholars understand it in different ways.

The passage describes the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, rebuilt under Nehemiah. The account is in the first person, as Nehemiah's own memory. Two groups of people who gave thanks walked on the wall, in opposite directions, until they met at the temple. The names show that it was a celebration of the whole people, not of just a few leaders.

For today: God notices each person, even those whom almost no one remembers. Your simple and steady service, though it goes unnoticed, is part of what God does with his people. Serve with gratitude and without seeking applause.
exp.6:66:
Besides the families who returned from exile in Babylon, it says there were also seven thousand three hundred thirty-seven male and female servants. Among them were two hundred forty-five singing men and singing women. The word "beside" here means "apart from" or "not counting."

Nehemiah records the list of those who returned with Zerubbabel to Judah. When he found this record, he copied it to show who made up the restored people. The figures in this list do not fully match those in Ezra 2, and scholars explain this in several ways, such as copying errors or counts made at different times. The actual reason is not known for certain.

For today: God pays attention to every person, even to those who serve without being noticed. Even the singers were recorded. Today you can serve with joy in ordinary things, knowing that God sees and values what you do.
exp.9:13:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam, Zattu, and Bani were "chief of the people," that is, heads of families or clans. The name Parosh is the one that appears here in the verse your reader sees.

Nehemiah 10 records a covenant signed after the people heard the law and confessed their sins (chapter 9). It does not describe a single character; it is a record of the leaders who signed, together with priests and Levites. They promised to obey God's law, not to marry neighboring peoples who would lead them away from Him, to keep the Sabbath, and to support the temple. These names also appear in Ezra 2, among the families who returned from exile.

God values the specific people who commit themselves to Him. Your name matters to Him, even if no one else remembers it. Think of one commitment of obedience you can take on today and keep it faithfully.
exp.6:68:
This verse ends the list of animals owned by the people who returned from exile in Babylon: four hundred and thirty-five camels and six thousand seven hundred and twenty asses. Asses were beasts of burden and transport, very useful for work and for travel.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, copying an official record. Nehemiah found this list of families and presents it to show who came back to Jerusalem and what resources they had to rebuild their lives. It is nearly the same list that appears in Ezra 2.
