Some figures differ a little between the two books, and it is not known for certain why; there are several possible explanations.

For today: God cares about the everyday, even about working animals and the names of people. What we have, little or much, can be put at the service of God and of his people, as those who gave for the work did afterward.
exp.11:14:
This verse is part of a list of priestly families. It says that Adna was the head of the priestly house of Harim, and that Helkai was the head of the house of Meraioth. The phrase "of Harim, Adna" means "in the family of Harim, the leader was Adna."

The book of Nehemiah (tradition attributes it to Nehemiah himself, though it is not certain that all the lists are his) records the priests in the time of the high priest Joiakim. They were listed to show who served in the temple and to bring order and continuity to worship after the return from exile.

For today: God notices people who seem to be just names. Their faithful service, even when quiet, matters. Serve steadily wherever you are, without needing applause.
exp.12:6:
He says that Nehemiah returned to Jerusalem and realized the wrong that Eliashib, the priest, had done. Eliashib had prepared a room for Tobiah inside the courts of the temple. The word "chamber" means a room, and the phrase that follows means to do something as a favor or out of consideration for someone.

Nehemiah speaks in the first person. He had been away, with King Artaxerxes, and when he came back he found that this room, formerly used to store the offerings and the tithes of the Levites, was now occupied by Tobiah, a man who had opposed God's people. That is why Nehemiah was indignant and had him thrown out.

For today: when no one is watching, it is easy to let worldly concerns or favors shown to others push aside what belongs to God. Let us honestly examine what has taken God's place in our lives, and give that space back to him.
exp.6:2:
Nehemiah gives orders to look after the city. The gates would not be opened until the sun was high, that is, well into the morning. When evening came, the guards were to close them and bar them (put the bar in place) while the people were still present. In addition, he appointed residents of Jerusalem as guards, each one during his own shift and in front of his own house.

Nehemiah, governor of Jerusalem, is speaking. The wall was already finished and the gates were in place. But the city was large and had few people, so it was exposed to danger. For that reason he entrusted the care of it to Hanani and Hananiah, a faithful man who feared God.

For today: God calls us to look after responsibly what he has entrusted to us, such as the home and the family. Each of us can watch over our own "door" with prayer and good habits, without becoming careless.
exp.11:21:
This verse says that the Levites and the priests were registered by their families during the time of the high priests Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan, and Jaddua. "Recorded" means written down in a list, and the "chief of the fathers" are the heads of each clan. The record reaches down to the reign of Darius the Persian.

The text is part of the lists in Nehemiah. The one speaking is the narrator of the book, traditionally Nehemiah, though some think someone else updated the list later. Little is known about which Darius is meant; scholars debate it. What matters is that the service of the temple was carefully kept in order.

Today it reminds us that God values faithful service, even when it is simple and hardly anyone notices. Serve your church with steadiness and gratitude, knowing that God knows your name.
exp.6:49:
This verse is part of a list of families. It names "the children of Reaiah, Rezin, and Nekoda," that is, the descendants of those three ancestors. Here "children" means family or lineage, not only direct sons and daughters. Apart from their appearance in this list, we know almost nothing more about these names.

Nehemiah, the leader of the people, had those who had returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem recorded. This particular group belongs to the Nethinim, people devoted to service in the temple. A nearly identical list appears in Ezra 2, and scholars explain the small differences between the two in several ways.

For today: God overlooks no one, not even those who seem insignificant. Their names were written down. If you serve quietly, without applause, your work matters and God sees it.
exp.3:0:
The explanation says that when Sanballat heard that the Jews were rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem, he became filled with anger and mocked them. Some older words: the phrase that reads as "it came to pass" in the verse is a way of saying "it happened," the word "wroth" means that he was filled with rage, "took great indignation" means that he was extremely angry, and "mocked" means that he laughed at them with contempt.

The one telling this is Nehemiah, who was leading the rebuilding after the exile. Sanballat, who seems to have been an authority in Samaria, opposed Jerusalem becoming strong again. His anger and his mockery aimed to discourage the people. The exact reasons for his opposition are not fully detailed in this verse.

For today: when you do something good and someone mocks or looks down on you, do not let that stop your work. Nehemiah responded by praying and pressing on. Pray, trust God, and continue with perseverance.
exp.7:10:
This verse tells us that the Levites quieted the people. "Stilled" means they calmed them down. They said to them: "Hold your peace, for the day is holy; neither be ye grieved." "Hold your peace" here means "calm down, stop weeping." "Holy day" is a day set apart for God.

Ezra was reading God's law, and the Levites were explaining it. The people wept as they heard it, perhaps because they realized how far they had strayed from it (the text does not say this exactly). Nehemiah, Ezra, and the Levites encouraged them to celebrate, because that day was a feast before God. Afterward, the people ate, shared, and rejoiced because they had understood the word.

For today: when God's Word confronts us, we may grieve, but we need not stay sunk in sorrow. God corrects us to bring us into his joy and forgiveness. Give thanks today for something, and share with someone who needs it.
exp.9:24:
This verse is part of a list of names. Rehum, Hashabnah, and Maaseiah are three of the leaders of the people who sealed a covenant before God. There are no difficult old words here, only Hebrew personal names.

The book is narrated by Nehemiah, after the people had returned from exile and the wall of Jerusalem had been rebuilt. After hearing God's law, the Israelites made a written commitment: to walk in the law, not to marry into neighboring peoples who worshiped other gods, to keep the Sabbath, and to support the temple. Of these three men we know nothing more than their names in this passage.

For today: God values those who commit themselves to Him, even when few remember them. Your everyday faithfulness, in the hidden places, also counts. Think of one concrete commitment to God and keep it consistently this week.
exp.7:0:
The explanation says that all the people gathered together as one, "as one man," in the square in front of the Water Gate, one of the entrances to Jerusalem. They themselves asked Ezra the scribe (the one who copied and knew the Scriptures well) to bring the book of the law of Moses, which God had given to Israel. "Gathered" here is simply the word used in the verse for the people coming together.

The account is written in the third person, recounting what happened. The walls of Jerusalem had already been rebuilt under Nehemiah. Now the people, in the seventh month, feel a hunger to hear the word of God. What stands out is that the initiative comes from the people, not only from the leaders.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we desire to hear the Bible with that same longing. A good practice is to set aside a fixed time, alone, with family, or at church, to read it together with attention and without rushing, willing to obey whatever God shows us.
exp.2:29:
It says that Hananiah, son of Shelemiah, and Hanun, the sixth son of Zalaph, repaired another section of the wall, "another piece," that is, a second section. Then Meshullam, son of Berechiah, repaired the part that lay across from his chamber, which was his room or dwelling. Each person is named with his father to identify him clearly.

Nehemiah himself is recounting the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem, around 445 B.C., after the return from exile. The city was in ruins and vulnerable. He organized the people into groups and families, and each one worked on a section. It is striking that Hanun is listed as the sixth son. Some understand that his brothers also helped, although the text does not explain this.

God uses small tasks done faithfully. Perhaps no one will remember your name, but your part counts. Ask God which is "the section across from your house": a nearby responsibility you can look after today, in your family, your church, or your work.
exp.2:27:
It says that the priests rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem starting at the Horse Gate. Each one worked on the section that lay in front of his own house. "Rebuilt" here means repairing or reconstructing what had been torn down. The Horse Gate was on the east side of the city.

This chapter is a list of those who worked on the wall under the leadership of Nehemiah, after the exile in Babylon. The account is told by Nehemiah himself. He records in detail who built each part, perhaps so that the effort of each family would not be forgotten. That the priests worked with their own hands is remarkable, because their usual labor was in the temple.

For today: God values simple, close-to-home service. We can begin by repairing what lies in front of our own "house": our family, our neighborhood, our church. Every small task counts when many work together.
exp.9:36:
This verse says that the people promised to bring to the house of God the first and best of their harvests: the dough (the flour kneaded into bread), the fruit of the trees, the wine and the oil. All of it was to go to the priests, to the storerooms or chambers of the temple. They also promised to give the tithe, that is, the tenth part, to the Levites, who would receive it in all the towns.

The speakers are the Israelites who returned from exile in the time of Nehemiah. After hearing the law, they made a covenant by signing a commitment. They knew that priests and Levites had no land of their own and lived from these offerings. In this way worship would not be neglected.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we put God first in what we receive, whether money, time or talents. We can set aside a part with gratitude and planning, supporting the church and those who serve, without pressure, with joy.
exp.6:17:
This verse says that 667 people from the family of Adonikam returned to Judah after the exile in Babylon. It is part of a list of families, and "children of" means descendants or members of that clan, not only direct sons.

Nehemiah reports that he found a record of the first people who came back with Zerubbabel. He reviews it to organize the people of Jerusalem, now that the walls had been rebuilt. That list confirmed who belonged to the people. A similar list appears in Ezra 2, where some of the numbers differ a little. The reason is not known for certain; some think it is due to different dates of recording or to errors in copying.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass. Every family counts. Value your place in the church and in your family, even when your service seems small or little seen. God knows it.
exp.5:8:
The explanation says that Nehemiah's enemies wanted to frighten them, thinking: "Their hands shall be weakened from the work, that it be not done." The "hands" stand for the strength to do the work. Nehemiah answers with a short prayer: "Now therefore, O God, strengthen my hands," that is: "Give me strength, Lord."

Nehemiah, who was leading the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem, is the one speaking. Sanballat and other opponents used threats and false rumors, such as accusing him of wanting to become king, to stop the work. Nehemiah does not defend himself only with arguments; he also asks God for help in the middle of the pressure.

For today: when fear or criticism tries to hold you back from something good that God has entrusted to you, pray a short and sincere prayer, like Nehemiah's, and keep moving forward with the next step, trusting that God gives you strength.
exp.6:42:
Among those who returned from exile in Babylon, the text says there were seventy-four Levites. The Levites were men from the tribe of Levi, assigned to help with the service of the temple. Here they are listed by family: Jeshua, Kadmiel, and Hodevah. "The children of" means descendants of that family.

Nehemiah copies a list of those who went back to Judah with Zerubbabel, years before the wall was rebuilt. He does this to record the lineage of the people and to know who belonged to each group. It is striking that the Levites are few compared with the priests, who numbered more than a thousand per family. Some think few Levites were willing to return, but the text does not explain this.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even those who seem few or little noticed. Serve faithfully where you are; your name and your work do not go unnoticed by Him.
exp.1:10:
Nehemiah recounts that he arrived in Jerusalem and waited there three days before doing anything. The text does not say what he did during those days, so we do not know whether he rested, observed the city, or simply prepared himself.

The speaker is Nehemiah, cupbearer to the king of Persia. He had traveled from far away carrying letters from the king to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem. His enemies, Sanballat and Tobiah, were already troubled by his arrival. That is why, in the verse that follows, he acts with caution and goes out to inspect the walls at night, without telling anyone his plan.

For today: it is not always necessary to rush. Before undertaking something important, take time to pray, observe, and ask God for wisdom. Patience can also be a form of faith.
exp.9:14:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions Bunni, Azgad, and Bebai, who appear among the "leaders of the people," that is, the heads of families or clans. In the older spellings used in some editions, a few of the names look different from current usage, but they were real people of that time.

The book of Nehemiah tells that, after the walls of Jerusalem were rebuilt, the people made a covenant sealed before God. The leaders put their names to it as a commitment to keep the law of Moses. It is not the speech of a single speaker; it is a written record of those who sealed the covenant. Scholars believe these names may stand for whole families, though this cannot be known with certainty.

God values people, even those whom almost no one remembers. These men had the courage to commit themselves publicly. Today we might ask ourselves: in what area should I take a clear step of obedience to God and accept my responsibility sincerely, without waiting for others to go first?
exp.10:11:
This verse counts how many priests lived in Jerusalem: eight hundred and twenty-two men who did the work of the house, that is, the temple. Adaiah is named, along with his list of ancestors, to show which priestly family he came from.

The passage is part of a list of those who settled in Jerusalem after the wall was rebuilt. Because the city had few inhabitants, some were chosen by lot to live there. The book is attributed to Nehemiah, though some scholars think it may have been completed or arranged by others. The list records who sustained the worship.

For today: God values faithful service, even the kind that almost no one sees. Think of a simple task you do in your church or family, and do it with gratitude, knowing that God knows it.
exp.8:37:
It says that, because of everything the people have just acknowledged before God, they make a firm agreement and put it in writing. The word "covenant" here refers to a solemn commitment. The leaders (princes, Levites, and priests) place their seal as a sign that they accept it.

The speaker is the people of Israel, around the time of Nehemiah, after returning from exile. They have just confessed their sins and God's faithfulness throughout their history. They live under the rule of a foreign empire and in great distress, and they recognize that this is connected to their sins. For that reason they want to renew their commitment to God.

For today: when you recognize a wrong before God, do not stop at sadness alone. Take a concrete and clear step of obedience, and if you can, share it with someone you trust who can help you follow through.
exp.8:21:
This verse says that God gave Israel kingdoms and peoples and divided them up among them by regions or territories. Israel took possession of the lands of King Sihon of Heshbon and King Og of Bashan, east of the Jordan River. The old wording you may see in other editions, "gave" and "divided," is simply the way the verse says God gave them the land and apportioned it to them.

It is part of a long prayer by the Levites, when the people, now returning from exile, gathered to confess their sins and remember God's faithfulness. They go over the history: the desert, the manna, the victories. They want to show that God kept his promises, even though the people often failed him.

For today: take time to remember the times God has provided for and cared for you. Recalling his past faithfulness strengthens your trust and leads you to give thanks, even when the path ahead feels uncertain.
exp.8:28:
This verse says that God warned his people many times to return to his law, but they acted with pride and did not obey. "Protesting" here means warning firmly. The phrase "stubbornly turning the shoulder" describes an animal that refuses to bear the yoke, and "stiffening the neck" means becoming obstinate, with a rigid neck. God's law is a path to life for those who live by it.

It is part of a long prayer of confession by the Levites, addressed to God, after the people returned from exile and gathered to hear the law. They review Israel's history: the people's rebellion, the punishment, and God's mercy again and again in response to their cry.

Today, when God warns us through his Word or through our conscience, it is wise to respond with humility and not with stubbornness. His correction seeks that we live well. And if we have failed, we can return to him, for he is merciful.
exp.11:38:
This verse describes the route taken by the second choir along the wall of Jerusalem. They passed the Ephraim Gate, the Old Gate, the Fish Gate, the Tower of Hananel and the Tower of the Hundred, and the Sheep Gate. In the end they stopped at the Prison Gate. The word for "stopped" means that they came to a halt. The "Prison Gate" is also called the "Guard Gate."

Nehemiah tells this in the first person. The rebuilt wall was being dedicated, and he was walking with half of the people while two choirs gave thanks to God. The names of the gates and towers show that they traveled a real and specific route. The exact location of each place is not known with certainty.

For today: gratitude can be something we live out and share. Remember with others what God has done, and give him thanks step by step, leaving nothing forgotten.
exp.10:13:
It says there was another group of priests, relatives of the ones before them, and that they were 128 mighty men of strength and courage. Their leader was Zabdiel, son of Gedolim. The phrase "mighty men of valour" means that they were capable, strong, and brave men. Some versions translate it as "brave and capable men."

The chapter is part of a list that the narrator of the book gives, tied to Nehemiah. After rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem, the city had few inhabitants. Lots were cast so that one out of every ten families would live in it, and this list names those who served in the temple and in the city. These 128 priests had the task of defending and serving.

For today: God notices those who serve, even when their names are little known. Ask yourself what strength or ability you have, and use it faithfully in your church or community, without seeking applause.
exp.4:17:
Here Nehemiah tells us what was prepared for his table each day: one ox, six choice sheep, and fowl, and every ten days an abundance of wine. The phrase "required not the bread of the governor" means that he did not demand the allowance or tax that was due to him as governor, and he gives the reason: the burden on the people was already very heavy.

The speaker is Nehemiah, governor of Judah. Earlier he had denounced the wealthy who were oppressing their poor brothers with debts. Now he shows that he himself did not take advantage of his office. He spent from his own resources to support more than one hundred and fifty people, and he worked on the wall without buying land.

For today: if you have authority or influence, do not use it for your own benefit. Serve generously, and think about the weight others are already carrying, doing what is right out of reverence for God rather than for applause.
exp.5:9:
Nehemiah tells how he went in secret to the house of Shemaiah, who was shut up in his house (it is not clear why; some think he was pretending to be in a serious situation). Shemaiah proposes that they hide inside the temple and shut its doors, because supposedly they would come to kill him that night. "Let us meet together" means "let us gather together."

Nehemiah leads the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem. His enemies, Tobiah and Sanballat, wanted to frighten him to stop the work. Later Nehemiah realizes that Shemaiah was paid to deceive him. If Nehemiah had hidden in the temple, he would have looked like a coward, and besides, entering there was not his place to do.

For today: not every advice that sounds religious comes from God. Before acting out of fear, compare it with the Word of God, ask for wisdom, and remain firm in what God has entrusted to you.
exp.9:18:
This verse is part of a list of names. Three leaders appear here: Hariph, Anathoth, and Nebai. Anathoth was also the name of a town of the priests near Jerusalem, so it could be a person or a place; it is not entirely clear.

After the return from exile in Babylon, the people made a solemn covenant with God. The leaders of the people signed and sealed the document, and Nehemiah appears first. This list of names shows that the leaders publicly committed themselves to obey God's law, not to marry foreign peoples, to keep the Sabbath, and to support the temple.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even those whom almost no one remembers. Your commitment to God, signed with your daily life, also counts. Put your name to your faithfulness.
exp.2:6:
This verse says that Melatiah of Gibeon and Jadon of Meronoth repaired the wall in the next section. They were men of Gibeon and of Mizpah. Their section reached to "the seat of the governor on this side of the river," an expression that many understand as the place or authority of the Persian governor of the region west of the Euphrates River.

Here no single character speaks; it is Nehemiah's account of rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem after the exile. The chapter lists who worked and in what place. It is notable that people from other nearby towns helped, not only people from Jerusalem, and that in the verse before, leaders from Tekoa did not want to take part.

For today: God values the work of ordinary people, even when their names are little known. Do willingly the part that falls to you in your church, family, or community, without expecting applause.
exp.6:46:
This verse continues a list of families called "netinim," that is, people dedicated to helping with the service of the temple. Three are named here: the children of Keros, of Sia, and of Padon. These are family names, and nothing more is explained about them.

Nehemiah, after rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem, found a record of those who had returned from exile in Babylon. He copied it to organize the city and to recognize who belonged to the people. Some scholars think the netinim were of foreign origin, but this is not entirely certain.

For today: God notices people whom almost no one remembers. Their names were written down because of their humble service. Today you can serve without seeking applause, trusting that God sees and values what you do in quiet.
exp.4:0:
It says that the people, together with their wives, began to cry out loudly in complaint, but not against enemies from outside; rather, against other Jews, their own brothers. The word "was" here is simply the verb "to be" in the past, and "cry" means a loud shout of complaint or pain.

This happens while the wall of Jerusalem is being rebuilt, in the time of Nehemiah. Those crying out are poor families. The verses that follow explain that there was famine, that they had pawned lands and houses to buy grain, and that they were in debt to fellow countrymen who were wealthier. Their pain was real and urgent.

For today: God is concerned with the cry of those who suffer, even within the community of faith. We can ask ourselves whether we are listening to those in need near us, and whether there is something concrete, such as helping, forgiving a debt, or acting justly, that we can do for them.
exp.6:5:
This verse begins a list of the families who returned from exile. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had carried many Jews away as captives. After that time, they came back to Jerusalem and to Judah, each one to his own city.

Nehemiah is the speaker, and he tells how God placed it on his heart to gather the people and record them by their family lines. Jerusalem had walls, but few people lived there and many houses were still unrebuilt. He found an old book containing the list of the first ones who returned with Zerubbabel. That list, very similar to the one in Ezra 2, helped repopulate the city and bring order to the people.

God remembers every person and every family. None of them is a mere number to Him. Today we can value those who serve without being seen, and remember that our place among God's people matters.
exp.11:40:
These verse lists seven priests: Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Michaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah. Each one held a trumpet. They were part of the procession that celebrated the dedication of the wall. The phrase "with trumpets" means they played these brass instruments to announce and accompany the praise.

Nehemiah tells this story in the first person. The wall of Jerusalem was already rebuilt, and the people formed two large choirs that walked in opposite directions along the wall. In the end they met at the house of God. The priests with trumpets led one of the groups. They wanted to dedicate the work to God and give him thanks.

For today: when God helps us finish something, it is worth stopping to thank him out loud and with joy. Also, each person has a part to play, even if it seems small, like blowing a trumpet, and together we make a complete song of praise.
exp.11:1:
This verse is part of a list of names: Amariah, Malluch, and Hattush. They are heads of priestly families who returned from exile in Babylon. The text does not explain who each one was; it only names them. Some spellings of the names differ between translations.

The book of Nehemiah gathers lists to record who returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, around 538 BC. The writer (traditionally Nehemiah, though some think others added material) wants to preserve the priestly line. In this way it was shown that service in the temple remained in the hands of legitimate families and that God had kept his promise to bring his people back.

God knows people by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. Your humble and little-seen service matters before him too. Serve him faithfully, without worrying about being famous.
exp.0:10:
Nehemiah asks God to listen attentively to his prayer and to the prayers of other servants who desire to honor his name. He asks that God give him success today and grant him favor in the eyes of the king. The cupbearer was the one who served wine to the king.

Nehemiah is a Jew living far from Jerusalem, serving the king of Persia. He has just learned that the city is in ruins, and he prays with sorrow, remembering God's promises to his people. The king is probably Artaxerxes. This prayer prepares the moment when Nehemiah will speak to the king to ask permission to go and rebuild.

Before taking an important step, he prays with humility and confidence. You can do the same: bring your plans and difficult encounters before God, and ask him to guide you and open doors, while doing your part with responsibility.
exp.7:6:
This verse names a group of Levites who helped the people understand God's law. The phrase "caused the people to understand" means that they explained or taught what was being read. The phrase "stood in their place" means that the people remained standing, attentive and in order, while they listened.

The narrator tells what happened when Ezra read the book of the law before the people, now that they had returned to Jerusalem. Many would not have grasped well the meaning of what was read, so these Levites helped. The verses that follow say they read clearly and gave the sense. Scholars do not agree on whether they translated, explained, or did both.

For today: it is not enough to hear the Bible; we must understand it. Seek help, such as a teacher, a study group, or a good translation, and do not be discouraged if at first it is hard. God wants his Word to be understood.
exp.4:8:
Nehemiah tells the leaders that what they are doing is not right. He asks them whether they should not live in reverence for God, so that the enemy nations would have no reason to mock them.

Nehemiah, governor of Jerusalem, speaks while the walls are being rebuilt. There was hunger and debt, and the wealthy were charging their own brothers excessive interest. Some were even taking their fields and their children as payment. Nehemiah gathered a large assembly and confronted them. Then he asked them to return everything they had taken.

For today: the way we treat money and those in need shows whether we truly respect God. We can ask ourselves whether we are taking advantage of someone in difficulty, and look for ways to help them with justice and generosity.
exp.1:14:
Here Nehemiah tells that he went up at night along the brook (the Kidron Valley, as it is commonly understood) and examined the damaged wall. Afterward he came back in through the same Valley Gate he had gone out by. "Examined" means he observed closely, and he went back, returning the way he came.

The speaker is Nehemiah, cupbearer to the king of Persia, who had come to Jerusalem to rebuild its walls. Before telling his plan to anyone, he wanted to see for himself how much damage there was. He went out at night, probably so as not to draw attention or provoke opposition too early.

For today: before acting, take time to observe the situation calmly and in prayer. Knowing the problem well helps you speak with clarity, plan with wisdom, and encourage others with real facts rather than assumptions.
exp.2:16:
After him, the Levites repaired another section of the wall. Rehum, the son of Bani, was in charge. Next to him worked Hashabiah, the ruler of half the district of Keilah, in his own part. The verse says that after those who had already been working, the Levites rebuilt another part of the wall.

This appears in the account of Nehemiah, who tells in the first person how the wall of Jerusalem was raised after the return from exile. The list names many people and places them section by section. In this way we see that the work belonged to the whole people, with leaders, priests, Levites and families, each in their own place.

Today, God also counts on you in a particular place. Your task may seem small or little seen, but it serves alongside others. Do your part faithfully, without comparing yourself to anyone.
exp.10:3:
This verse says that people from two tribes settled in Jerusalem: Judah and Benjamin. Then it begins a list of the leaders from Judah. The first is Athaiah, and his ancestors are named, going back to Perez, a son of Judah.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recording the names after the walls had been rebuilt. Jerusalem had few inhabitants, so some people volunteered and others, according to the chapter, were chosen by lot to move there. The people blessed the volunteers. Many scholars think this helped protect and strengthen the city.

For today: God notices people who serve, even when they are little known. Ask yourself where you can volunteer to help in your church or community, even if it costs you some comfort.
exp.11:22:
This verse says that the heads of the families of the Levites were recorded in "the book of the chronicles," that is, an official record of that time. That list reached down to the days of Johanan, son of Eliashib. The Levites were the tribe assigned to serve in the temple.

Here the narrator of the book reviews who served in the temple after the return from exile. The record was kept so it would be known who had the right to serve and so that order was maintained in worship. Scholars debate who wrote this section and when it was completed, so we cannot say for certain.

For today: God values those who serve, even when almost no one knows them. Many names were written down because of their faithfulness. Serve steadily in your church or your family, trusting that God sees and remembers your work.
exp.6:10:
This list counts the family of Pahath-moab, which had two branches: the descendants of Jeshua and those of Joab. In total there were 2,818 people. The phrase "children of" means descendants, not only direct sons and daughters.

Nehemiah found this record of the families who returned from exile in Babylon to Judah and Jerusalem. He used it to organize the people after the wall was rebuilt. The parallel list in Ezra 2:6 gives 2,812, and it is not known for certain why there is a difference. It may be due to different moments of counting or to copying, but this is only a possibility.

For today: God does not see faceless crowds, but families and people with names. Your service, even if it seems small or little seen, counts before Him. Today you can encourage someone who feels forgotten and remind them that they belong to God's people.
exp.2:25:
This verse says that the Nethinims, who were helpers of the temple, lived in Ophel and worked on that part of the wall. Their section reached as far as the place opposite the water gate toward the east, and to a tower that stood out. Ophel was a hill south of the temple. The parenthetical phrase only clarifies where they were.

Nehemiah is the one narrating. He tells how the people rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem, dividing the work into sections. The Nethinims were servants of the temple, probably of foreign origin, and here they appear as an active part of the work. The exact details of the towers are hard to pinpoint today, and scholars do not fully agree.

For today: God values those who serve in less visible places. Do the task that falls to you gladly, near where you live or serve, without comparing yourself to others. All work done as a team counts toward God's work.
exp.9:29:
The explanation says the people promised not to give their daughters in marriage to the peoples of the land, that is, to the inhabitants of Canaan and the neighboring nations, nor to take their daughters as wives for their sons.

The speaker is the people of Judah, after the return from exile in Babylon, in the time of Nehemiah. They had made a solemn covenant to obey the law of Moses. The main reason for this promise was to protect faithfulness to God, since the law warned that marriages with idolatrous peoples could turn the heart toward other gods (Deuteronomy 7:3-4). It was not about contempt for other peoples, but about spiritual loyalty.

For today: take care with the decisions that most shape your faith, such as marriage, close friendships, and commitments. Ask God for wisdom to choose what draws you closer to Him.
exp.1:0:
Nehemiah recounts that, in the month of Nisan in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, it fell to him to serve wine to the king. He took up the cup and handed it over. He says that before this he had never been sad in the king's presence.

Nehemiah speaks as the king's cupbearer of Persia, a position of great trust. Four months earlier, in the month of Kislev, he had received news that Jerusalem was still in ruins, and since then he had been praying with grief. Now his sorrow shows on his face, which was risky before a king. Many place this year around 445 B.C., although the exact date is debated.

God can open doors just when our burden becomes visible. If something truly hurts you, bring it to God in prayer first, as Nehemiah did, and then act with courage and respect when the opportunity comes.
exp.11:20:
This verse is part of a list of the heads of priestly families. It says that in the house of Hilkiah, the leader was Hashabiah, and in the house of Jedaiah, the leader was Nethaneel. "Heads" here means the leaders or chiefs of each family.

The book was written by Jewish tradition from the time of Nehemiah, and here the account lists the priests who served in the temple in the days of the high priest Joiakim, after the return from exile in Babylon. The names were recorded to preserve the order of the service and the priestly inheritance of each family. Some names repeat between lists, and scholars do not always agree on the details.

For today: God takes notice of those who serve, even when hardly anyone remembers them. If your service is simple and hidden, do not lose heart; God knows your name and values your faithfulness.
exp.2:15:
Verse 16 tells of another man, also named Nehemiah (not the governor), son of Azbuk, who repaired a section of the wall of Jerusalem. He was ruler of half the district of Beth-zur. His stretch went as far as the place opposite the tombs of David, the pool that had been made (a dam or reservoir built by human hands), and the house of the mighty men. This last phrase may refer to a barracks or a place for elite soldiers, though this is not known with certainty.

The book is written in the style of a narrative, probably by Nehemiah himself. The Jews had returned from exile and Jerusalem was still in ruins. Here the names and places of those who rebuilt the wall are recorded, because each family and each leader had their part in the work.

For today: God sees and remembers the work of each person, even work that seems small or little known. Do with willingness the part that falls to you, in your family or in your church, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.5:2:
Nehemiah sends word to his enemies that he is doing a great work and cannot come down to meet with them. If he left the work to go, the work would stop.

Nehemiah speaks while he is rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem. Sanballat and Geshem invite him to a meeting in the plain of Ono, but the text says they were planning to harm him. Although we do not know in detail what they would have done, Nehemiah recognizes the trap and does not fall into it. The enemies insist several times, and he answers in the same way.

For today: not every invitation to talk or to help is a good opportunity. When God has given you a task, learn to say no calmly and firmly to whatever only distracts you or wears you down. Ask him for wisdom to tell apart what builds up from what gets in the way.
exp.11:18:
This verse is part of a list of names. "Of Joiarib, Mattenai" means that Mattenai was the head of the priestly family of Joiarib. The same is true of Uzzi, head of the family of Jedaiah. They were descendants of priests who served in the temple.

The text is part of the account in the book of Nehemiah, which tells of the rebuilding of Jerusalem after the exile. This list records the heads of the priestly families in the days of the high priest Joiakim. They were written down to keep the order of worship and the memory of the people. It is not known with certainty who wrote this list, but its purpose seems clear: to keep a record of who served.

For today: God knows and values those who serve without being famous. There are names that almost no one remembers, but their faithfulness counts. Serve faithfully wherever you are, even when no one applauds you.
exp.4:12:
Nehemiah shakes out the folds of his garment, where a person kept whatever they carried, as a gesture showing what would happen to anyone who did not keep his promise. He asks that God shake him out of his house and his labor, that is, out of his goods and what he has earned, until he is emptied. The people answer "Amen," which means "so be it," they praise God, and they carry out what was promised.

Nehemiah speaks as governor of Judah. Some wealthy Jews were charging interest and taking the lands and homes of their poorer brothers, who were in debt and hungry. Nehemiah confronted them and asked them to return everything. This act sealed their commitment with a solemn oath.

For today: when we make a promise, especially to someone in need, we must keep it. Examine whether in your work or your business you treat with justice and compassion those who have less than you.
exp.9:1:
It says that Seraiah, Azariah, and Jeremiah are among those who put their name, or their seal, on a document. It is part of a list of priests who signed a commitment. The word for the governor is not explained here, and in this passage it refers to Nehemiah.

After rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem and hearing the reading of the Law, the people recognized their failings. Then they made a written agreement to obey God. The text of Nehemiah lists the leaders who signed it. The names repeat in other lists of priests, but it cannot be stated with certainty who each one was.

God takes commitments seriously and values people, not just ideas. These names, though they may seem simple, show that each one took on his part. Today we can clearly decide on one concrete act of obedience, place it before God, and bring it to someone we trust who can help us keep it.
exp.6:44:
The porters were the men in charge of guarding the gates of the temple and watching who came in. Six families are named: Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub, Hatita, and Shobai. Together they numbered one hundred and thirty-eight people.

This verse is part of the list of exiles who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel. It does not speak of any one particular person; it is a record that Nehemiah found and copied again. It served to confirm who belonged to the people and who could serve in the temple. This same list also appears in Ezra 2, with some differences in the numbers and names, which can be explained in several ways.

For today: God values quiet work, like opening a door or looking after a place. Hardly anyone remembers these porters, but God did name them. Serve faithfully even when no one sees you.
exp.10:29:
This verse follows a list of towns in southern Judah where some Israelites settled who did not stay in Jerusalem. The towns named are Zanoah, Adullam, Lachish and Azekah, together with their villages, that is, the small settlements around them. It says the people lived "from Beersheba" as far as the valley of Hinnom, that is, from the far south to near Jerusalem. The "fields" mentioned here refers to the farmland nearby.

Nehemiah, or whoever compiled his book, records who settled where after the return from exile. Jerusalem needed more inhabitants, so lots were cast: one out of every ten lived in the city and the rest in other towns. This list shows how the promised land was resettled. Some details of location are debated among scholars.

God pays attention to every place and every person, even when they seem ordinary. Serve where you are, whether in a great city or a small village. Your place also matters to God.
exp.4:6:
It says that Nehemiah thought the matter over calmly before acting. Then he rebuked the nobles and the rulers, asking them whether they were charging their own brothers interest. Here, charging interest means demanding excessive interest from someone who is in need. In the end, he gathered a large crowd to deal with the matter in public.

Nehemiah, governor of Judah, speaks while the wall of Jerusalem is being rebuilt. Some poor Jews were crying out because, through hunger and debt, they had handed over their lands and even their children as servants. The wealthy among their own people were taking advantage of them, and Nehemiah became angry when he heard their complaint.

For today: before correcting an injustice, it is wise to stop, think, and pray. We should also examine whether, in our businesses, loans, or work, we deal fairly and compassionately with those who are in difficulty, especially with our brothers and sisters in the faith.
exp.8:0:
It says that on the twenty-fourth day of that month, the people of Israel gathered together to fast. They dressed in sackcloth, which was rough clothing worn as a sign of mourning, and they put earth upon their heads or bodies. These were outward signs of sorrow, humility, and repentance.

The one who tells the story is the author of the book of Nehemiah, though we cannot know his name for certain. This takes place after the wall of Jerusalem had been rebuilt and after the feast of Tabernacles had been celebrated. As they heard the law of God, the people saw their failures. For this reason they gathered together, separated themselves from foreign influences, and confessed their sins and the sins of their fathers.

When God shows us something wrong in our lives, we can respond with sincere humility. More than the outward sign, what matters is a heart that stops, recognizes its sin, and returns to God with confidence in his forgiveness.
exp.6:40:
This verse is part of a list of priestly families. It says that the descendants of Pashur (another way of spelling Pasur) numbered one thousand two hundred forty and seven people. "The children of" does not refer only to direct children, but to the whole family or clan descended from that ancestor.

The text is a record of those who returned from exile in Babylon to Judah. Nehemiah, the leader who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem, found this census and copied it. An almost identical list appears in Ezra 2. It served to confirm who were legitimate priests and Levites, and so to organize worship in the temple.

For today: God pays attention to each family and each person, even when they are just a name in a list. Your service, though it may seem small or little seen, does not go unnoticed by Him. Serve faithfully where you are.
exp.3:21:
Nehemiah asks that each man, together with his servant, stay overnight inside Jerusalem. In this way, at night everyone will help guard the city as watchmen, and by day they will keep working on the project. "Servant" refers to a helper or attendant, and "watchman" is the one who keeps guard.

Nehemiah, who was leading the rebuilding of the walls, is speaking. His enemies were threatening them, and they could attack by surprise. Because the people lived in nearby villages and the wall was long, Nehemiah organized shifts for watching and for working. In this way the city was protected without stopping the construction.

For today: trusting God does not remove our responsibility. We can pray and, at the same time, work with order and care. If you have an important task, ask God for help, organize your time well, and do not neglect what you must protect.
exp.10:1:
This verse says that the people of the town blessed, that is, spoke well of and thanked, the men who offered themselves of their own free will to live in Jerusalem. The word "dwell" means to live or make one's home. "Willingly" means they did it without anyone forcing them.

We are at the time when Jerusalem already had its walls rebuilt, but there were not enough people living inside. The leaders already lived there, and the rest of the people cast lots so that one family in every ten would move. It was a sacrifice, because they left their lands and their towns. Moreover, these volunteers joined those chosen by lot. The text does not say in detail what form that blessing took.

Today we can recognize and encourage, with sincere words, those who serve gladly and pay a price, in the church, the family, or the workplace. A timely word of thanks strengthens the one who gives from the heart.
exp.11:0:
These are the priests and the Levites who went up with Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and with Jeshua: Seraiah, Jeremiah, Ezra.

This verse begins a list of the priests and Levites who returned to Judah from exile in Babylon. They went up with Zerubbabel, a descendant of King David who served as governor, and with Jeshua, the high priest. The phrase "went up" is used because Jerusalem sits on high ground, and that is how people speak of traveling there. The first names listed here are Seraiah, Jeremiah, and Ezra.

The author is the narrator of the book, traditionally associated with Nehemiah, though some think other hands helped arrange the lists. This passage records the religious leaders of the first return, around 538 B.C. Recording their names helped show that the temple service continued in an orderly way. This Ezra may be a priest of that period, and it is not clear whether he is the same scribe from the book of Ezra.

God remembers those who serve faithfully, even when they seem unknown. Today you can serve with humility and steadiness, trusting that God values your work.
exp.10:15:
This verse mentions two Levites, Shabbethai and Jozabad, who were among the leaders of their tribe. They were put in charge of overseeing the outside work of the house of God. "Overseers" means those in charge or supervisors. The "outside work" probably refers to organizing and maintenance tasks outside the temple itself; the text gives no further details, and some think it included administrative matters.

Nehemiah 11 is a list of those who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile. The city was sparsely populated, so lots were cast to have one out of every ten families live in it. The author, traditionally Nehemiah, records the names to remember those who served in rebuilding the life of the people.

For today: God values service that almost no one sees. These men did not sing or lead worship, but their practical work supported the worship. If you help with simple tasks in your church or community, do it with joy, knowing that God sees it and takes it into account.
exp.11:44:
This verse says that the priests, the Levites, the singers and the gatekeepers carried out their service in the temple. "Keeping the charge" means carrying out with care what God had entrusted to them. "Purification" refers to the rites of cleansing, through which forgiveness of sins was sought. Everything was done according to what King David and his son Solomon had commanded.

The text comes from the account of Nehemiah, and it is not a speech. It takes place after the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, in the midst of great joy. The people supported with their offerings those who served in the temple, and so the worship was kept in good order. The exact details of each task are not explained here.

For today: faith is sustained by faithfulness in what is small and constant. We can support with gratitude and generosity those who serve in our church, and carry out with joy the work God has entrusted to us, even when it goes unnoticed.
exp.1:3:
The passage tells us that the king asked Nehemiah what he wanted to request. Before answering, Nehemiah prayed silently to the God of heaven. The words "said unto me" are the same as "told me," and "For what dost thou make request?" means "What do you want to ask of me?"

Nehemiah served as cupbearer to King Artaxerxes, a position of trust in the palace. He was sad because Jerusalem still lay in ruins, and the king noticed it. It was dangerous to show sadness before the king, so Nehemiah was very afraid. The Bible does not say how long that prayer lasted, but it seems to have been brief, offered in the moment.

For today: you do not need a special place or many words to pray. In a difficult conversation, an interview, or an important decision, you can lift up a short, sincere prayer to God before you speak. He hears you at any moment.
exp.3:22:
It says that Nehemiah and those with him did not take off their clothes to sleep. His "brethren" are close relatives or companions, and the "servants" are his young attendants. The "men of the guard" were the men who kept watch over him. The last phrase is hard in Hebrew; some translations understand it as each man taking off his clothes only to wash them, and others as each one carrying his weapon in his hand, even when going for water.

Nehemiah speaks while he is rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem. His enemies threatened to attack, so half the men worked while the other half stood guard with spears. He tells that everyone lived on constant alert until the work was finished.

Today, when an important task faces opposition, we need perseverance and care. We can pray and work with discipline, accepting passing discomforts, without neglecting spiritual watchfulness or service to God.
exp.12:25:
Nehemiah reminds the Israelites of the case of King Solomon. He was the greatest king of his time, loved by God and set by Him over all Israel. Even so, foreign women led him into sin.

Nehemiah speaks as governor, back in Jerusalem. He finds that many Jews had married women from neighboring peoples, and their children could no longer even speak Hebrew. The problem was not where these women came from, but that these marriages were pulling the people away from the God of the covenant. That is why he gives them the example of Solomon, whose heart turned away (1 Kings 11).

For today: no one is so strong that they cannot fall. Watch over the influences and relationships that shape your heart, and seek friendships and decisions that draw you closer to God, not farther from Him.
exp.5:1:
Nehemiah is the man in charge of rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem. The wall was already standing, though the gates were still missing. His enemies had not managed to stop the work with mockery or threats, so now they offer him a friendly meeting. The Bible does not spell out how they planned to harm him, but Nehemiah recognized it as a trap. Ono was some distance from Jerusalem, and that would have left him exposed.

For today: not every friendly invitation is a good one. Before accepting anything that would pull you away from what God has entrusted to you, ask for wisdom and examine the intentions behind it. You can say "no" firmly and without a fight.
exp.6:18:
This verse says that the descendants of the family of Bigvai, that is, his "children" in the sense of family or clan, were two thousand and sixty-seven people who returned from exile.

Nehemiah speaks in the first person. After rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem, he found the record of the first people who returned from Babylon and copied it to repopulate the city. Ezra 2:14 gives Bigvai with 2,056, a different figure. Some believe this is due to differences in copying or to the count being taken at different times, but we do not know this for certain.

For today: God knows every person and every family, even when for us they are only numbers. Think of someone who goes unnoticed in your church or your family and give them a word of appreciation today. To God, everyone counts.
exp.11:7:
This verse names the Levites who returned from exile with Zerubbabel: Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, Sherebiah, Judah, and Mattaniah. Mattaniah, along with his brothers, was in charge of the songs, that is, the hymns of praise and thanksgiving in worship. "Was over" means he led or had charge of that task.

Nehemiah is the one who compiles these lists, although the text does not say who wrote each part. His purpose is to keep a record of the families of priests and Levites, to show that the temple service continued in an orderly way. The names are tied to the days of Jeshua, the high priest of that generation. The Levites are already mentioned earlier with the task of music and thanksgiving.

For today: God values faithful service, even the kind that seems small or hardly seen. Seek to do your part in the church with steadiness and gratitude, without expecting recognition, because God remembers every name.
exp.0:0:
Nehemiah begins his book by saying that these are his words, that is, his personal account. He presents himself as the son of Hachaliah and notes when everything happened: in the month Chisleu (roughly November to December), in the twentieth year. He was in Shushan, which was the capital of the kingdom, that is, a major city of the Persian empire.

The one speaking is Nehemiah, a Jew who lived far from his homeland, in exile. Throughout the whole book we learn that he served the Persian king. Many understand that the "twentieth year" refers to the reign of King Artaxerxes, though the verse does not say so. This verse sets the scene: soon painful news about Jerusalem will arrive.

For today: God can use an ordinary person in his daily work, far from where he might expect to be. Pay attention to what God places before you in your workplace, because something great may begin there.
exp.7:11:
It says that, after hearing the reading of the law, all the people went off to eat and drink, to share portions of food with others, and to celebrate with great joy. The reason was that they had understood what had been taught to them. The phrase "went their way" simply means they left and went on about their day, and "to send portions" means sending part of the food to those who had none.

The people had returned from exile, and Ezra was reading the law with the help of the Levites, who explained it. As they heard it, the people were weeping. Nehemiah, Ezra, and the Levites told them that the day was holy and that they should not grieve, because the joy of the Lord was their strength. This verse shows how they responded.

For today: when you understand something of the Word of God, do not keep it to yourself. Let it fill you with gratitude and share it generously, for example by inviting someone to eat with you or by helping someone who is in need.
exp.6:57:
This verse continues a list of names. It mentions three more families: the children of Jaala, of Darkon, and of Giddel. They belong to the group called "the children of Solomon's servants," descendants of people who worked for King Solomon. Here "children" means descendants, not only direct sons.

The passage is a record of those who returned from exile in Babylon to Judah. Nehemiah found this list and copied it (Neh. 7:5). It already appears in Ezra 2, with small differences in some names. It mattered to know who belonged to the people and who served in the temple. At the end, the total of the group is given: 392.

God knows people by their names, even those whom almost no one remembers. These families were not famous, but their names were written down in the Bible. If you serve quietly and without applause today, remember that God sees and values your faithfulness. Serve with joy, without seeking recognition.
exp.6:4:
Nehemiah tells us that God put it into his heart to gather together the leaders, the officials, and the people so that they might be registered according to their families. Nehemiah then found an old book containing the genealogy of those who had first returned from exile.

Nehemiah, the governor, is speaking. Jerusalem already had walls and gates, but there were almost no people living inside and few houses had been built. The community still needed to be rebuilt. That is why he wanted to organize the people and confirm who they were, probably so that it could be known who could live in the city and serve in it. The list that follows helps us see the continuity with those who had returned earlier.

For today: when you finish a big task, do not stop at what is visible. Ask God for direction to care for what matters most, which is people, community, and the roots of faith. He can place in your heart the next step.
exp.10:4:
This verse gives the name of another inhabitant of Jerusalem from the tribe of Judah: Maaseiah, with his list of ancestors going back to Zechariah and Shiloni. The phrase "the son of" means descendant, not always a direct son. "Shiloni" probably connects him to the family of Shelah, son of Judah, although some understand it differently.

It is part of a list from the book of Nehemiah. After the wall was rebuilt, Jerusalem had few inhabitants, and lots were cast so that some families would move to live in the city (Nehemiah 11:1). The record shows who accepted that commitment and which families they came from.

For today: God notices the people who serve, even when almost no one names them. Serve faithfully where God places you, without thinking about applause.
exp.10:26:
This verse is part of a list of places where some of the descendants of Judah lived. It mentions Hazar-shual, Beer-sheba, and the villages around them. The villages are small towns near a larger city.

Nehemiah 11 tells how the region was resettled after the return from exile in Babylon. Jerusalem was the main city, and a few were chosen to live there, while others settled on their ancestral lands. The text is a historical record, not a speech. Beer-sheba lay at the southern edge of Judah, which shows how far the people reached as they occupied their land again.

God cares for the small places and for ordinary people, not only for the great cities. Your place of life or work, though it may seem unimportant, may be where God wants you to serve faithfully. Ask him today to help you be steady where you are.
exp.8:15:
The explanation says that Israel's ancestors, after receiving so much from God, acted with pride. The phrase about "dealt proudly" means they were tenacious, like an animal that will not lower its neck to be led. That is why they did not obey God's commandments.

This is part of a prayer of confession in Jerusalem, in the time of Nehemiah. The Levites recall Israel's history: God delivered them, gave them the law, bread from heaven, and water from the rock. But they responded with rebellion. The prayer does not end there, but emphasizes that God is merciful and did not abandon them.

For today: when God has given us so much, pride makes us deaf. Today you can humbly recognize where you have been stubborn, and listen to God again, trusting in his mercy.
exp.3:14:
The enemies of Israel learned that Nehemiah and the people knew about their plan to attack. Then God brought their scheme to nothing (the wording means that he undid it). After that, everyone returned to the wall, each one to his work. The phrase about the young men is replaced here by the verse's own wording: "every one unto his work" is the same idea as each person going back to his task.

Nehemiah is the one who tells this in the first person. Jerusalem was rebuilding its wall, and hostile neighbors mocked and threatened to attack. Nehemiah organized a defense, encouraged the people not to be afraid, and reminded them that the Lord is great. When the danger passed, they did not stop to celebrate but went on working.

For today: when you face opposition or fear, trust that God is at work, but also do what is yours to do with wisdom. After the trial, return steadily to your responsibility.
exp.11:15:
This verse is part of a list. It says that, in the priestly household of Iddo, the head was Zechariah, and in that of Ginnethon, Meshullam. "Of" means "of the family of." These are the names of the heads of priestly families.

The book of Nehemiah presents this record of the priests in the days of the high priest Joiakim, after the return from exile in Babylon. Traditionally the book is attributed to Nehemiah, although some scholars think the list was completed by others. Its purpose was to keep a record of who served in the temple and to ensure that worship continued in an orderly way.

For today: God pays attention to specific people, even when the world forgets them. There are names that seem insignificant, yet God preserved them in His Word. Your faithful service, even when it is quiet and without applause, also matters to Him.
exp.7:17:
This verse tells that Ezra read from the book of God's law every day of the feast, from the first day to the last. The people kept the festival for seven days, and on the eighth day there was a special assembly, held as it was prescribed, that is, according to what had been commanded.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recounting what happened in Jerusalem after the return from exile. The people were celebrating the Feast of Tabernacles, which remembered how God cared for Israel in the wilderness. The law commanded this feast, and they kept it with great joy, living in booths and listening to the Word.

For today: the joy of faith grows when we listen to God's Word with steadiness. We can set aside a time each day, even a brief one, to read the Bible and give thanks to God.
exp.10:17:
This verse says that the total of the Levites who lived in Jerusalem, called "the holy city," was 284. "Levites" were the men of the tribe of Levi, appointed to serve in the temple. "Holy city" refers to Jerusalem, the place where the house of God stood.

Nehemiah 11 is a list of those who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile. The city had few inhabitants and newly rebuilt walls, so lots were cast so that one out of every ten families would live there. The narrator records the numbers and the names, among them those who led the praise and looked after the work of the temple.

For today: God values those who serve faithfully, even in tasks that go unseen. A number in a list reminds us that no faithful service escapes His notice. Serve where you are, without seeking applause.
exp.9:34:
This verse says that the people committed themselves to bring the firstfruits each year to the house of the Lord, that is, to the temple. The firstfruits are the first and best of the harvest, both from the ground and from the trees. It was a way of acknowledging that everything they received came from God.

The speakers are those who returned from exile in the time of Nehemiah: leaders, priests, Levites and the people. They had made a signed covenant to obey the law of Moses. After years of neglect, they wanted to support worship in the temple and once again put God first.

For today: before you spend or share what you receive, set aside the first part for God, with gratitude and not out of obligation. It can be money, time or service to others. In this way you remember that all that you have comes from Him.
exp.9:0:
What it says: This verse begins a list of the people who signed, or sealed, a written agreement. The first name given is Nehemiah, called "the Tirshatha," which was a Persian title for a governor. He is said to be the son of Hachaliah. Then Zidkijah appears, and the names continue in the next verse.

Context: This is not a speech by a character; it is the book's account, giving the names of the leaders who signed. After the people heard God's law and confessed their sins (ch. 9), they made a firm agreement to obey it (9:38). The leaders signed first, and Nehemiah, the governor, heads the list.

For today: Whoever leads should set the example. If you say you want to obey God, make your commitment concrete and visible, starting with yourself, so that others are encouraged to follow you sincerely.
exp.6:65:
It says that the whole group of Israelites who returned from exile in Babylon added up to 42,360 people. "Congregation" means the assembly or the people gathered together. "Whole" means the total, counting everyone together. This figure does not include the servants, the singers, or the animals, which are mentioned afterward.

The one telling this is Nehemiah, who found a written record of the families who had come back with Zerubbabel. Before this verse, it is recounted that some priests could not prove their ancestry and were set apart from service. Nehemiah records everything carefully so he can reorganize the people in Jerusalem. The numbers in this list resemble those in Ezra 2, although some figures differ, and it is not known with certainty why.

For today: God counts his people and gives each one a place. You are not a lost number; serve faithfully where you are.
exp.10:10:
This verse names Seraiah, a priest who lived in Jerusalem. His family line is given back five generations, to Ahitub. He is called the one in charge of God's house, that is, the main person responsible or appointed over the temple. Here the word "ruler" means leader or supervisor, not the son of a king.

Nehemiah 11 is part of a list of those who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile. The city was sparsely populated, and by lot one family in every ten was chosen to live there. The author, who probably compiled official records, notes names and positions to remember who served in the temple. Scholars discuss how some names in these lists fit with other genealogies.

God notices the people who serve, even in less visible tasks. Today you can serve faithfully in your church or community, knowing that God remembers your faithfulness even when few people notice it.
exp.8:34:
It says that Israel's ancestors had a kingdom, received many blessings from God, and lived in a broad and fertile land (the word "large and fat" means rich and fruitful). Even so, they did not serve him and did not turn from their evil deeds. "Turn" here means turning away from their wrong path toward God.

It is part of a long prayer of confession, offered in the time of Nehemiah, when the people had already returned from exile. The Levites review the history of Israel and acknowledge that God was just and faithful, while the people were disobedient. That is why they now live under the rule of foreign kings and in distress.

For today: blessings do not always draw us closer to God; sometimes they make us forget him. Ask yourself whether your gratitude shows in obedience. Today, thank God for something specific and change an attitude you know does not please him.
exp.11:41:
This verse continues the list of priests who blew trumpets at the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem. It mentions more priests' names: Maaseiah, Shemaiah, Eleazar, Uzzi, Jehohanan, Malchijah, Elam, and Ezer. Then it says that the singers sang loudly, under the direction of Jezrahiah.

The one telling the story is Nehemiah, who speaks in the first person ("I"). The wall was already finished, and the people held a celebration with two great choirs that gave thanks to God in the temple. The text takes care to mention names and order, because the praise was offered with preparation and responsibility.

For today: praise to God deserves joy and also order. If you serve in your church, your place matters, even if no one knows you. Serve with eagerness and with faithfulness.
exp.10:33:
This verse continues a list of towns where the descendants of Benjamin lived. It names three places: Hadid, Zeboim and Neballat. They are the names of villages and settlements, not people. The Reina-Valera 1909 writes "Neballath," with the older spelling.

The book of Nehemiah tells how Jerusalem was rebuilt after the return from exile. In this chapter, the author records who stayed in the city and who went back to live in other towns of Judah and Benjamin. What is known about the exact location of some of these sites is limited. The list shows that the restoration was an effort of the whole people.

For today: God notices small places and ordinary people, even when no one else remembers them. Your steady service in your family, your church or your neighborhood also counts, even when it goes unnoticed.
exp.10:6:
This verse begins the list of the families from the tribe of Benjamin who settled in Jerusalem. It names Sallu, the son of Meshullam, and traces his family line back through several generations until it reaches Jesaiah. We would write "Isaiah" today, but this is a different Hebrew name, so it should not be confused with the prophet.

Nehemiah describes how Jerusalem was repopulated after the return from exile. The city had walls, but very few people lived in it. So the leaders settled there, and the rest cast lots so that one family out of every ten would move. It was a sacrifice, because it meant leaving their fields and villages. The lists of names and genealogies showed who belonged to God's people and what their responsibility was.

God knows and values each person by name, even those whom history barely remembers. Today you can serve faithfully in a place that is not very visible, such as your church or your community, knowing that God sees and honors that commitment.
exp.12:2:
When they heard the law, the people separated from Israel all the foreigners who were mixed in with them.

The one telling the story is Nehemiah, governor of Jerusalem. He had read Deuteronomy 23:3-6, which forbade Ammonites and Moabites from entering the assembly of God, because they had treated Israel badly in the wilderness. The people responded with immediate obedience. Scholars debate how strict this separation was and whether it applied to every foreigner or only to those who put Israel's faith at risk.

Today we can learn to let the Word of God correct our lives right away. When Scripture shows us something we need to change, the best response is to obey with humility, taking care that nothing draws us away from faithfulness to God.
exp.6:33:
The explanation says that 1,254 descendants of "the other Elam" returned from exile. It is called "the other" because another Elam had already been mentioned in the list (verse 12), with the same number. It is not known for certain whether this was a different clan or a different place; the Bible does not make it clear.

The passage is a list of the families who returned to Judah from Babylon. Nehemiah says he found this record when God put it in his heart to gather the people, after the wall of Jerusalem had been rebuilt. The list served to establish who belonged to the people, to repopulate the city, and to reorganize the life of the temple. It is nearly the same as the one in Ezra 2.

For today: God pays attention to every person and every family, even to those almost no one remembers. Your name and your service, though they may seem small, matter to Him. Serve faithfully wherever you are, without needing applause.
exp.6:69:
Some of the heads of the families gave help for the work. The Tirshatha, which was the Persian title for the governor, gave to the treasury a thousand drams of gold (gold coins), fifty basons (vessels for the service of the temple) and five hundred and thirty garments for the priests.

This passage is within the list of the Jews who returned from exile in Babylon. The narrator is noting how many came back and how they helped rebuild the life of the people and the worship of God. Here the Tirshatha seems to be Nehemiah, although some scholars think it could refer to the earlier governor. The figures in this list are also compared with those in Ezra 2.

Today we can learn that serving God includes giving generously, according to our means. Those who lead should be the first to set the example, and all of us can contribute something for the good of the community.
exp.12:22:
This verse says that Nehemiah saw, in those days, some Jews who had married women from Ashdod, from Ammon and from Moab. "Saw" is the word for "vi," and "married" is the word for "tomado mujeres," meaning they had taken wives from those peoples. Ashdod was a Philistine city; the Ammonites and Moabites were neighboring peoples of Israel.

Nehemiah speaks in the first person. He had already corrected other problems in Jerusalem, such as the Sabbath. Now he is concerned about the faith of the people, because the children no longer spoke Hebrew, and the text connects this with the law that warned against alliances that would draw Israel away from God. Some scholars believe the problem was mainly religious, not ethnic.

For today: take care with what most shapes your heart and your home. Before important decisions, such as courtship or commitments, ask yourself whether they bring you closer to God or pull you away from Him, and seek counsel with humility.
exp.10:20:
It says that the Nethinims lived in Ophel, a raised area south of the temple, in Jerusalem. The Nethinims were servants of the temple, helpers to the Levites in humble tasks. Ziha and Gispa were their leaders, that is, the ones in charge of directing them.

The book of Nehemiah tells how Jerusalem was resettled after the return from exile. Here the narrator makes a list of who lived in the city and what role each group had. Some scholars think the Nethinims descended from people who joined the service of the sanctuary from ancient times, but their exact origin is not entirely certain. Living near the temple allowed them to serve easily.

For today: God takes into account even the work that goes largely unseen. If your service in the church or in your family goes unnoticed, remember that God knows it and values it. Serve it with gladness and faithfulness.
exp.7:9:
Here the Israelites are told to go and celebrate: to eat good food, drink sweet wine, and share with those who have nothing to eat. The rich, abundant meals are what is meant here. Prepared simply means ready. God asks them not to be sad, because the joy that comes from the Lord sustains and strengthens them.

Nehemiah the governor speaks, together with Ezra and the Levites. The people had returned from exile and were listening to God's law, which they were now beginning to understand. They wept, perhaps realizing how far they had strayed from it. But that day was holy, a time to rejoice in God.

For today: when you feel guilt or sadness, come to God with confidence, and let his joy lift you up. Then share with someone in need.
exp.5:15:
When Nehemiah's enemies heard that the wall was finished, they were afraid. They were humbled: they lowered their gaze in shame. And they recognized that this work had been accomplished with God's help.

The one telling the story is Nehemiah, who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem. Tobiah, Sanballat, and others mocked, threatened, and tried to frighten him. Even so, the wall was completed in fifty-two days. The verses that follow show that there were still people in Judah tied to Tobiah, so the problems did not disappear entirely.

When you do what is right and face opposition, keep going with prayer and perseverance. The results may not convince everyone, but they can show that God is at work. And if you accomplish something, give God the credit.
exp.0:2:
Here the men who came from Jerusalem answer Nehemiah. They tell him that the Jews who were left in the province of Judah, those who had returned or had not been taken away as prisoners, live in great suffering and shame. The survivors are the ones who were left behind after the others were carried off. Their state is one of humiliation and disgrace. Furthermore, the wall of Jerusalem was still broken down and its gates were burned with fire.
