Nehemiah was the king's cupbearer in Susa, far from his homeland. He asked about Jerusalem of his brother Hanani and others who had come from Judah. Without walls or gates, the city was defenseless and exposed to the contempt of its neighbors. This news moved him to weeping and to prayer.

For today: when you learn of someone else's pain, do not ignore it. Let it touch your heart, bring it to God in prayer, and ask him what you can do to help.
exp.0:1:
He says that Hanani, one of Nehemiah's brothers, came with some men of Judah. Nehemiah asked them questions about the Jews who had survived and remained after the exile, and also about Jerusalem. The word "asked" in the verse covers the sense of his question; the text does not fully clarify whether "brothers" refers to a close relative or a fellow countryman.

Nehemiah speaks here, serving in Susa, the capital of the Persian kingdom. Far from his homeland, he wanted to know how his people and his city were doing. His question shows a heart concerned for them. The answer he receives, in the verses that follow, will move him to weeping, fasting, and prayer.

For today: ask sincerely about those who are suffering or far away, and let what you hear move you to pray and to act, not only to be informed.
exp.2:1:
This verse tells how the men of Jericho worked on the section beside the part built by Eliashib and the priests. After them, Zaccur, the son of Imri, worked. "Built" here means rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem. "Next to them" means "beside that section."

It is part of an account in the book of Nehemiah, which describes how the people rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem after the return from exile. The text is a list of workers, and the narrator carefully notes who did each part. Why so many names are included is not explained, but many think it is to acknowledge each person who took part.

For today: God values each person's work, even when it goes unnoticed. Do your part faithfully, whether great or small, and rejoice in working alongside others for a common purpose.
exp.11:29:
The explanation says that the priests and the Levites, who were in charge of the service in the temple, first purified themselves. Then they purified the people, the city gates, and the wall. The text does not explain the details of the rite; other passages of the Old Testament mention washings and sacrifices, but here it is not specified.

The one telling the story is Nehemiah, in the first person. The dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, now rebuilt, is being prepared. They had gathered the singers to celebrate with gratitude and music. Before the procession, everything is set apart for God.

For today: before asking God to bless something important, such as a home, a job, or a ministry, begin by examining your own heart. Ask for forgiveness and cleansing, and then give thanks to him with joy.
exp.8:23:
The explanation says that the descendants of those who came out of Egypt entered the promised land and took possession of it. God is the one who subdued the Canaanites, who were the inhabitants of that land, and handed them over into the hands of Israel. The phrase "that they might do with them as they would" means that Israel could deal with them as God allowed.

Here the people of Israel speak, led by the Levites, in a prayer of confession after returning from exile. They review their history to acknowledge that God kept his promise to Abraham, while they, on the other hand, were unfaithful. Some matters about the conquest are difficult, and they are understood within that time and within God's judgment on the wickedness of those peoples.

For today: remember with gratitude how God has kept his promises to you. A thankful heart protects us from forgetting God when things are going well.
exp.12:16:
Nehemiah says he firmly corrected the leaders of Judah, the nobles. He asked them what evil thing this was that they were doing. To profane something means to treat as common what God had set apart as holy. Here it refers to using the sabbath day for work and trade.

Nehemiah was governor of Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. He saw that people were treading grapes, loading goods, and buying fish from merchants of Tyre on the sabbath. He blamed the leaders because they were supposed to set an example and stop this practice. Then he reminded them that despising God's commands had brought judgment on their ancestors.

For today: we can ask ourselves what the pace of work and profit takes from our time with God. A simple practice is to set aside a weekly time of rest, prayer, and fellowship with other believers, even when it costs us something.
exp.9:7:
This verse ends a list of priests who signed a covenant. Maaziah, Bilgai and Shemaiah are the last three names. The phrase "these were the priests" shows that all the names before it, from verse 2 on, belong to priestly families. Here the names may stand for households or families, not only for individual people.

The book tells how, after hearing the Law and confessing their sins, the people made a written commitment (Nehemiah 9 and 10). The leaders, the priests and the Levites sealed it. They committed themselves to obey God's Law, not to mix with the neighboring peoples in practices contrary to it, to keep the Sabbath, and to support the temple. Scholars do not agree on every detail about each name.

God values people who commit themselves by name. Today you can put in writing a concrete decision of obedience, such as praying every day or serving in your church, and share it with someone who will encourage you to keep it.
exp.12:5:
Nehemiah says he was not in Jerusalem when the problem with the chamber happened. In the thirty-second year of King Artaxerxes, he went to see the king, and after some time the king gave him permission to return. The phrase "But in all this time" means "but while all this was happening." The phrase "after certain days" means "after some time." He is called the king of Babylon because Artaxerxes ruled the Persian empire, which had inherited that region.

Nehemiah speaks in the first person. He explains why the priest Eliashib was able to give Tobiah, an enemy of the people, a room inside the temple: he was far away. The Bible does not say how long he was gone, only that it was "certain days."

For today: the good we accomplish can weaken when no one is there to look after it. Faithfully care for your faith, your family, and your church, and do not let neglect open the door to what does not belong.
exp.6:0:
This verse says that when they finished building the wall of Jerusalem, Nehemiah set the doors in place. Afterward, gatekeepers were appointed (those who looked after the entrances), singers (those in charge of the music and praise in the temple), and Levites (men of the tribe of Levi, devoted to serving the temple).

Nehemiah speaks in the first person. He had been the king of Persia's cupbearer, and he returned to Jerusalem to lead the rebuilding of the wall. Once the work was finished, he did not leave it unattended, but organized the people to protect the city and to keep up the worship of God.

For today: finishing a project is not the end, and it must also be cared for. When God gives us something good, such as a family, a church, or a job, it is wise to assign responsibilities and keep praise as a priority.
exp.6:56:
This verse begins another group in the list of those who returned from exile: the descendants of "Solomon's servants." Three families are named: Sotai, Sophereth, and Perida. "Servants" here does not refer to ordinary slaves, but to workers or attendants connected with the temple and the kingdom of Solomon. Some of the names are spelled a little differently in Ezra 2.

Nehemiah himself explains that he found this genealogical record of the first people who returned to Jerusalem, and he includes it in his book. The list served to confirm who belonged to the people and who could serve in the temple. We do not know for certain who these families were; only their names have been preserved.

God remembers people whom almost no one remembers. These families did nothing famous, but they were written down for having served and returned. Today you can take encouragement if your work seems small or hidden: God sees it and values it. Serve faithfully, even when no one applauds you.
exp.9:28:
This verse says that the people joined with their leaders and bound themselves, with a solemn promise, to live according to the law that God gave through Moses. The people clave to their brethren, their nobles, and entered into a curse and an oath, so the word "clave" means they joined themselves closely to them. A "curse" here is a solemn self-binding declaration made publicly, and an "oath" is a promise made before God.

The people of Judah are speaking, after returning from exile in Babylon. The leaders had already sealed the covenant, and now the others join them: priests, Levites, whole families, and everyone old enough to understand. They had seen that turning away from God's law brought suffering, and they wanted to begin again.

For today: a sincere decision to obey God is strengthened when we do not make it alone. We can seek out a family or brothers and sisters in the faith, and commit together to take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.6:28:
This verse is part of a list of families and towns. It says that 743 men from three places (Kirjath-jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth) returned to Judah. The word "men" here simply means men, and the names spelled differently are towns of Judah and Benjamin.

Nehemiah copies here the record of the exiles who came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel. He finds it when God puts it on his heart to gather the people and count them. This list, nearly the same as the one in Ezra 2, helped people recognize who belonged to the community and to divide the work of rebuilding.

For today: God does not see faceless crowds; every person and every small town counts for Him. Today you can value your place in your church or community, even when it seems barely visible. Serve faithfully in the simple things, because God remembers and uses the work of those who take part in His work.
exp.8:18:
This verse says that God did not abandon Israel in the wilderness, even though they had failed him. Because of his great mercy, he kept guiding them. The pillar of cloud led them by day, and the pillar of fire gave them light by night, so that they would know where to go. The word "mercies" means kindness and compassion that they did not deserve.

Here the Levites are speaking, during a great prayer of confession in the time of Nehemiah, when the people had already returned from exile. They remember Israel's history: its rebellion, such as the golden calf, and God's constant faithfulness. They want to acknowledge their sins and also God's patience.

For today: when you fail, do not hide from God. Acknowledge your mistake and return to him, trusting that his mercy is still greater than your failure. He can keep guiding you step by step.
exp.9:5:
This verse is part of a list of names: Daniel, Ginnethon and Baruch. The verses that follow say that they were priests. The spelling "Ginnethon" is old; today it is usually written "Ginnetho." It is a list without explanations, just names.

Nehemiah 10 records those who signed a covenant with God after the return from exile in Babylon. The account comes from the book of Nehemiah itself, which preserves the names of the leaders, priests, Levites and heads of the people. They committed themselves to obey God's law, not to marry people from neighboring nations, to keep the Sabbath and to support the temple. Beyond this text, nothing more is known about these three names, and it is not wise to assume details that the Bible does not give.

For today: God values people who commit themselves to Him, even when few remember them. You can serve faithfully in ordinary things, without seeking recognition, trusting that God sees and remembers your commitment.
exp.0:9:
The explanation says that the Israelites are God's servants and his people, whom he has already rescued with great power and with a strong hand. The sentence about the word "redeemed" means that God freed them by paying a price or by intervening with power, as when he brought them out of Egypt. Their strength or might is shown by his power at work.

Nehemiah is praying in Susa, far from Jerusalem. He has just learned that the city lies in ruins and that his people are suffering. He acknowledges the people's sin and reminds God of his promises to Moses: if they returned to him, he would gather them together again. Here he bases his request on what God has already done before, not on his own merits.

Today, when you face a great need, pray by remembering how God has helped you before and what he has promised. That remembrance strengthens trust and encourages you to ask with humility and hope.
exp.11:39:
The verse tells that the two groups of singers, which had marched in opposite directions along the wall, came to a stop at the house of God, that is, the temple. Nehemiah took his place there with the half of the rulers, who were the leaders or authorities of the people. The verse's wording "stood" means that they came to a halt and took their place.

Nehemiah speaks in the first person. The dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, now rebuilt, is being celebrated. With two processions of thanksgiving, the people walked around the wall and ended up gathered in the temple to worship. The two groups began apart, but they ended together before God.

For today: all our effort and our achievements should end in gratitude and worship of God. Also, although each person serves in different ways, the common purpose is to gather to give thanks to Him.
exp.10:35:
This verse closes the list of towns where the people settled. It says that some Levites, that is, members of the tribe dedicated to service in the temple, lived scattered among the territories of Judah and Benjamin. The word "divisions" in the verse refers to groups or portions of land. Some scholars understand it as groups of Levites who joined Benjamin, and others as areas where they lived.

The account of Nehemiah, which according to tradition he wrote himself, lists who settled in Jerusalem and in other towns after the return from exile. This record shows that the rebuilding included putting the life of the people in order and also the life of service to God.

Today, the Levites remind us that serving God does not happen only in a special place. Ask yourself where God has placed you, in your family, your work, or your church, and serve there faithfully, even though no one notices.
exp.5:0:
This verse tells how Nehemiah's enemies, Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem the Arab, learned that the wall of Jerusalem was finished and that no gaps remained in it. The word "breach" in the verse means an opening or gap in the wall. Only the doors were still missing, the wooden gates that would be set into the entrances.

The one telling the story is Nehemiah himself, who recounts his experience in the first person. He had returned to Jerusalem to rebuild its walls, and these men had opposed him from the start, with mockery and threats. Now that the work was almost complete, they tried a different strategy: inviting him to a meeting away from the city. The text says they intended to harm him.

For today: when you are close to finishing something good, a distraction may appear that seems friendly. Ask God for wisdom to recognize it, and stay firm in what He has entrusted to you.
exp.1:17:
Nehemiah tells the Jews that God had taken care of him and had given him favor with the king. He speaks of the hand of God, a way of saying that God was acting on his behalf. Hearing this, the people said, "Let us rise up and build." The expression "they strengthened their hands for good" means that they were encouraged and set to the good work with real willingness.

Nehemiah speaks as the cupbearer of King Artaxerxes, who had learned that Jerusalem's walls lay in ruins and its gates had been burned. He asked the king for permission and went to the city. First he observed in secret, and now he encourages the people by showing them that God and the king supported the project.

For today: when we share how God has helped us, we encourage others to act. Tell your testimony simply and invite others to work together on something good.
exp.3:7:
They agreed together, all of them, to go and fight against Jerusalem and to cause it harm. Where the wording says they "plotted," it means they made a plan in secret. Where it says they came together "with one voice," it means they were united, acting as one.

Nehemiah himself tells the story, in the first person. The Jews had already built the wall up to half its height, and the people were working with enthusiasm. Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabs, the Ammonites, and the people of Ashdod became very angry when they saw the gaps being closed. They most likely feared losing their influence, although the text does not fully explain this.

For today: when you do something good and make progress, opposition may appear. Just as Nehemiah did in the next verse, pray to God first and then act wisely, without abandoning the work.
exp.5:7:
Nehemiah answers firmly to a false letter. He says to Sanballat: "There are no such things done as you say; you are making them up out of your own mind." The word "making them up" means to fabricate a lie. "Á decirle" is "to say to him," and "de tu corazón" means "out of your own mind."

Nehemiah was overseeing the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem. His enemies, Sanballat and others, could not stop him, so they accused him of plotting a rebellion to make himself king. The letter mentioned Geshem and sought to frighten him. Nehemiah did not defend himself with long arguments; he denied the lie and kept working, as seen in his prayer: "Strengthen my hands."

When someone accuses you falsely or tries to frighten you, respond with truth, with calm, and without wasting time on quarrels. Pray asking God for strength and keep doing what He has entrusted to you.
exp.2:28:
This verse says that Zadok, son of Immer, repaired the wall in front of his own house. After him worked Shemaiah, son of Shecaniah, who was the keeper of the east gate. Repaired means that he mended or rebuilt that section. In front of his house means in the stretch of wall that was next to his home.

Nehemiah tells how the people rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem after the exile. He lists the names one by one because each person had an assigned section. Many priests and families worked near their own homes. About the Zadok of this passage we know nothing more; there is no certainty that he is the same man mentioned in other texts.

For today: God values simple work done in the place where we are. We can serve faithfully in what is close to us, such as the home, the family, or the church, without seeking recognition. A small section finished well helps the whole work move forward.
exp.9:22:
This verse is part of a list of names: Hoshea, Hananiah and Hashub. In the older version they appear as "Hoseas," "Hananias" and "Asub," but the reader sees the King James spelling, which matches the names as given here. They are three of the leaders of the people who signed a solemn agreement. There is no direct teaching here, only the names of real people.

Chapter 10 follows the great reading of the Law and the people's prayer of confession. Nehemiah appears first in the list, and then come priests, Levites and leaders of the people. With their signatures, they committed themselves to obey God's Law and to care for the temple. About these three men in particular, the Bible gives no further details, and we do not know for certain whether they were the same men who appear under these names in other passages.

God values people who make a commitment with their own names attached. Today we can ask ourselves: what concrete step of obedience am I willing to take before God and my community, without stopping at good intentions?
exp.6:6:
This verse gives the names of the leaders who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel: Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum and Baanah. Then it announces "the number of the men," that is, the count of the men of the people of Israel. This Nehemiah is not the governor who narrates the book, but another man with the same name.

Nehemiah speaks, saying that God put it in his heart to gather the nobles and the people to register them by families. He found an old record of the first ones who returned to Jerusalem and Judah. This was done to put the community in order and to protect its identity. The list also appears in Ezra 2, with some differences that are explained in several ways.

For today: God remembers each person by name. Value your place in the church and in the family, even when no one notices, and serve with faithfulness.
exp.1:18:
Verse 19 tells how three men from the region, Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem, heard that the Jews were rebuilding the wall. They mocked them and treated them with contempt. "Laughed us to scorn" means they laughed at them in derision. Then they accused them of rebelling against the king of Persia.

The one telling the story is Nehemiah, the king's cupbearer, who arrived in Jerusalem with royal permission. The people had just been encouraged to build. The three neighbors were men with power in the area, and it is likely they saw the project as a threat to their influence. That is why they tried to discourage the people with mockery and accusations.

When you do something good that God has placed on your heart, someone may mock you or doubt your motives. Do not stop because of that. Like Nehemiah, respond calmly, trust God, and keep working.
exp.11:42:
That day, the people offered many sacrifices and celebrated with joy. The animals offered to God are called "sacrifices," and the shouting of happiness is the loud cheer of gladness. The verse says God had made them rejoice with great joy. Everyone took part: men, women, and children. Their joy was heard from far away.

This is part of Nehemiah's account of the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem. The narrator describes the celebration, with choirs, trumpets, and priests. The people had finished the work despite opposition, and they recognize that it was God who gave them this joy. The following verses show that this joy was also expressed in organizing the offerings to support the service of the temple.

For today: when God helps us finish something difficult, it is good to pause, thank him together with our community, and celebrate together. A shared joy can encourage others and show that God is the one who gives true gladness.
exp.10:28:
This verse is part of a list of towns in southern Judah where some Israelites settled. It names three places: En-rimmon, Zareah, and Jarmuth. These are the names of ancient towns, and "villages" refers to the small settlements nearby that depended on them.

Nehemiah recounts how the region was resettled after the return from exile in Babylon. Jerusalem needed more inhabitants, so some lived in the city (chosen by lot) and others returned to their own lands and towns. This list shows that the people were recovering their territory, from Beersheba to the valley of Hinnom. The exact location of some of these places is debated.

God pays attention to people and places that seem small. These nearly forgotten names remind us that every family that returned to its land was part of the restoration. Your place of service, though simple and little seen, matters to God. Serve faithfully where you are.
exp.12:4:
It says that the priest Eliashib prepared a large room inside the temple for Tobiah. Before this, that place was used to store the offerings, the incense, the temple utensils, and the tithes of grain, wine, and oil. Those tithes were meant for the Levites, the singers, and the gatekeepers, besides the portion for the priests.

Nehemiah speaks here, recounting what he found when he returned to Jerusalem after being away. Eliashib, who was in charge of the temple rooms, had family ties with Tobiah, a man who had opposed Nehemiah. By giving him that holy space, he displaced what supported the service of the temple.

For today: let us take care that what is dedicated to God is not displaced by comforts or relationships. Let us examine whether our priorities leave room for what sustains worship and for those who serve.
exp.4:16:
This verse says that Nehemiah received each day at his table one hundred and fifty Jews and leaders of the people. He also ate with people from the nations around them who came to visit. The rulers are the leaders or chiefs of the people, and the surrounding lands are the regions nearby.

Nehemiah, governor of Judah, speaks here after rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem. Before him, other governors had burdened the people with heavy taxes. Nehemiah, out of fear of God, did not do this. He paid for that generous hospitality from his own pocket, although he could have demanded the allowance due to him as governor, because the people were already heavily burdened.

For today: if you have some kind of authority or influence, use it to serve and not to gain advantage. Ask yourself how you can give, and not demand, especially from those who already carry a heavy load. Sincere generosity comes from respecting God.
exp.12:1:
It says that the Ammonites and Moabites were excluded from the congregation because they did not meet Israel with bread and water when Israel was on its way. Furthermore, they hired Balaam to curse the people. But God turned that curse into a blessing.

The one telling this is the narrator of the book, who is probably Nehemiah. He refers to what the people heard when the law of Moses was read (Deuteronomy 23:3-5). After returning from exile, the community sought to be faithful to God and to avoid influences that would draw them away from Him. Some scholars point out that this rule was applied with a sense of spiritual protection.

For today: God can transform what others do against us into something good. Trust Him when you feel attacked or rejected, and seek to be hospitable to others, as God expects of His people.
exp.6:3:
The verse describes how Jerusalem was after the wall had been rebuilt. The city was "espaciosa y grande," that is, it had a great deal of ground, but very few people were living in it. Furthermore, the houses had not yet been rebuilt. The rebuilding of the houses is the point of the phrase "vueltas a construir," which means they had not yet been built again.

It is Nehemiah who speaks, the one who led the rebuilding of the wall. He had already posted guards and officials to watch over the gates, but he realized that a protected city was not enough: it needed inhabitants. So in the following verse he says that God put it in his heart to gather the people and register them by families.

For today: finishing a visible work does not always mean that everything is complete. After reaching a goal, ask God to show you what comes next. Often what comes next is caring for people and building community, not only raising structures.
exp.11:25:
This verse closes the list of the priests and Levites, and says in what period they lived. It mentions Joiakim, the high priest, son of Jeshua and grandson of Jozadak. It also names Nehemiah, the governor (the civil leader), and Ezra, a priest and scribe, that is, an expert in God's Law who copied and taught it.

Nehemiah 12 is a historical record, and the narrator seems to be Nehemiah himself. Before the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, the names are recorded of those who served in worship, such as singers and gatekeepers. This shows that the service followed the order established since David. The names belong to different generations, and the verse places them all in that time.

For today: God notices faithful service, even the kind that goes unseen. Serve where God has placed you, with steadiness, without seeking applause. He remembers every name.
exp.12:11:
This verse says that all the people of Judah brought back the tithe, that is, the tenth part of their grain, their new wine and their oil. They brought it to the storerooms, which were the temple treasuries where what was needed to support the service of God was kept.

Nehemiah, the governor, is speaking during his second period in Jerusalem. On his return, he found that the Levites were not receiving their support and had gone off to work their fields. For this reason the temple had been neglected. Nehemiah rebuked the leaders, reorganized the service, and the people responded with obedience. Then he appointed trustworthy officers to distribute what had been received.

For today: if God has given us something, let us help generously and in an orderly way those who serve in our church. When we give faithfully, the service of God is sustained and those who carry it out are cared for.
exp.6:38:
This verse begins the list of the priests who returned from exile. It says that the descendants of Jedaiah, of the family of Jeshua, numbered 973 people. "Children of" means descendants, not necessarily direct sons. "House" refers to a family or lineage.

Nehemiah copies here a record of the families who came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel. He found it when he wanted to gather the people and organize Jerusalem, which had few inhabited houses. This list also appears in Ezra 2, with small differences that some explain by time or by the way the numbers were counted. The priests were important because they led worship in the temple.

For today: God remembers people, not only famous leaders. Every name and every number matters to Him. Serve faithfully where you are, even when no one applauds; your place among God's people is important.
exp.2:18:
He says that Ezer, son of Jeshua and ruler of the city of Mizpah, repaired another section of the wall of Jerusalem. That section stood facing the ascent that led up to the armoury, right at the corner.

Rebuilt is the sense here: he repaired or reconstructed it. Ruler here refers to a local governor or leader. Another piece is a second section assigned to him.

This chapter is a list of those who worked on the wall under Nehemiah's direction after the return from exile. It is not about one particular person; the narrator notes who rebuilt each part. The text says nothing more about this armoury, so it is best not to invent details.

For today: God values the work of each person, even when their name is not famous. Faithfully doing the task that falls to you, alongside others, is also a way of serving him.
exp.2:4:
The explanation says that the people of Tekoa, a town near Jerusalem, repaired the section of wall that followed the previous one. But their nobles did not put their necks to the work: they would not bend down or submit themselves to the labor of their Lord. Some understand "their Lord" to be God; others take it to mean their masters or supervisors. The text does not make this entirely clear.

It is part of the list of builders that Nehemiah writes about the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem after the exile. He records in detail who worked and where. It is notable that the people of Tekoa did repair a second section later (verse 27), but their leaders were left without credit.

For today: serving God sometimes means getting your hands dirty. No one is too important to help in the common work. Ask yourself where you can help with humility, without expecting recognition.
exp.2:30:
Malchiah, the son of a goldsmith, repaired a section of the wall of Jerusalem. His section reached as far as the house of the Nethinims (servants of the temple) and of the merchants, facing the Miphkad gate, and to the corner room. It is not known for certain exactly where each of these places was.

Nehemiah tells in the first person how the wall was rebuilt after the exile. He lists those who worked, each in their own section. Many repaired near their own homes or their places of work. This shows that the work was shared by people of many different kinds: priests, craftsmen, merchants, and servants of the temple.

For today: God uses small, well-defined tasks. Faithfully do the section that has been given to you, in your home, your work, or your church, without comparing yourself to others. Your part counts toward the whole work.
exp.1:4:
Nehemiah answers the king with great respect: if it pleases the king, and if he has found favor in the king's sight, he asks to be sent to Judah, to the city where his ancestors are buried, so that he can rebuild it.

Nehemiah speaks as the cupbearer of the Persian king Artaxerxes. He had just received news that Jerusalem still lay in ruins, with its gates burned. His sadness caught the king's attention, and the king asked him what he wanted. Before answering, Nehemiah prayed silently to God, and then he made his request clearly and humbly.

For today: when you carry a burden for something that needs fixing, pray first and then take a concrete step. Ask with respect, with a clear plan, trusting that God can open doors and move hearts.

sum.5: Nehemiah turns down the invitations, the false accusations, and the threats of his enemies, who wanted to frighten him into stopping the work. He prays to God for strength and holds firm. The wall is finished in fifty-two days, and even the enemies acknowledge that God was at work in this project.
sum.11: Nehemiah 12 lists the priests and Levites who returned with Zerubbabel, along with their descendants. It then describes the dedication of Jerusalem's wall. The people purified themselves, and two large choirs walked along the top of the wall to the house of God, singing, playing music, and offering sacrifices. Their joy could be heard from far away. After this, arrangements were made for the support of the priests, Levites, singers, and gatekeepers.
sum.2: In Nehemiah 3, priests, rulers, merchants, craftsmen, families, and people from various towns divide up the work and rebuild the wall and gates of Jerusalem, many of them working in front of their own homes. It teaches the value of working together, each person in their own part. Only some of the leaders from Tekoa refused to cooperate.
sum.4: When Nehemiah heard the cry of the poor, who were in debt and hungry, and some were even selling their own sons, he rebuked the wealthy for charging interest to their fellow Israelites. They promised to return the lands and the interest they had collected, and the people praised God. Nehemiah also set an example: out of reverence for God, he did not burden the people, and he was generous with them.
sum.7: All the people gathered together, and Ezra read the law of Moses from early morning until noon, while the Levites helped everyone understand it. When the people began to weep, Nehemiah told them that the day was holy and that the joy of the LORD was their strength. Then they discovered the Feast of Booths and celebrated it with great joy.
sum.9: In Nehemiah 10, the leaders, priests and Levites sign a covenant, and the rest of the people join them under oath to live according to the law of God given through Moses. They commit themselves not to marry their children to the peoples of the land, to observe the Sabbath and the seventh year, and to support the temple with offerings, wood, firstfruits and tithes. They conclude by saying, "We will not neglect the house of our God."
sum.3: While the Jews were rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem, Sanballat and Tobiah mocked them and then plotted to attack them. Nehemiah responded by praying and posting guards. He encouraged the people to trust in God, and everyone worked with one hand on the task and the other on the sword.
sum.10: The leaders of the people settled in Jerusalem, and the rest cast lots so that one out of every ten families would move to the holy city. The people blessed those who volunteered. The chapter lists who lived there, including Judahites, Benjaminites, priests, Levites, and gatekeepers, and the other cities where the rest of the people settled.
sum.8: The people of Israel gather together with fasting, confess their sins, and listen to the law. The Levites pray, recalling God's faithfulness from Abraham through the time in the wilderness, despite the people's repeated rebellion. They acknowledge that God is just and merciful, and in the end they make a written covenant to return to Him.
sum.6:
With the wall finished, Nehemiah appointed guards and put his brother Hanani and Hananiah, the commander of the citadel, in charge of Jerusalem. They were faithful men who feared God more than most. He gave orders that the gates were not to be opened until the sun was hot, and that they were to be shut and barred while the guards were still on duty, and he posted residents of Jerusalem at their watch posts, each in front of his own house.

The city was large but sparsely populated, and its houses had not yet been rebuilt. So Nehemiah gathered the nobles, the officials, and the common people to be registered by family. He found the genealogical record of those who had first returned from exile, and he read through the list of names. It included the families, the priests, and the Levites, and the record was kept carefully so that each person's place could be known.

Some of the heads of families gave gifts toward the work, and these contributions were recorded as well. Then the people settled back into their own towns, and all of Israel went to live in the cities that belonged to them.
sum.0: Nehemiah, who lived in Susa, learns from his brother Hanani that the Jews who returned to Jerusalem are suffering, and that the wall is broken down and its gates have been burned. He wept, fasted, and prayed to God, confessing the sins of the people and his own, recalling God's promises, and asking for favor before the king, whom he served as cupbearer.
sum.12: Nehemiah returns to Jerusalem and finds that the people have grown careless. The priest Eliashib had given Tobiah a room in the temple, the Levites were not being paid, trading was taking place on the Sabbath, and some people had married foreign wives. Nehemiah corrects all of these things firmly and restores proper order to worship, and he asks God to remember him for good.
sum.1: Nehemiah, the king's cupbearer, showed his sadness over Jerusalem, prayed to God, and the king sent him with letters and support to rebuild the city. Once in Jerusalem, he inspected the fallen walls at night and encouraged the people to build, trusting in the good hand of God, even though their enemies mocked them.
